s: Current team Slack mirror with full history. Libbitcoin Time 2026: the development history of the libbitcoin repositories. History Libbitcoin was announced on the Bitcoin forum in July 2011, two and a half years after the genesis block. The plan was to "rewrite bitcoin" as a library anyone could build on, pluggable and configurable at every level, under a lesser AGPL license drafted for the project. In 2013 the libbitcoin manifesto made the case for why it mattered: a Bitcoin of many implementations has no single point of failure, and no single party controls its standard. The same year brought obelisk, a query server, and sx, a command line toolkit, the ancestors of Bitcoin Server (bs) and Bitcoin Explorer (bx). From 2014 the code was divided into the six repositories it has today, from system primitives to the server, and versions 2 and 3 followed in 2014 and 2017. Version 4 is the first major release since 2017, the result of a decade of R&D by a small team of dedicated volunteers. History of the archived repositories (blockchain, protocol, client and consensus) is included only where it was carried into a current repository. bitcoind is Bitcoin Core at its master (October 2026) with its secp256k1, without its wallet application, its GUI, its other executables or its other embedded dependencies (leveldb, crc32c, minisketch, univalue, ctaes and libmultiprocess). Wallet functionality that bitcoind itself uses, such as addresses, keys, descriptors and PSBT, is included, as is libbitcoin's. Its contributors and commits are those that touch its code or its functional tests, and those of secp256k1 (to August 2026). Its secp256k1 lines exclude 18,235 lines of precomputed tables, and its functions and structs are those of the secp256k1 public headers. Its Python tests are the functional tests, excluding those of the wallet application, and its words are those of the bitcoincore.org website, meeting notes included. Lines are non-blank lines of C++ in the library (include and src) and in its tests (test). Library lines exclude 60,969 lines of data tables in system (word lists, Unicode tables and the embedded GPU kernels). The server's embedded web interface, which can be compiled out, is excluded, as is bitcoind's GUI. Runtime tests are C++ test cases, compile-time tests are static_assert statements in the tests, and Python tests are the server's endpoint tests (3,894 lines of Python, not in the test lines). Classes, methods and public functions are counted from the compiler's view of the public headers: class and struct definitions, their member functions by access, and free functions.

Libbitcoin is a full stack of C++20 Bitcoin software, from primitives to a personal full node and internet scale query server. Bitcoin Server (bs) is one node that speaks the protocols your software already uses: point Electrum wallets, lnd and btcwallet, bitcoind tooling or your own explorer at it. It includes an integrated block explorer and administrative dashboard. Download Bitcoin Server Bitcoin Explorer (bx) is its command line client: generate keys and addresses, construct and decode transactions, inspect scripts, and query a server. For developers, every layer beneath them, from Bitcoin primitives to the full node, is a C++ library for any application, and the running node is a server for client applications over all common Bitcoin interfaces and protocols. To report a vulnerability, see Vulnerability Reporting.
Query performance measurements of Bitcoin Server (bs) across machines and configurations, some with Bitcoin Core, Fulcrum, or Frigate comparisons.

Index efficiency: multiple of other product (log scale) Index efficiency is Libbitcoin's query rate relative to the other server, divided by the size of its index relative to the other's, both at block 950,000 (index sizes are on the footprint page). Each value is a multiple: 2.5× means Libbitcoin delivers 2.5 times the query rate per byte of index, and below 1× it delivers less. Address history rates are entries per second, silent payments rates are blocks scanned per second, and other rates are calls per second.

P2P/S block throughput (linear scale) P2P/S block/tx throughput (log scale) Bitcoind JSON-RPC block/tx throughput (log scale) Bitcoind REST block/tx throughput (log scale) Bitcoind REST hex block/tx throughput (log scale) Native REST block/tx throughput (log scale) The other charts measure one connection at a time. Throughput is what a server delivers under many: each connection count requests its own set of blocks or transactions back to back for 20 seconds, repeating the set if it runs out, from 16 client processes, with both servers configured to accept the full connection count. Each set is requested twice in succession and the second, warm pass is shown. Block series purge the cache and restart the server before every connection count; transaction series do so once per series. On the linear block chart, the dashed line marks the block rate that 10 Gbps of network can carry, so a block curve above the line means the network, not the server, would be the limit. Bitcoin Core serves only unconfirmed transactions over P2P, so P2P transactions are shown for Libbitcoin alone. Bitcoin Core serves P2P blocks from a single thread and levels off at about 1,100 blocks per second from two connections, with latency growing in proportion to the load; Libbitcoin serves them concurrently and reaches about 7,900 per second by 64 connections. Over encrypted (BIP324) P2P, Libbitcoin reaches about 4,500 blocks per second and Bitcoin Core about 630, while Libbitcoin transactions are about as fast as unencrypted, since BIP324 drops the per-message double SHA-256 checksum and Libbitcoin's ChaCha20 is hardware accelerated. Bitcoin Core does not serve HTTPS or websockets, so the HTTPS and websocket series (secure ones dashed), and the native chart, show Libbitcoin alone. HTTPS uses 256 listening ports, one per connection. TLS carries data in records of at most 16 KiB, so a 1.5 MB block is sent as about a hundred separately encrypted and authenticated records; that per-record work is inherent to HTTPS and secure websockets and weighs most on large responses. The HTTPS and secure websocket curves level off where the test client's TLS saturates its processes; Libbitcoin uses under six cores at those rates, and the rate rises with more client processes. Plain HTTP transactions level off near 185,000 per second.

Chain object rate (log scale) Address output rate (log scale) Libbitcoin only, in binary data format over HTTP. Addresses are grouped by history size as in the Electrum interface, and an address response is its outputs, so the rate is outputs returned per second of call time.

Chain object rate: comparative (log scale) Address history rate: comparative (log scale) The Electrum interface is compared with Fulcrum 2.1.3, which indexes from Bitcoin Core at default settings. Addresses are grouped by history size, and the largest class adds 27 addresses of 100k to 2.2M entries. The 0 entries class uses 300 script hashes that own no output, the query a wallet makes most often when it scans past its last used address, and is plotted in calls per second. Address history rates are entries returned per second of call time.

Silent payments scan rate, GPU: comparative (log scale) Silent payments scan rate, CPU: comparative (log scale) The Sparrow interface is compared with Frigate 1.6.1, which indexes silent payments from Bitcoin Core. A silent payments scan subscribes one scan key to a range of blocks ending at 950,000, and is timed from the subscription to the notification of completion. Each of three repetitions purges the standby list, scans cold with a new key, then scans warm with the same key. Rates are blocks of the range per second, and each range is labeled with its approximate span of time. GPU scans use each server's default GPU backend. CPU scans use Frigate's CPU backend, UltrafastSecp256k1 field arithmetic on BMI2/ADX, which has no SIMD path, and Libbitcoin's AVX-512 IFMA scan. A scan the server ended without completing, other than by timeout, is marked as a server failure. Libbitcoin's other CPU paths are shown warm, in order of rate above the Libbitcoin AVX-512 IFMA warm bar. AVX-512F builds the IFMA 52 bit multiply-add from 32 bit multiplies, and AVX-IFMA is measured as AVX-512 IFMA restricted to its 256 bit registers.

Chain object rate: comparative (log scale) Each server is a peer to a single client connection over loopback. A block is a witness block by getdata, headers and cfheaders are 2,000 per request, and cfilter is one block per request.
Chain object rate: comparative (log scale) The bitcoind JSON-RPC interface is compared with Bitcoin Core 32.0.
Chain object rate: comparative (log scale) The bitcoind REST interface is compared with Bitcoin Core 32.0.

Transaction notification dispatch rate: comparative (log scale) Block notification fan-out time: comparative (log scale) Chain object rate: comparative (log scale) Each server is at block 950,000 with an empty pool. Transaction dispatch is measured with 16 to 256 subscribers on one ZMTP endpoint (CurveZMQ dashed, Libbitcoin only), while one P2P peer offers the transactions of blocks 950,001 to 950,009 at 500 per second. For each notification, the span from its arrival at the first subscriber to its arrival at the last is taken, and the rate is the subscribers reached after the first per second of the median span. At 256 subscribers Libbitcoin delivers each notification to all of them in 1.5 to 1.7 ms (2.7 to 3.2 ms over CurveZMQ), Bitcoin Core in 8 to 10 ms. Block fan-out is measured with 256 to 6,144 rawblock subscribers on one ZMTP endpoint, while one P2P peer offers nine blocks 6 seconds apart. For each block, the time from its push to its arrival at the last subscriber is taken, less the same time measured with one subscriber (the server's download, validation and organization of the pushed block, which precede any broadcast), and the median over the nine blocks is plotted. At 256 subscribers Libbitcoin reaches the last of them 23 ms after its fan-out begins, Bitcoin Core 61 ms; at 6,144 subscribers, 754 ms and 1,514 ms. Libbitcoin sends to subscribers from 32 threads and Bitcoin Core from one; on Windows, Defender network inspection, Web Threat Defense and the Windows Firewall examine each TCP send under a shared kernel lock, so the parallel sends contend where the single sender does not, and Libbitcoin's delivery CPU per block is several times Bitcoin Core's at the larger counts. The chain object rate times each of the 28,142 transactions of blocks 950,001 to 950,009, offered in block order by one P2P peer (inventory, then the transaction when requested), from its send to the arrival of its rawtx notification on a ZMQ subscription. Rates are 1000 / mean latency over the 24,517 transactions both servers accepted. Libbitcoin accepted 1,421 more transactions, as Bitcoin Core's clustered mempool imposes a hardwired capacity limit for performance reasons. Both rejected 2,204 transactions that were not yet valid at block 950,000: 1,522 are time-locked to a later block, 55 have unsatisfied relative lock times (BIP68), and 627 spend outputs of those.

Servers run one at a time on shelly (Threadripper PRO 9985WX, 512 GB, Windows 11), each with a store at block 950,000, called over loopback from the same machine. Libbitcoin 4.0 serves from its own store (address index load factor 5). Bitcoin Core 32.0 has txindex, txospenderindex and the basic block filter index. Unless noted, each method is called 300 times, one call at a time on one connection, with requests drawn from random blocks across the chain. Each of three repetitions purges all caches and restarts the servers, then makes a cold pass and a warm pass on the same requests. Calls are timed to the last response byte, and rates are calls per second (1000 / mean ms). Bitcoin Core and Fulcrum hold all headers in memory, so their warm header bars are hatched.

How the libraries of Bitcoin Server (bs) fit together: the stack, the node, the store and the server. Bitcoin Server (bs) is a stack of C++ libraries, each built on those below it. This page outlines how the layers fit together. The node and the store are each described in depth, against their source, in Node Architecture and Database Architecture.

Layer Role libbitcoin-system Bitcoin primitives and consensus rules: blocks, transactions, script execution, hashing and cryptography. libbitcoin-database The store: append-only, memory-mapped tables and the queries over them. libbitcoin-network Connections, sessions and protocols: the Bitcoin P2P network, and the HTTP, websocket, JSON-RPC, TLS and ZMQ services. libbitcoin-node The full node: header and block sync, validation, confirmation and the transaction pool. libbitcoin-server The client interfaces of Bitcoin Server, and bs. The libraries are listed under Developers.

Synchronization is headers-first. Peer protocols prove and archive each peer's headers, and a chain of chasers carries them from there to confirmation: Blocks are downloaded from many peers at once and validated concurrently, while organization and confirmation follow in order. The chasers communicate only through an event bus, and share state only through the store. Further chasers maintain the transaction pool, fee estimates, store snapshots and disk space. Quiescing the pipeline allows store snapshot, remap and shutdown.

The store is strictly relational, without a query engine. Every relation is resolved by one of two physical operations chosen when the table is designed: navigation, following a link that is a row's position, or search, a hash lookup through a table's head. Table bodies are append-only and published by small heads, so every write becomes visible atomically, and a snapshot is a copy of the heads. All files are memory-mapped, and grow by remapping. A store that closes cleanly reopens as it was; one that does not is restored from its last snapshot.
Bitcoin Server adds client interfaces to the node, on the services of libbitcoin-network, serving from the node's store. The interfaces are listed in BS Interfaces.

The protocol evolves by addition: new consensus rules and new P2P protocol versions. None is hardwired. Each is implemented on its own and selected by configuration, so each is developed and tested in isolation, read and verified as one unit of code, and enabled or disabled on its own. The full stack runs with any individual rule or protocol version disabled. Old rules and versions are never dropped, in consensus or in P2P: a node validates the whole chain under the rules of each height, and serves a peer at any version it implements, within the configured bounds. There is no way to know which rules miners enforce or which versions peers run, so none can be assumed unused. It also lets the node be operated at any historical level, back to its minimums: the rules of the satoshi client v0.3.0 in consensus (before BIP16, forks were implemented on an ad hoc basis, without coordination), and version 31402 in P2P. Some rules and versions are not implemented, which is often a judgement call, such as the forks made by bitcoind without prior specification, listed in chain/enums/flags.hpp, and Erlay (BIP330) in P2P.

The consensus rules define which blocks are valid. A fork is a new rule. Rules only accumulate: a rule that disables part of an earlier one is itself a new rule, applied with the earlier rule, which remains. A fork (in fact the coin itself) is classified by the rules alone, by the validity of blocks without the rule and with it: Fork Without the rule and with it Example Soft A block valid without the rule is invalid with it BIP66 requires strict signature encoding Hard A block invalid without the rule is valid with it BIP90 imposes the rule of BIP34 above a fixed block A rule that makes any block valid that is invalid without it is a hard fork, whatever else it does. A rule that leaves the validity of every block as it is without it is not a fork. The classification is independent of how a fork is deployed, and of whether any chain is observed to split because of it. A split is an event: nodes enforcing different rules diverge only when a block is mined that is valid under one set and not the other. A hard fork that no block exercises splits nothing, and remains a hard fork: BIP90 has not split the chain, because no block in its history is valid under one and not the other. A soft fork can split the chain: in July 2015, after BIP66 activated, miners that did not validate extended a block invalid under it. Whether a split is likely or unlikely is an estimate of how miners and nodes will behave, not a property of the rule. A soft fork is not backward compatible. Nodes that do not adopt the rule accept blocks that are invalid under it, as the BIP66 split shows. The chain without the rule does not survive only because majority hash power enforces the rule, by not extending blocks that are invalid under it, and that enforcement is indistinguishable from censorship. Under a hard fork, nodes that do not adopt the rule reject blocks that the nodes that adopt it accept. Each flag in chain/enums/flags.hpp is labeled with its type, and with its purpose: feature, security, determinism, inflation, deflation or arbitrary.

Each fork is one flag (chain::flags), enabled by its own member of the configured forks ([forks]), and activated by its own deployment. The chain state computes the flags active at each height from the configured forks and the chain, and each rule is a predicate of the chain types applied only under its flag. Activation is configured as well: activation times, version thresholds, burial heights, checkpoints and BIP9 deployments are all settings of [bitcoin]. BIP54 (proposed) is implemented as five forks, one per rule, each switched and deployed independently. See Activation, and the [forks] and [bitcoin] settings.

Each P2P protocol is a class, and each protocol version that extends it is a class derived from that of the previous version, named by the version that introduced it. A derived class adds only what its version adds, and overrides only the handlers that it extends: protocol_ping_60001 derives from protocol_ping_106 and adds the nonce and pong of BIP31. The earlier class remains, for peers at the earlier version. Protocol Library Versions Version handshake network 106 → 70001 → 70002 → 70014 → 70016 Ping network 106 → 60001 Address in, address out, seed network 209 → 70016 Alert network 311 Reject network 70002 Header in, header out node 31800 → 70012 → 70014 Block in node 31800 Block out node 106 → 70001 → 70012 → 70014 Transaction in node 106 → 70001 → 70013 → 70016 Transaction out node 106 → 60002 → 70001 → 70013 → 70016 Client filters out node 70015 A session attaches to each channel the most derived class of each protocol that the negotiated version and the configuration allow. The version is bounded by protocol_maximum and protocol_minimum, and each optional feature has its own switch, such as enable_compact, enable_address_v2 and enable_witness_tx, so a channel can run any version with any of its features disabled. See [peer] and Sessions and protocols.

Every published bs and selector binary is built in a Guix container from a pinned, bootstrappable toolchain. Each release build is made twice, by two builders on separate runners, and the release continues only if the two are bit-identical. Anyone with a Linux machine and Guix can rebuild a release from its tags and compare the result with the published files.

double-build.yml, in libbitcoin-server, is run by hand or by Build to Release. Run by hand, it takes a branch or tag (ref) for all five repositories, by default the branch it runs on. Called by the release, it takes the release's tag for each. Job Does resolve Resolves each ref to one commit in each repository (git ls-remote, the tagged commit of an annotated tag), so that both builders build the same commits sdk Packages the macOS SDK from Xcode on macos-latest, and the MSVC headers and libraries and the Windows SDK on windows-latest, as deterministic tar archives, and records their versions and hashes toolchain Builds each Guix toolchain from the pinned Guix commit, on each runner architecture, and caches its store closure under a hash of the Guix definitions guix Two builders per build. Each restores the toolchain, checks out the five repositories, builds in the Guix container and hashes its output compare Tabulates the hashes of both builders for every build; if any differ or any is missing, writes a diffoscope report per file and fails The two builders of a Linux build run on different architectures: builder a on ubuntu-24.04 (x64) and builder b on ubuntu-24.04-arm (arm64), each cross-compiling for its target. The macOS and Windows builds run both builders on ubuntu-24.04.

The build definition is in .github/guix of libbitcoin-server: File Defines channels.scm The Guix commit that pins every package manifest.scm The packages in the container for each host toolchains.scm The Linux cross toolchains, GCC 14 and binutils 2.46 against glibc 2.31 patches/ Patches to GCC and glibc for reproducible output guix-build.sh Starts the container for one build build.sh Configures, builds and packages one build inside the container package-sdk.sh Packages the Apple or Windows SDK Host Compiler Linker Platform files x86_64-linux-gnu, aarch64-linux-gnu GCC 14 (Guix cross) binutils 2.46 glibc 2.31 x86_64-apple-darwin, arm64-apple-darwin clang 19 lld 19 Apple SDK from Xcode, macOS 13.3 minimum x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-pc-windows-msvc clang-cl 21 lld-link 21 MSVC headers and libraries, Windows SDK guix-build.sh runs guix time-machine at the pinned commit, then guix shell --container --pure --no-cwd, so that nothing from the host reaches the build except the sources (shared at /distsrc), the output directory and the SDK. Inside, build.sh: sets LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, TZ=UTC, HOME=/tmp and umask 0022, maps the source and every Guix store path out of the debug information (-ffile-prefix-map), and omits the compiler command line (-gno-record-gcc-switches), builds with builds/cmake/install-cmake.sh of the project, from the local sources, release and static, without tests and without an install RPATH, separates and packages the debug symbols, with fixed timestamps, and strips the binary, writes SHA256SUMS for the binary and its symbols. Windows builds link with -Brepro. The Windows SDK is spelled for a case-insensitive filesystem, so the compiler and linker read it through a case-insensitive overlay.

A release names the tag of each of the five repositories it was built from. Rebuilding it needs a Linux machine, x64 or arm64, that allows unprivileged user namespaces. First, install Guix 1.5.0 with its binary installer. Clone the five repositories side by side in one directory, each at its release tag: $ git clone --branch <system tag> https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-system src/libbitcoin-system $ git clone --branch <database tag> https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-database src/libbitcoin-database $ git clone --branch <network tag> https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-network src/libbitcoin-network $ git clone --branch <node tag> https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-node src/libbitcoin-node $ git clone --branch <server tag> https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server src/libbitcoin-server Set the variables of the build, from its entry in the guix matrix of .github/workflows/double-build.yml at the server tag, and run guix-build.sh with the source and output directories. For bs-linux-x64: $ HOST=x86_64-linux-gnu BASENAME=bs-linux-x64 \ FLAGS="-march=x86-64 -mtune=generic" \ LINKFLAGS="-static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc" \ bash src/libbitcoin-server/.github/guix/guix-build.sh src build A build with tags also sets OPTIONS from its entry, as OPTIONS="-Denable-avx2=ON -Denable-shani=ON" with FLAGS="-march=x86-64-v3 -mtune=generic" for bs-linux-x64-avx2-shani. A selector build also sets PROJECT=libbitcoin-system and PROGRAM=selector. The first run builds the toolchain from source, which can take hours; later runs reuse it from the Guix store. Then compare build/SHA256SUMS with the hashes of the published files: $ sha256sum bs-linux-x64 bs-linux-x64.debug The checkout directory and the build machine do not affect the output. The macOS and Windows builds also need the SDK the release was built with: set SDK to the directory unpacked from the archive that package-sdk.sh writes, and DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=13.3 for macOS. The archive is identical only from the same Xcode, or the same MSVC and Windows SDK versions. Each build's toolchain.txt, in the artifacts of the Double Build run, records those versions and the archive's hash.

Architecture of the libbitcoin build: the model, the generator, the generated build files, options, install scripts and CI. Every libbitcoin repository carries three build systems (autotools, CMake and Visual Studio), install scripts for each, CI workflows and editor settings. None of these files is written by hand. They are generated by libbitcoin-build from one XML model of the repositories, processed through a set of GSL templates, and committed to each repository. This page describes the model, the generator, and what the generated files do; instructions for building are in Building and Build options. Paths are relative to the root of libbitcoin-build at master c045b17 (2026-10-26), and of libbitcoin-system at master 2d560dc1 (2026-10-28) for generated files.

version4.xml is the one description of everything that is built. It has three parts: a repository element per libbitcoin repository, registrar elements holding definitions shared by all repositories, and a templates element that lists the templates and where their output goes.

A repository declares its version, languages and targets. A target is the library, its test executable, or a binary (a console application or examples). Each target names its source and header directories, its dependencies, its options and its compiler settings. Simplified, from libbitcoin-system: <repository name="libbitcoin-system"> <version major="4" minor="0" /> <library name="libbitcoin-system"> <sources path="src" recursive="true" /> <headers path="include" recursive="true" root="true" /> <option name="avx2" type="enable" default="no" msvc="/p:Option-avx2=true" /> <compiler standard="20"> <flag option="avx2" environmental="true" type="public"> <symbol value="-mavx" /> <symbol value="-mavx2" /> </flag> </compiler> </library> <test name="libbitcoin-system-test" option="tests" type="with" default="yes" /> </repository> The library dependencies form the chain that every install script and CI job follows. libbitcoin-server adds the bs binary and libbitcoin-explorer the bx binary; tests depend on their library. Other libraries can optionally be linked, each in place of the library's own implementation, which is the default: Library Can link Effect libbitcoin-system libsecp256k1, UltrafastSecp256k1 (compatibility layer) Replaces the internal secp256k1 compatibility header (src/crypto/secp256k1/interface.hpp)

The registrars hold what would otherwise be repeated in every repository. A repository refers to a dependency or an option by name, and the generator resolves it against the registrar. Registrar Contents dependency For each library and external dependency: its source (GitHub owner and tag, archive URL, NuGet package), its build methods (gnu, cmake, preset, msbuild, nuget), the options used when it is built as a dependency, and its CMake package and target (bitcoin::system) build-options The install script options (--build-config, --build-link, --prefix, --build-limit, --hardware-optimized and others), with variable names, types and help text presets The CMake presets (nix-gnu-debug-static and so on), composed from base, debug, release, static and shared settings actions The GitHub actions used by the workflows, pinned by commit hash A toolchain element defines the Visual Studio toolset (v145), the solution configurations (StaticDebug, StaticRelease, and hidden dynamic and LTCG variants) and the platforms (Win32, x64, ARM64).

The generator is the iMatix GSL code generator: a GSL template is a script that walks an XML tree and writes text. generate4.sh (or generate4.cmd) clears output/ and calls generate.sh version4.xml, which runs three stages: Stage Script Effect Generate process/generate_artifacts.sh.gsl Runs gsl once per template listed in version4.xml, writing every repository's files under output/version4/ Copy statics process/copy_statics.sh.gsl Adds the fixed files (property sheets from props/version4/, nuget.config, build_base.bat), substituting repository, dependency and target names in their paths Copy projects process/copy_projects.sh.gsl Copies each repository's output into the sibling repository clone; arguments restrict the copy to matching repositories The process scripts are themselves generated from the model, so the list of templates exists only in version4.xml.

Each template writes one kind of file into each repository. Templates are under templates/; [library] is the repository name, [suffix] the name without libbitcoin-, and [target] a library, test or executable project. Template Artifact gnu/configure.ac.gsl builds/gnu/configure.ac gnu/Makefile.am.gsl builds/gnu/Makefile.am gnu/pc.in.gsl builds/gnu/[library].pc.in shell/runner.sh.gsl builds/gnu/test_runner.sh shell/install-gnu.sh.gsl builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh cmake/CMakeLists.txt.gsl builds/cmake/CMakeLists.txt cmake/CMakePresets.json.gsl builds/cmake/CMakePresets.json cmake/config.cmake.in.gsl builds/cmake/[library]-config.cmake.in shell/install-cmake.sh.gsl builds/cmake/install-cmake.sh shell/install-presets.sh.gsl builds/cmake/install-presets.sh msbuild/sln.gsl builds/msvc/vs2026/[library].sln msbuild/vcxproj.gsl builds/msvc/vs2026/[target]/[target].vcxproj msbuild/vcxproj.filters.gsl builds/msvc/vs2026/[target]/[target].vcxproj.filters msbuild/packages.config.gsl builds/msvc/vs2026/[target]/packages.config msbuild/debug.natvis.gsl builds/msvc/debug.natvis shell/build-msvc.cmd.gsl builds/msvc/build-msvc.cmd yml/ci.yml.gsl .github/workflows/ci.yml yml/ci-expanded.yml.gsl .github/workflows/ci-expanded.yml yml/version-tag.yml.gsl .github/workflows/version-tag.yml vscode/code-workspace.gsl builds/vscode/[suffix].code-workspace vscode/settings.json.gsl .vscode/settings.json src/include.hpp.gsl include/bitcoin/[suffix].hpp src/version.hpp.in.gsl include/bitcoin/[suffix]/version.hpp.in src/version.cpp.in.gsl src/version.cpp.in git/gitignore.gsl .gitignore git/CODEOWNERS.gsl .github/CODEOWNERS The Visual Studio property sheets are maintained as files under props/version4/, not generated: shared sheets per platform and configuration (x64.props, ReleaseLIB.props, DebugSEXE.props), an import sheet per library, and a project sheet per target. The project sheet maps the target's options to preprocessor definitions. The import sheet of a library adds its include path, its .lib, and the path to its build output in the sibling repository, for any project that depends on it.

The model names source directories, not files. The autotools and Visual Studio templates read those directories in the sibling repository clones at generation time (lib/filesystem.gsl), and write every matching file into Makefile.am and the .vcxproj explicitly: .h, .hpp and .ipp headers, .c and .cpp sources, and for Visual Studio .rc resources. A file added to a repository is therefore not part of those builds until the generator runs again. CMakeLists.txt lists directories instead (file( GLOB_RECURSE ... CONFIGURE_DEPENDS )), and collects the files when CMake configures. The aggregate header include/bitcoin/[suffix].hpp is generated from the same discovery of the header directories.

An option in the model becomes a configure argument (--enable-avx2), a CMake option (enable-avx2), an install script argument passed to both, and, through its msvc attribute, a build-msvc.cmd argument mapped to an MSBuild property (/p:Option-avx2=true). Its define elements become preprocessor definitions and its flag elements compiler flags.

The intrinsics options of libbitcoin-system add compiler flags. Each flag in the model carries a short test program, which the generated configure.ac and CMakeLists.txt compile with the flags to verify that the compiler supports them. Option Implies GNU, Clang and clang-cl flags cl sse41 -msse4.1 WITH_SSE41 avx2 aesni -mavx -mavx2 /arch:AVX2 avx512 avx2, aesni -mavx512f -mavx512bw -mavx512vl /arch:AVX512 avx512ifma avx512, avx2, shani, aesni -mavx512ifma -mavx512vl WITH_AVX512IFMA avxifma avx2, shani, aesni -mavxifma /arch:AVX2, WITH_AVXIFMA shani aesni -msse4 -msha WITH_SHANI sha512 -mavx2 -msha512 /arch:AVX2, WITH_SHA512 aesni -msse4.1 -maes -mpclmul WITH_AESNI vaes -mavx2 -maes -mpclmul -mvaes -mvpclmulqdq /arch:AVX2, WITH_VAES sha2 aes +sha2 WITH_SHA2 sha3 sha2, aes +sha3 (with armv8.2-a) WITH_SHA3 aes +aes WITH_AES An option also turns on each option it implies, with that option's flags and definitions. The implications are emitted into each build system: as assignments after the options in CMakeLists.txt and configure.ac, and as conditional properties after the option defaults in the MSBuild .props files. The implied options are those that every processor with the extension is known to have, and the release builds are named for the options set, omitting those implied (Build selection). The flags are public. configure.ac substitutes them into the pkg-config Cflags, and CMakeLists.txt attaches them to the library target with PUBLIC visibility, so dependents compile with the same instruction sets. The definitions in the cl column are defined for both cl and clang-cl, and clang-cl also takes the same flags as Clang. For cl, which has no per-extension flags, the width options raise an Option-arch property (highest wins), which x64.props and Win32.props map to EnableEnhancedInstructionSet, defaulting to AdvancedVectorExtensions2. EnableEnhancedInstructionSet is not set for clang-cl, and in CMake /arch is passed only to cl. The ARM options combine into one flag, -march=armv8-a+<extensions> (armv8.2-a when sha3 is on), since ARM extensions are suffixes of a single -march or -mcpu value. The build fails if an ARM option is on and CFLAGS or CXXFLAGS already hold -march or -mcpu. Clang-cl on ARM64 takes the same flag. When an option is off, the build still compiles its test program without the flags, and reports an environmental override if it compiles (as when CFLAGS already enables the instruction set).

Option Scope Effect --with-valgrind libbitcoin-system defines WITH_VALGRIND (valgrind memcheck client requests) --with-cuda libbitcoin-system defines WITH_CUDA (default on) --with-secp256k1 libbitcoin-system defines WITH_SECP256K1, the native secp256k1 interface (default on); off, adds the external secp256k1 dependency --with-performance-tests, --with-slow-tests libbitcoin-system tests define WITH_PERFORMANCE_TESTS, WITH_SLOW_TESTS --with-verbose libbitcoin-network defines WITH_LOGV (public), compiling verbose logging --with-self-tests libbitcoin-server defines WITH_SELF_TESTS (public), compiling the built-in store tests --with-web bs defines WITH_WEB, compiling web pages into the console application --enable-ndebug, --enable-isystem autotools define NDEBUG (default on); use -isystem for dependency includes --with-tests, --with-examples, --with-console, --with-tools per target whether the target is built Every target also compiles as C++20 with the warning and hardening flags of its compiler element (-Wall, -Wextra, -fstack-protector-all and others). The install scripts set -Og -g1 or -O3 from --build-config, and with it --hardware-optimized adds -march=native -mtune=native. --build-valgrind=<filter> runs the libbitcoin-system tests matching the filter under valgrind after the normal test run.

An install script builds its repository together with everything below it in the dependency chain, in order. For libbitcoin-server, install-gnu.sh runs: build_gnu "libbitcoin-system" ... --without-tests --without-examples build_gnu "libbitcoin-database" ... --without-tests --without-tools build_gnu "libbitcoin-network" ... --without-tests build_gnu "libbitcoin-node" ... --without-tests build_gnu "libbitcoin-server" ... test_gnu "libbitcoin-server" ... Each libbitcoin dependency is cloned at the tag in the dependency registrar (or taken from --build-src-dir with --build-use-local-src), built with the registrar's dependency options, and installed to --prefix before the next starts. Only the target repository runs its tests. --build-limit stops after external dependencies or after libbitcoin dependencies, or builds the target alone. The libraries find each other through pkg-config (PKG_CHECK_MODULES) or through find_package and the exported CMake targets. install-cmake.sh and install-presets.sh follow the same sequence with CMake. build-msvc.cmd restores each solution's NuGet packages and builds the library projects of the chain in order, then the target's binaries and tests. The test project runs its tests as a post-build step in release configurations.

The ci element of each repository lists entries, each a runner image with a compiler, packages and options, and its jobs. A job names a build method (gnu, cmake, presets or msvc), a configuration and a link mode. For libbitcoin-system: Image Compiler Jobs windows-latest, windows-2025-vs2026 MSVC (vs2026, x64) StaticDebug, StaticRelease macos-latest Clang gnu and cmake, debug and release, static and dynamic ubuntu-24.04 Clang 18, 19; GCC 13, 14, 15, 16 gnu, cmake and presets ubuntu-24.04 GCC 13 one gnu job with lcov coverage ubuntu-24.04 GCC 14 and Clang 18 with valgrind gnu release static, intrinsics off, --with-valgrind --build-valgrind=secp256k1_ctime_tests ubuntu-24.04-arm GCC 14 and Clang 18 with valgrind gnu release static, AES and SHA-2 intrinsics, --with-valgrind --build-valgrind=secp256k1_ctime_tests Each job checks out the repository and runs its install script with --build-use-local-src and the job's --build-config and --build-link. The script builds the dependency chain, the repository and its tests, and prints the test logs. Two workflows are generated from the same entries. Jobs marked gate="true" in the model form ci.yml, which runs on push and pull request when source, test or build paths change. ci-expanded.yml holds every job and runs on manual dispatch. The coverage job sends lcov output to Coveralls, excluding the paths in the entry's coverage element. version-tag.yml creates a version tag on manual dispatch (Versioning).

ci.yml of libbitcoin-server, as run on GitHub Actions: Every job must pass for the run to pass. libbitcoin-build has its own CI, which clones all six repositories and runs generate4.sh on Ubuntu and macOS.

A build's version is <major>.<minor>.<patch>. The major and minor numbers (4.0) are set in the model. The patch number is the commit height of the repository's checkout, git rev-list --count HEAD, so each repository numbers its own builds and every commit raises the number. The version carries the full commit hash and a dirty flag, set when git status --porcelain reports any change. Built outside a git checkout, the hash is unknown, the patch number 0 and the flag clear. Each library has two configurable files, named by the configurable elements of its model: File Generated as Contents include/bitcoin/[suffix]/version.hpp.in version.hpp The LIBBITCOIN_[SUFFIX]_VERSION ("4.0"), _MAJOR_VERSION and _MINOR_VERSION macros, and the declaration of build_version() src/version.cpp.in version.cpp build_version(), which returns the semantic version, the commit hash and the dirty flag version.hpp is written when the build is configured, and holds only the major and minor numbers, so a new commit does not change it. version.cpp is written again by every build, from the state of the checkout at that build, and is replaced only when its content changes, so an unchanged state recompiles nothing: Build system version.cpp autotools A FORCE rule in Makefile.am substitutes the values with sed CMake A custom target reruns CMakeLists.txt in script mode, which calls configure_file Visual Studio The ConfigureFiles target of Git.props, before compilation, writes both files under build/ bs --version prints each library's version, its hash shortened to eight digits, and -dirty for a dirty build: libbitcoin-system.... 4.0.10444 8a3cb4da version-tag.yml, run by manual dispatch on a branch (master by default), computes the tag v<major>.<minor>.<patch> from the same commit count, adds an optional suffix, and pushes it as an annotated tag. It fails if the tag exists. maintenance/create-version-tag.sh in libbitcoin-build does the same locally, and pushes only when given a remote.

Two kinds of generated source are committed to the repositories, because they need tools that a build does not: the CUDA kernels of libbitcoin-system and the web sites of libbitcoin-server. Each is made by a Python script, run from the repository root: one compiles C++ to PTX, the other TypeScript to minified script and stylesheets, and each embeds the result in C++ sources that the build compiles like any other. Run the script again after changing the sources it reads, and commit what it writes.

tools/generate_cuda_ptx.py compiles src/crypto/secp256k1/cuda/kernels.cu to PTX, the portable assembly of NVIDIA GPUs, and writes src/crypto/secp256k1/cuda/ptx.cpp: python3 tools/generate_cuda_ptx.py The PTX is generated entirely from the constexpr scalar sources of libbitcoin-system. The kernels are compiled by clang for the device only, with no CUDA toolkit: -x cuda --cuda-device-only --cuda-gpu-arch=sm_75 -nocudainc -nocudalib -std=c++20 -O3, defining WITH_PTX and NDEBUG. They include the library headers and the generated version.hpp, so a build must have run first. On Windows the script uses the clang of Visual Studio (the C++ Clang Compiler component) under vcvars64.bat, and elsewhere clang++ on the path, or the compiler given by --clang. The PTX is raw deflated (level 9) and written as a byte array with its inflated size, compiled only when CUDA is enabled (HAVE_CUDA). At run time the library loads the CUDA driver (nvcuda.dll or libcuda.so.1), inflates the PTX and passes it to cuModuleLoadData, and the driver compiles it for the GPU. sm_75 is the oldest GPU architecture the PTX supports.

tools/generate_embedded_pages.py builds the admin site and the block explorer and writes them into console/embedded/, from which bs serves them unless folders.admin or folders.native names a directory (Configuration File): python3 tools/generate_embedded_pages.py Source Output web/admin-dashboard/dist/index.html, style.css, script.js admin_html.cpp, admin_css.cpp, admin_ecma.cpp web/blockexplorer/dist/index.html, style.css, script.js native_html.cpp, native_css.cpp, native_ecma.cpp web/shared/favicon.svg icon.cpp Each site is a TypeScript and React project built by Vite. The script installs its packages exactly as recorded in its package-lock.json (npm ci --ignore-scripts), which requires network access, then runs its build (tsc && vite build), which writes the three files to dist/. A Vite plugin (web/licenses.mjs) prepends to each script and stylesheet the notice of every third-party package it contains. The script uses npm on the path, or the one given by --npm, or on Windows the Node.js bundled with Visual Studio. The sites require Node.js 20.19 or later. Text files are embedded as raw string literals of 8,000 bytes each, and the favicon as a byte array. Every page is generated before any is written, so a failure leaves the committed pages unchanged. font.cpp in the same directory is not generated.
How release builds of Bitcoin Server (bs) are packaged for package managers, as a container image, and as apps for node platforms. Packages contain the signed builds of a release (Release builds).

Manager Platform Architectures Package Installs apt (deb) Linux x64, arm64 libbitcoin-server_<version>_<arch>.deb (amd64, arm64) The best variant the processor supports, linked as /usr/bin/bs Homebrew macOS x64, arm64 Formula libbitcoin-server.rb bs-macos-arm64-sha3 or bs-macos-x64-avx2, as bs winget Windows x64, arm64 Libbitcoin.Server, an Inno Setup installer (libbitcoin-server-<version>-windows-<arch>-setup.exe) The best variant the processor supports, as bs.exe, with its directory added to the system PATH unless that installer task is unchecked Docker Linux x64, arm64 Image ghcr.io/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server:<version> (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) Runs the best variant the processor supports (§5) Umbrel umbrelOS x64, arm64 App bitcoin-server (libbitcoin-server-<version>-umbrel.tar.gz), on the Docker image As Docker (§5.2) StartOS StartOS 0.4 x64, arm64 Package bitcoin-server (.s9pk), on the Docker image As Docker (§5.3)

The deb packages, the Windows installers and the Docker image each hold two variants of bs and the selector, which prints the tags of the processor (Build selection). The optimized variant is used if the selector prints each of its required tags, and the baseline variant otherwise, at install for a deb or an installer, and at each start for the image. The baseline variant is built for the architecture's floor and requires no tags, so it runs on every processor of its architecture. Platform Architecture Baseline Optimized Requires Linux, Docker x64 bs-linux-x64 bs-linux-x64-avx2-shani avx2, shani Linux, Docker arm64 bs-linux-arm64 bs-linux-arm64-sha2 sha2 Windows x64 bs-windows-x64.exe bs-windows-x64-avx2-shani.exe avx2, shani Windows arm64 bs-windows-arm64.exe bs-windows-arm64-sha2.exe sha2 The Homebrew formula holds one build per architecture, with no selector: bs-macos-arm64-sha3 and bs-macos-x64-avx2. Both builds require macOS 13.3, and every Mac that runs it has the tags of its build: every Apple silicon processor, and every Intel processor of a Mac supported by macOS 13 (2017 and later).

package-release.yml, in libbitcoin-server, is run by hand with a release tag. Each job that takes builds from the release downloads them with their signatures, and fails unless every signature verifies. Its jobs: Job Does version Takes the version from the tag (without its v) debian Builds a deb per architecture (dpkg-deb), and assembles the variants of each architecture for the image docker Builds the image for both architectures and pushes it to the GitHub container registry windows Builds an installer per architecture (Inno Setup) manifests Writes the Homebrew formula, the winget manifests and the Umbrel app startos Builds a StartOS package per architecture, with the image pinned by digest publish Attaches the packages, formula, manifests and apps to the release, with their SHA-256 checksums (packages-sha256.txt)

The container image is pushed to the GitHub container registry by the docker job. Every other package is published as an asset of the release, and reaches its distribution repository from there: Package Repository Submission deb A libbitcoin apt repository The deb is added, the index regenerated and its Release file signed with the repository key Homebrew formula A libbitcoin tap (libbitcoin/homebrew-tap) The formula is committed to the tap winget manifests microsoft/winget-pkgs A pull request with the manifests, validated and merged by Microsoft Docker image ghcr.io/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server Pushed by package-release; the package is public Umbrel app A libbitcoin community app store, or getumbrel/umbrel-apps The app is committed to the store, or submitted to Umbrel by pull request StartOS package A StartOS registry The package is submitted to the registry The formula, manifests and Umbrel app refer to the release's download URLs, so each is submitted once the release is published. Package Users install with deb apt install libbitcoin-server, once the repository and its key are added Homebrew formula brew install libbitcoin/tap/libbitcoin-server winget manifests winget install Libbitcoin.Server Docker image docker pull ghcr.io/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server:<version> Umbrel app The app store in umbrelOS StartOS package The registry in StartOS

The image runs bs as user and group 1000, with its data in the /data volume and its configuration in /data/bs.cfg. On first start, when /data/bs.cfg does not exist, the image copies its default configuration there: [folders] root = bitcoin console = log events = log [admin] bind = 0.0.0.0:8080 connections = 10 [native] bind = 0.0.0.0:8180 connections = 10 Port Service 8333 P2P 8080 Admin (management console) 8180 Native (block explorer, REST and WebSocket) docker stop sends SIGTERM, which starts closing the store. A syncing node can take longer to close than the 10-second default timeout, after which Docker kills the node, so run the container with --stop-timeout 600.

The app runs the image, pinned by digest, with its data under the app's data/bs directory. Port Service 8186 Admin, through Umbrel's app proxy (the app's Open button, behind the Umbrel login) 8187 Native (block explorer) 8334 P2P (inbound.bind), since Umbrel's Bitcoin Node app holds 8333 Backups exclude bitcoin/, which holds the network directory with the store, logs and peer address cache. The stop grace period is 5 minutes 30 seconds, for the store to close.

The package runs the image, pinned by digest, on x86_64 and aarch64. Interface Port Service Web UI 8080 Admin (management console) Block Explorer 8180 Native (block explorer) Peer 8333 P2P StartOS serves the web interfaces over HTTPS, with its own certificate authority. Its health check is that the admin port is listening. The stop timeout is 5 minutes, and backups exclude bitcoin/. The package requires 15 GiB of RAM as StartOS reports it, which admits a 16 GB machine (StartOS compares against the total the kernel reports, about 2.3% under the installed RAM). StartOS does not offer the package on a smaller machine.
The published builds of bs are made by two GitHub Actions workflows, both run by hand: one tags each repository with a version, and one builds, signs and publishes the server from those tags.

Each of libbitcoin-system, -database, -network, -node and -server has a version-tag.yml workflow. Its inputs are a branch (master by default), a tag description and a tag suffix. It computes the version from the branch: Part Source Major LIBBITCOIN_VERSION_MAJOR in builds/cmake/CMakeLists.txt Minor LIBBITCOIN_VERSION_MINOR in builds/cmake/CMakeLists.txt Patch The number of commits on the branch (git rev-list --count HEAD) The tag is v<major>.<minor>.<patch> followed by the suffix, and is created as an annotated tag and pushed. The workflow fails if the tag already exists.
manual-release.yml, in libbitcoin-server, takes a tag for each of the five repositories, and an optional suffix for the release title. Its four jobs run in order.
Checks out each repository at its tag, and fails unless each tag exists as a tag (not a branch or commit).

Runs the Double Build with the five tags. Each build is made twice in a pinned Guix container, cross-compiled on Linux runners, and the job fails unless both builders produce bit-identical files (Deterministic builds): Build Host Compiler named for the hardware extensions it requires, and runs on every processor that has them (Build selection). The same job also builds the selector of libbitcoin-system, which reports the build for the processor, for the packages that choose a variant at install (Packaging). It is built for each of the six hosts with no instruction set options: selector-linux-x64, selector-linux-arm64, selector-macos-x64, selector-macos-arm64, selector-windows-x64 and selector-windows-arm64. Linux builds link the C++ and GCC runtimes statically (-static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc) and require glibc 2.31 or later. Windows builds end in .exe. After the build, each builder: separates the debug symbols from the binary and strips it, runs --version and --hardware where the runner can execute the build, and shows the linkage (file, and readelf for Linux), records the runner image, the Guix commit and any SDK versions in toolchain.txt, and hashes its files, uploads its files for the comparison. Builder a also uploads the build and its symbols for signing, kept for one day. Every build is compiled with debug information, and its symbols are published beside it: Platform Symbols Linked to the binary by Linux <build>.debug (compressed) GNU build ID and .gnu_debuglink macOS <build>.dSYM.zip UUID Windows <build>.pdb.zip PDB signature

Runs in the release environment, which holds the signing key and its passphrase as secrets, and does not start until a maintainer approves it. It downloads every build, imports the key into a temporary keyring, and writes a detached, armored signature beside each build and symbols file (<file>.asc). It then deletes the key and the keyring, imports the public key, and fails unless every signature verifies as a good signature. The builds, symbols and signatures are uploaded as one artifact.

Also in the release environment, and also waits for approval. It creates a release at the server tag (with the suffix, if any), as a draft prerelease, with the builds, their symbols and the signatures as its assets. Existing assets are not overwritten. The release notes link the tag of each of the five repositories it was built from, and show the public key that signed it. The draft is public once a maintainer publishes it.

How the release builds of Bitcoin Server (bs) are divided by hardware extension, how each build is named, and how the selector finds the build for a machine. The builds are made by the release workflow (Release builds) and installed by the packages (Packaging).

Each architecture has a floor, the lowest target any build is compiled for. A build that uses a hardware extension is compiled for the lowest architecture level that every processor with that extension is known to reach, so its target can be above the floor. Source-anchored architecture documentation for libbitcoin-database: heads, bodies, maps, tables, the memory-mapped store and queries. This is a top-down, source-anchored description of libbitcoin-database, the store beneath libbitcoin-node. It covers the storage primitives (heads, bodies and maps), the tables built from them, the memory-mapped storage and its recovery model, and the query layer that the node uses. The relational concepts (natural, foreign and search keys, navigation versus search, append-only bodies published by heads, recoverability, and reliability) are from the 2021 design document for the version 4 store. Every behavioural claim is anchored with file:line references into the C++ source. The citations were verified against libbitcoin-database master at commit d29fa3df (2026-10-20). Paths are relative to include/bitcoin/database/ unless they begin with src/.

# File Topic 00 00-overview Layers, the relational model, navigation versus search, file layout 01 01-reliability Fail-stop and recoverable: assumptions, the clean-close guarantee, recovery, and why repair is impossible 02 02-primitives Links, keys, heads, bodies and maps, with figures of each head type 03 03-tables Every store table: map type, link, row, fields, and relations 04 04-storage Memory maps, growth and remap, disk full, snapshot and restore, locking 05 05-queries Query families, archival commit order, block state, confirmation, pool
00 → 01 → 02 → 03, then 05 §2–§3 for how a block is written and confirmed. Read 04 when working on store lifecycle or performance.

01 states the reliability model. 02 §5 and 04 §5 give the publication model: every write becomes visible through a single atomic cell or size store, and recovery is a head snapshot over append-only bodies. 05 §2 is the archival commit order that the node's organizeN/validateN/confirmN faults rely on. The numbered invariants are listed below.
The node architecture treats the store as an oracle. 05 is the interface it calls, and 04 §4–§6 are the suspend, disk-full and snapshot behaviours that chaser_storage and chaser_snapshot drive.
Every non-trivial claim has a path:N citation. Re-grep from the repo root after source changes and update the commit above.

These pages follow the type declarations in tables/. Consensus rules (script, BIP30/34/68 checks) live in libbitcoin-system. 05-queries describes the store reads behind them, not the rules.

Typed reads and writes over links. store store.hpp, impl/store/ Owns every storage and table, the envelope, and the transactor lock. Lifecycle and recovery. tables tables/ One schema per table: link width, key, row and the element serializers. primitives primitives/, impl/primitives/ The head, body and map templates. memory memory/, impl/memory/, src/memory/ Memory-mapped files, growth, flush, and the remap lock.
2. A relational store without a query engine

The store is strictly relational, but every relation is resolved by one of two physical operations chosen when the table is designed: Navigation. A row holds the link of a row in another table. A link is that row's position (record ordinal or byte offset), so following it is a multiply and an add: no hash, no search, no lock beyond the remap lock. Links are the store's foreign keys (FK). Tables do not store their own primary keys; a row's PK is its position. Search. A hash head maps a key to the newest row with that key, and rows in a bucket chain to older rows. Search is how a natural key (NK) from outside the store becomes a link. The 2021 design names the key kinds used throughout: Key Meaning Implementation PK Row identity The row's link (position). Never stored in its own row. FK Reference to another table's PK A link field, e.g. tx.outs_fk, ins.sequence.input_fk. NK Unique property derived from the row Block hash (header), txid (tx). SK Indexed search value The hash-head key: block hash, txid, point, output script hash, wtxid. NP Natural point: txid + index The ins key, the prevout an input spends. FP Foreign point: tx FK + index Proposed in 2021; not used. ins is keyed by NP. Invariant (Table-1). The only public entries to the archive are the two natural keys exposed by the chain: block hash and txid. Every other archive object is reached from one of them by navigation, or by a height index once confirmed. Optional entries are output script hash (address index) and wtxid (pool).

Two associations cannot be written when their parent is written, because the store is append-only and blocks and transactions arrive out of order: Header → transactions. Headers are archived first (headers-first sync), and a block's transactions arrive later. The association is a single txs row written once the header and all its transactions are archived. In 2021 this was a search; it is now an array map indexed directly by the header link, so it is navigation (tables/archives/txs.hpp:36-46). Output → spending input. An output can be archived before or after any input that spends it. The ins hash map is keyed by the spent point (NP), so spenders of an output are found by search on that point (tables/archives/ins.hpp).

Bodies are append-only. A row is allocated, written, and only then made reachable: by a head push (search), an array or headmap cell (index), or a foreign key written into a row that is itself published later. A reader therefore never reaches a partly written row, without any read lock on the row (02 §4.1, 05 §2). This one property gives both concurrency (readers and the single writer of each row do not coordinate) and recovery: a consistent state is a copy of the heads, since every body row beyond what the heads publish is unreachable (04 §6).

Category Tables Character archive header, input, output, ins, outs, tx, txs The blockchain itself. Append-only, never pruned. index candidate, confirmed, strong, state, duplicate, wtxid, scan, scan_prefix Mutable state over the archive: chains, confirmation, validation. cache prevout, pool, spends, ecdsa, schnorr, silent, prevalid, presilent, envelope Derived or transient data; prunable, truncated per batch, or rewritten in place. optional filter_bk, filter_tx; address search in outs Enabled by configuration at creation. Details per table are in 03-tables.

Each table has a head file and, unless it is a headmap, one body file per record (store.hpp:346-359, tables/names.hpp). <path>/ ├── flush.lock present while open; left behind by a faulted close ├── process.lock exclusive OS file lock ├── heads/ the live heads │ ├── archive_header.head │ ├── index_candidate.head headmap: the whole table │ └── ... ├── primary/ newest snapshot of heads/ ├── secondary/ previous snapshot (transient during rotation) ├── temporary/ snapshot being written ├── archive_header.data ├── archive_ins_point.data multi-record bodies: <name>_<record>.data ├── archive_ins_sequence.data └── ... Heads are a few percent of the store. Bodies are the bulk and are never copied (04 §6).

Node architecture — the chasers that drive these queries

Companion to 00-overview and 03-tables. Every table in the store is an instance of a small set of templates in include/bitcoin/database/primitives/. A table is a head and a body, each backed by its own storage (file). The head is the small, fixed or slowly growing part that indexes the body; the body holds the elements and is append-only. A map template pairs one head type with one body type and exposes the query interface. Citations are to libbitcoin-database master at d29fa3df, relative to include/bitcoin/database/. Template Head Body Lookup Store tables hashmap hashhead record or slab search by key header, tx, duplicate, wtxid hashmaps hashhead keyed record + records search by key, then link ins, outs, pool arraymap arrayhead record or slab index by dense integer txs, prevout, filter_bk, filter_tx arraymaps arrayhead records index, then link scan nomap nohead record or slab link only input, output, spends, scan_prefix, batch banks nomaps nohead records link only ecdsa, schnorr, silent banks headmap (is the head) none index into the head candidate, confirmed, strong, state, envelope

A link is an unsigned integer of Size bytes, of which the low Bits are significant (primitives/linkage.hpp:32-66). The all-ones value of Bits is terminal, which is both the null link and the mask used to read a link out of wider bytes. Serialization is non-endian. A link is a record ordinal in a record body (position = link × row size) and a byte offset in a slab body. Because a slab consumes the link domain by bytes, slab links are wider: input, output, txs, prevout and filter_tx all use 5-byte links, while most record tables use 3 or 4 bytes. Several links are deliberately narrower than their bytes so that a flag can be merged into the spare bit wherever the link is stored (tables/schema.hpp:105, :135, :181): Link Bytes / bits Freed bit carries header 3 / 23 the strong index's "positive" flag (strong.hpp) tx 4 / 31 the coinbase flag in prevout and spends records output 5 / 39 the outs "excluded" flag (op_return or oversize) Invariant (Link-1). terminal is never a valid element link. Every walk, iterator and head lookup stops on terminal, and a terminal bucket is an empty bucket.

A key is a fixed-width byte array (a hash), a chain::point (hash and index), or a keys::search<Width> that stores only Width bytes and verifies a match against the element itself (primitives/keys.hpp:30-53). A zero-width search key stores no key bytes at all: the outs (address) and wtxid tables find candidates by bucket and confirm them against the output script or the pool's witness hash. Bucket selection takes the low eight bytes of the key modulo the bucket count, which is uniform because the keys are already hashes. A point mixes its index into the hash with FNV-1a, and a null-index (coinbase) point is always bucket zero (impl/primitives/keys.ipp, bucket, hash). The bucket filter draws its entropy (thumb) from the key bytes that follow the bucket bytes, so the two do not overlap.

The head file is [body count][cell 0 .. cell buckets-1], every slot one cell wide (primitives/hashhead.hpp:171-179). The bucket count is fixed at creation and recorded in the store envelope, so a store keeps its geometry across configuration changes. A new head is filled with ones (all buckets terminal). A cell holds the link of the bucket's newest element in its low Link::bits. When CellSize is wider than the link, the remaining high bits are a bucket filter: a small bloom filter over the keys pushed into the bucket (hashhead.hpp:43-48). Push computes the new cell (new link, filter OR the key's k bits) and installs it with a compare-exchange loop, so the filter can never lag the conflict stack. The element's next is written from the observed top and fenced before the exchange publishes it (impl/primitives/hashhead.ipp, set_cell, next_cell). A word-aligned cell is a lock-free atomic; an unaligned cell is guarded by a mutex. Search first tests the key's k bits against the cell. If any is clear the key is not in the bucket and no body memory is touched (screened). k is derived from the expected element count and bucket count (optimal_k), and the envelope's stored value overrides it at open, so a store keeps the k it was built with. Only three tables have spare cell bits, and so a working filter: Invariant (Head-Hash-1). A cell's filter is a superset of the keys reachable from its link. A clear filter bit is therefore a proof of absence, and a set bit only a possibility.

The same [body count][bucket ...] layout, but the bucket index is the key itself, a dense integer such as a header link (primitives/arrayhead.hpp:29-111). There is no hash and no conflict list. The head expands as keys grow, through the storage's growth path. Each bucket is read and written atomically: as an atomic word when the bucket is integral-sized, otherwise under a head mutex held only for the copy (impl/primitives/arrayhead.ipp:142-210). Align pads each bucket to a full word; every store table uses align = false.
A single cell holding the body count, and nothing else (primitives/nohead.hpp:29-82). The body is reachable only by links that other tables hold.

A head-only table: the head file is an array of cells with no count cell and no body (primitives/headmap.hpp:30-195). The logical file size is the count, so publishing the size publishes the newest cell. A value is either a link (masked to terminal) or an opaque integer no wider than the cell. A cell size of max_size_t makes the head a byte-addressed slab (used only by the envelope). Because a headmap has no body, its whole content is in the head, and it is restored with the heads at snapshot (impl/primitives/headmap.ipp:51-62).

bodys<Link, Key, Sizes...> wraps a storage and converts between links and positions (primitives/body.hpp:29-120). Each row is a set of records, one per size and one file per record, all addressed by the same link. A body of one record, body<Link, Key, Size>, is the special case bodys of one size, and is what most tables use. Records: position = link × record size, in each record's own file (memory/mmaps.hpp). Allocation is unified across the record files under one lock. Slab (one record of Size == max_size_t): position = link. Elements carry no length prefix; each element's own serialization (typically a varint count) determines its extent, so an empty element is not storable. Allocation reserves space and advances the logical size before the element is written; the element becomes reachable only when something publishes its link (a head push, or a foreign key written in another table). Invariant (Body-1). Bodies are append-only. The only exceptions are wholesale: batch banks are truncated to zero per batch, and prune reclaims the prevout, pool, spends, wtxid and batch bodies (impl/store/store_prune.ipp).

A hash head over a body whose elements are [next][key][value] (primitives/hashmap.hpp:38-275). Elements in a bucket form a stack through next, newest first. Two-phase commit. allocate and set write a complete element with its next unset, and commit pushes it onto the bucket. Until the commit the element is unreachable by search, so a reader can never see a partly written element (set, commit, put = all three). Search. first / find screen the cell, then walk the stack comparing stored keys (impl/primitives/hashmap.ipp:519-538). Duplicates. Keys are not unique. it(key) returns an iterator that walks the whole conflict stack, skipping keys that do not match (primitives/iterator.hpp). This is the multimap of the 2021 design. Get by link. get(link) bypasses the head entirely, so a hashmap is a key-link bimap: search by key yields the link, and the link is a foreign key that other tables store. Slab hashmaps (variable elements, byte-offset links) are supported by the template; the store uses record hashmaps throughout and keeps variable data in no maps and array maps. Invariant (Map-Hash-1). An element is searchable if and only if its commit completed, and once searchable it remains so (heads are never popped, only cleared wholesale by prune or restore). Caution. An iterator holds the body's shared remap lock until it is released. Writing to the same table while holding one will deadlock against the remap that the write's growth requires (primitives/iterator.hpp:29-41, impl/query/query.ipp:50-58). Reads through the iterator use its own accessor (get(iterator, ...)).

An array head over a body: at(key) reads the bucket and get reads the element (primitives/arraymap.hpp:36-125). put(key, element) appends the element and stores its link into the bucket, expanding the head as needed. Buckets are mutable, so a key can be repointed while the old element stays in the body unreachable. In the store every array map is keyed by header link: txs (block to its transactions), prevout (block to its spent-output cache), filter_bk and filter_tx (block to its BIP157 header and BIP158 filter). These replace the search that the 2021 design needed for Header→Txs: the header link is already known, so the association is a direct index.

A no head over a body, addressed only by link (primitives/nomap.hpp:29-148). Inputs and outputs are slab no maps: a transaction's inputs and outputs are found through foreign keys held by ins and outs, never by search.

The three maps are general over record(s); hashmap, arraymap and nomap are the case of record(1) (primitives/hashmaps.hpp:28-317, arraymaps.hpp, nomaps.hpp). In a hashmaps, record zero is keyed and searched; the other records are read by the same row link. A query that needs one record reads only that record's file, which keeps hot data dense in memory. Table Form Records (width) ins hashmaps point, keyed (39), sequence (13) outs hashmaps address, keyed (4, or 0 when address indexing is off), puts (5) pool hashmaps context, keyed (38), id0..id3 (8 each) scan arraymaps identity (4), point (33), outputs (7) ecdsa nomaps identity (6), message (32), key (33), signature (64) schnorr nomaps identity (3), message (32), key (32), signature (64) silent nomaps identity (4), sum (33), hash (32), outputs (7)

Each map is a pair (head, body) of byte arrays plus a logical size. All publication is either a single atomic cell store (head) or a size store (headmap, body count), so the reachable state is always a prefix-closed subset of the written state. The hash head is a set of per-bucket stacks with a monotone filter per stack. Search is filter ⊇ keys(stack) then a linear walk. The array head and headmap are total functions from a dense domain to links, mutable pointwise; the bodies they reference are append-only.

Companion to 03-tables and 04-storage. query<store> (query.hpp, impl/query/) is the whole interface the node uses. Apart from the two chain reorganization mutexes, its state is the store.

Family Source Purpose store query.ipp Transactor, fault and disk-full state, snapshot, reload, prune, pooling latch extent, sizes extent.ipp, sizes.ipp Head and body sizes, bucket counts, record counts, enabled options initialize initialize.ipp Genesis navigate navigate/*.ipp Key to link: to_header, to_tx, to_txs, to_state, parents, children, spenders, to_block archive archive/*.ipp Read and write headers, txs and blocks, as objects or wire bytes properties properties_*.ipp, fee_rate.ipp, merkle.ipp Sizes, heights, values, fee rates, merkle over the confirmed index consensus consensus/*.ipp Block state, chain state, work, prevouts, strong, block_confirmable height height.ipp, locator.ipp, sequences.ipp Candidate and confirmed push and pop, locators, ancestry, mtp confirmed confirmed.ipp Non-consensus confirmation and spent tests pool pool.ipp Pooled tx records, confirmability, ancestors and descendants batch batch/*.ipp Signature and silent-payment batch banks address address/*.ipp Script-hash history, unspent, balance filters filters.ipp BIP157/158 unspent unspent.ipp, amounts.ipp Unspent output totals and set commitments Writes return a code. A write fails on a full or faulted storage, and the node maps each failure to a fault of its own (node 00 §9).

set_code(tx_link, tx, bypass, prune) is the only query that writes several tables for one object (impl/query/archive/chain_writer.ipp:128-271). The tx row is allocated first, so its link is known to every component, but it is published last. Invariant (Archive-1). A transaction is findable by txid only after its inputs, outputs, ins, outs and its own row are written and its points are searchable. Finding a tx therefore implies its spends are navigable, and finding a spender implies its tx row is complete (chain_writer.ipp:188-201, :214-219). The point push precedes the tx commit because a spender found by point search navigates to its tx through ins.sequence.tx_fk; that row must be complete by then, though it need not yet be searchable. When the pool is enabled, a tx already archived and pooled with a matching witness is reused rather than archived again (chain_writer.ipp:94-125).

set_code(header_link, header, ctx, ...) puts the header row (allocate, write and push in one call), then merges its initial flags into state: milestoned, checkpointed, and scanned or filtered when those features are off (chain_writer.ipp:301-354).

A block is associated once its header and every tx are archived (chain_writer.ipp:424-547): Each tx not already archived is written as in §2.1, each under its own transactor. Under one transactor, set_txs: if the block is already known strong, write strong for each tx; put the txs row at the header link; merge associated into state. Invariant (Archive-2). associated implies a complete txs row, and a txs row implies every tx it lists is archived and searchable. The txs element is written before its array cell is set (impl/primitives/arraymap.ipp:189-213).

state holds one flag byte per header (types/block_state.hpp:28-62). Flag Set by associated block association (§2.3) valid validation succeeded confirmable block_confirmable succeeded unconfirmable validation or confirmation failed (if mark_unconfirmable is configured) milestoned header archival under a milestone (bypass) checkpointed header archival under a checkpoint (bypass) scanned silent-payment scan complete, or silent disabled filtered BIP158 filter written, or filters disabled Predicates: is_validated = (valid or confirmable) and not unconfirmable; is_confirmable = confirmable and not unconfirmable; is_bypass = milestoned or checkpointed. set_block_unknown clears the three validation flags. All updates are atomic read-modify-writes of the cell (impl/primitives/headmap.ipp:364-402, impl/query/consensus/consensus_states.ipp).

candidate and confirmed map height to header link. A push reserves space outside the transactor, then writes the cell into unpublished capacity and publishes it by advancing the size; a pop truncates (impl/query/height.ipp, impl/primitives/headmap.ipp:281-322). Query Effect push_candidate(link) Append to candidate; re-evaluate currency pop_candidate() Mark the store dirty; truncate candidate by one push_confirmed(link, strong) Optionally set strong for the block's txs; append to confirmed pop_confirmed() Clear strong for the block's txs; truncate confirmed by one strong records, per tx, the block that makes it strong. A tx is strong when its cell holds a positive association. Confirmation of a spend is then find_strong(parent): the parent's own cell, or the cell of any duplicate of its txid (impl/query/consensus/consensus_strong.ipp:83-121). Invariant (Confirm-1). A tx is strong only if a block containing it is strong: a candidate being confirmed, or confirmed. strong is set for a block's txs before the block is pushed to confirmed and cleared before it is popped (impl/query/height.ipp:80-133). Invariant (Confirm-2). Each chain has a single writer, serialized by its reorganization mutex (height.ipp:54-133), and readers see a height only after its cell is written.

block_confirmable(link) checks every spend of a validated block against the strong index (impl/query/consensus/consensus_block.ipp:33-104): The prevout row was written during validation (set_prevouts, consensus_prevouts.ipp:78-118). It holds each spend's parent tx link, coinbase bit and sequence, so confirmation searches nothing per input, and it holds the txs that spend any of the block's points that appear in duplicate (get_doubles, :191-229). A block with no double-spent points has no conflicts, and that is decided by the duplicate filter.

The pool is an index over archived transactions, not a separate store. set_pooling() is a one-way latch recorded in the envelope with the tx and scan counts at the moment of latching; it marks the store dirty (impl/store/store.ipp:263-279). set_pooled(link, tx, ctx, time) writes, under one transactor, the spends rows for the tx's prevouts, the wtxid row and the four id records, and last the pool record, keyed by tx link, which publishes it (impl/query/pool.ipp:460-536). is_pooled(link) is a search of pool by tx link. Prune keeps only pool records that can still confirm, compacting them through a separate directory (impl/store/store_prune.ipp:125-338).

Signature and silent-payment verification are batched through the two-bank cache tables. One bank fills while the other is verified; a drained bank is truncated to zero. prevalid and presilent list the headers whose rows are in the bank (impl/query/batch/*.ipp). The node side of this protocol is in node 04 §5.
