Companion to 00-overview and 04-storage. The store is fail-stop and recoverable. Under the assumptions every system must make, it either holds exactly what was written or it is condemned and returned to a known-good state. It never opens a store whose contents it cannot vouch for, and it never repairs one. Citations are to libbitcoin-database master at 10e63cfe, relative to include/bitcoin/database/, and to libbitcoin-server where marked.

The common phrase "a reliable store" bundles properties that have to be kept apart. Term Meaning Reliability A rate: how often a component fails. Fail-stop A shape: when a component fails, it stops detectably. It never returns wrong data as good. Fail-partial The alternative: a failed component may keep running and return wrong or stale data as good. Crash consistency After a hard shutdown, the store is always in a state its contract allows. Recoverable A stop is not terminal: the store can be returned to a known-good state. A component that halts every week is fail-stop and unreliable. One that runs for years and then silently serves stale data is reliable and fail-partial, and it is the second that destroys data, because every layer above it was built on failures being announced.

Two assumptions underlie every claim on this page. Neither is particular to libbitcoin. No software can do without them. Fail-stop hardware. Software runs on its hardware, so it cannot certify that hardware. Any check it makes, a checksum, a comparison, a re-validation, executes on the same processor and memory and reads the same storage it would be checking. Hardware fail-stop is therefore assumed, not constructed. Drives, controllers and ECC memory approximate it well, because their detection sits outside the part that fails. Correct software in normal operation. A defect that writes wrong state through a clean shutdown produces a well-formed store. No mechanism inside the store can see it, for the same reason: the check would share the defect. Everything that follows holds under these two assumptions, and only under them.

"Working hardware" has a precise meaning here: every fault below the software either does not occur or surfaces as a detectable stop, an error return or a halt, and never as wrong data returned as good. With correct software above it, that leaves no path by which an error can enter the store unannounced. Each failure is either absent (software, by assumption) or announced (hardware, by assumption). The assumption covers the whole substrate the software touches, not only the drive. A fail-stop drive beneath memory without ECC still admits silent error, because data can change after the drive has delivered it correctly. ECC memory, interface CRCs and drive-internal ECC each buy fail-stop behavior for their own segment.

The fail-stop property cannot be conferred from above. Drive firmware sits inside the failure domain it would certify. Firmware defects are themselves a main source of fail-partial behavior: lost writes acknowledged as complete, misdirected writes, stale reads. Software checks (page checksums, scrubbing, re-validation) execute on the processor and memory they would be checking. They shrink the surface for undetected error, but what remains is exactly what fail-stop excludes, wrong data accepted as good. A checksum also blesses whatever the code computed, so it cannot see the software's own errors either. So software checks are probabilistic mitigation, not a guarantee. A store that assumes fail-stop hardware and does not checksum is not omitting a protection. It declines a permanent cost for a check that cannot deliver the property it suggests.

A component that is always correct and never stops would be stronger than fail-stop. No single device can guarantee it. Masking is finite. Every masking mechanism is redundancy within a bound: an error-correcting code corrects up to its distance, a mirror survives one loss. Past the bound, a code used for correction can miscorrect, decoding to the wrong value and returning it as good. The same redundancy buys either more masking or more detection, and pushing a device toward never stopping moves its failures toward fail-partial. No physical object is unconditionally available. Power loss or destruction stops any device. Fail-stop survives even that, since destruction is a stop, which makes it the strongest model a single device can hold. Continued correct service through faults requires redundancy across independent failure domains, and its guarantee is conditional on a fault budget.

RAID is that redundancy across drives, and it assumes fail-stop members. A member that stops is an erasure at a known location, so the array reconstructs it from the others and keeps serving. A code that corrects n erasures corrects only n/2 errors at unknown locations, so the announcement is worth twice the redundancy. Normal reads do not check parity, so a fail-partial member's wrong data passes through. A parity update computed from it writes the error into the parity, and a later rebuild restores it with confidence. RAID masks the stops of fail-stop members and does nothing for silent faults.

bs requires fail-stop hardware and nothing more: An announced hardware error stops bs, either as a storage fault (§5) or by ending the process. Either way flush.lock remains and the store is condemned (§3). ECC memory is the part of the substrate most often missing. Without it, the assumption of §2 does not hold for memory. RAID beneath the store, or a mirrored volume, masks a drive that stops, so bs keeps running through it. It adds availability, not correctness. The store's guarantee is the same with or without it. Checksumming filesystems and scrubbing reduce the chance of silent hardware error. They are worth having on doubtful hardware, but they do not change the guarantee either.

The store does not ask whether its contents after a crash are valid. That question has no reliable answer. It asks whether the store closed cleanly, which is decidable. Open creates flush.lock and holds it, with an exclusive OS process lock, for as long as the store is open (impl/store/store_open.ipp:37-45). Close flushes every table, records each body's count in its head, and removes flush.lock only if no storage faulted (impl/store/store_close.ipp:89-96). A fault returns error::integrity and leaves the lock in place. At open, a present flush.lock means the store did not close cleanly. It is not opened. Only restore accepts it (impl/store/store_restore.ipp:41-46), and the server routes startup there automatically (server:console/executor_runner.cpp:128-131). The predicate never depends on code that ran during the crash, so it cannot be wrong about the crash. It deliberately over-approximates: some condemned stores were in fact intact. That availability cost is what keeps the guarantee free of exceptions. The clean-close state itself is sound because the store admits only two kinds of durable change, each consistent at any instant a fault can strike: Atomic directory renames on one volume: snapshot promotion and rotation, all-old or all-new. Append-only body writes with logical truncation: content below any recorded count never changes once written, so every body state that can exist on disk is a valid extension of every recorded count. Mutable state lives in heads, which are replaced only as a whole (04 §6). Every deletion that matters is an atomic rename. Non-atomic deletion touches only directories already defined as garbage. Invariant (Reliability-1). A store opens only if it closed cleanly, and a store that closed cleanly holds exactly what was written. Invariant (Reliability-2). No snapshot directory that restore could prefer is ever modified in place.

A condemned store is returned to a state whose correctness rests on something other than the damaged store: Restore from a snapshot. The store keeps one snapshot, its heads as of a quiescent point. Restore prefers /primary, falls back to /secondary only when a crash interrupted the snapshot that was replacing it, and truncates every body to the counts the snapshot recorded (impl/store/store_restore.ipp:60-86, 04 §6). Because bodies are append-only, those counts describe a state that existed exactly. Recreate and resync. With no snapshot, restore recreates the store in place and the node rebuilds it from the network (impl/store/store_restore.ipp:79-82). Both paths end in a state the store did not have to vouch for. The snapshot was taken while the store was known good. The network is an independent source. Invariant (Reliability-3). Recovery never trusts content of the condemned store beyond the counts recorded by a snapshot taken at a quiescent point.

Repair is not a choice the design declines. It is not possible, because nothing can certify a repaired store as correct. The store cannot vouch for itself. Any check of its contents shares fate with those contents. Full validation of the whole chain is not an authority either. It proves that the data satisfies the consensus rules, not that the store holds what was written. It runs over the suspect store. Indexes, associations and derived state can agree with each other and with the rules and still be wrong. The hardware cannot be checked by software running on it (§2). A repaired store would be trusted on no grounds at all. Rollback to a known-good state, or a rebuild from the source, is the only recovery there is.

Faults while running are announced, never absorbed. Disk full is recoverable. The storage records the space it needed, the node suspends, and once space is freed a reload resumes service without condemning the store (04 §4). Any other storage fault implies a code or hardware error, outside the assumptions of §2. Corruption of the store itself is excluded by construction (§3), so a fault is never ambiguous. It is latched as the first error code and cannot be cleared (impl/memory/mmap.ipp:227-239). The node stops using the store, reports the fault, and close leaves flush.lock in place. The next start will restore, but restoring before the cause is found is not a good idea. The fault means an assumption failed, and until the code or hardware is fixed, restore and resync run on the same platform with none of the guarantees above.

Bitcoin Core keeps its chain state in LevelDB. Under the same two assumptions, it can offer no comparable guarantee. LevelDB is fail-partial, and corrupts on good hardware. Chrome ships LevelDB and SQLite side by side across the same machines, drives and power loss. LevelDB corrupts at rates that forced dedicated recovery machinery, and SQLite does not. Bitcoin Core's chain state corruption after power loss on ordinary machines fits the same pattern. The faults follow the software, not the hardware. Its recovery repairs the only copy. Log recovery stops at the first bad record and discards everything after it. RepairDB keeps what it can parse and drops the rest. ReplayBlocks reconciles the chain state from the damaged store itself. Each result is then trusted, with no authority to check it against. Its integrity checks certify nothing. The startup VerifyDB examines the last 6 blocks by default, reading them and their undo data from the same suspect store and comparing them with chain state from the same process. A pass shows only that the parts agree with each other. It certifies neither the rest of the store nor even the blocks it examined. A full-depth run over every block has the same flaw. Its errors are ambiguous. A corruption error implies one of three causes: bad hardware, bad software, or corruption of the store itself (for example by uncontrolled process termination). Because LevelDB is not crash consistent, the third is always possible, so the error cannot say which occurred. Every recovery available, an in-place repair, -reindex from the block files on the same disk, or even a full resync from the network, assumes the store was the cause. None can rule out the other two, so each may resume on the hardware or software that caused the error. libbitcoin Bitcoin Core Failure model of the store fail-stop fail-partial After a hard shutdown clean close or condemned, decided without examining contents examined, repaired, then trusted After a reported error bad hardware or software, since the store cannot corrupt itself bad hardware, bad software or store corruption, indistinguishable Recovery snapshot restore or rebuild repair, reindex or resync, each assuming store corruption Recovered store rests on a snapshot taken while known good, or the network the damaged store's own contents, unless resynchronized

A single component can be at best fail-stop and recoverable. Keeping service through faults requires redundancy across independent failure domains, and redundancy is only sound over members that fail by stopping, since it must know which member failed. Bitcoin already provides that redundancy: thousands of independent nodes, any one of which can stop while the rest serve. The network is the array and nodes are its members, and like RAID (§2.4) its contract holds only over members that stop rather than lie. For a node, the correct design is therefore exactly fail-stop and recoverable. Masking faults inside the node would duplicate, conditionally and less well, what the network provides as a whole.

Companion to 02-primitives and 05-queries. Heads and bodies sit on the storage interface (memory/interfaces/storage.hpp:31-143), implemented by mmap<Widths...> (memory/mmap.hpp:43-551): one memory-mapped file, or a multi-record aggregate of several files that share one size and one set of locks (memory/mmaps.hpp).

Each storage keeps a chain of sizes as atomics (memory/mmap.hpp:431-437): settled ≤ frontier ≤ logical ≤ capacity ≤ file Size Meaning logical Bytes allocated to rows. This is what size() reports and what a head records as the body count. frontier End of the contiguous run of rows whose writes have completed. settled Rows flushed and moved to a read-only file mapping (staged bodies only). capacity Mapped and usable without a remap. file Bytes reserved on disk. Invariant (Storage-1). The size chain is monotone in that order at every observable point (impl/memory/mmap.ipp:188-223).

allocate(count) claims rows by a compare-exchange on logical while the claim fits in capacity, which is the common case and takes no lock (impl/memory/mmap_storage.ipp:457-470). A claim past capacity takes the growth mutex (one grower at a time), then the remap lock exclusively, and grows (:472-497). Growth targets required × (1 + rate/100) (default rate 5%) for native maps, and whole chunks of min(256 MiB, RAM/256) for staged bodies (impl/memory/mmap.ipp:119-160). If the disk refuses the target, the surplus is halved toward the exact requirement before giving up (impl/memory/mmap_private.ipp:150-184).

Growing a map can move it, which invalidates every pointer into it. Each storage therefore has a shared mutex over its mapping (memory/mmap.hpp:443-445): Every read and write goes through an accessor (memory), which holds the shared side for its lifetime and bounds access at the logical size (memory/accessor.hpp:30-34, impl/memory/mmap_dispatch.ipp:112-132). Growth, unload, reload and shrink take the exclusive side. Accessors are short-lived: a query takes one, reads or writes a row, and releases it. A table iterator holds one for its life, which is why writing to the same table while iterating it will deadlock (impl/query/query.ipp:50-58). On macOS the shared mutex is a pthread_rwlock_t, because the libc++ shared_mutex serializes readers (locks/shared_mutex.hpp:26-63). Invariant (Storage-2). No pointer into a storage outlives the shared lock under which it was obtained, except the unguarded get_raw used for fixed-size heads that never remap (impl/memory/mmap_dispatch.ipp:89-104).

Mode Platform Used by Behaviour native Windows (all storages) — File-backed shared mapping. Flush is FlushViewOfFile and FlushFileBuffers (src/memory/mman.cpp). A background reader touches head pages to keep them resident (impl/memory/mmap_native.ipp:197-250). staged Linux, macOS bodies Writes land in anonymous memory and are written to the file with pwrite at flush, then the flushed range is remapped read-only from the file (settled). A worker settles and evicts under memory pressure; writers are throttled at the staging bound (impl/memory/mmap_body.ipp). managed Linux, macOS heads An anonymous copy of the head with a dirty-page bitmap. Dirty pages are written back lazily and at flush (impl/memory/mmap_head.ipp). shared Linux, macOS the strong head A file-backed shared mapping (impl/store/store.ipp:76). Bodies are staged because they are append-only, and heads stay resident because they update in place. The strong head is the exception: it is appended in tx order and goes cold behind its top, so it maps its file and its pages can be dropped (store.hpp:338-344).

A storage has two error states (memory/mmap.hpp:431-436): space: the bytes a refused growth needed. Set when fallocate returns ENOSPC or the free-space probe fails; the map stays loaded (impl/memory/mmap_private.ipp:218-282). fault: the first unrecoverable error code, latched. Any other resize or map failure sets it and unmaps. At the query level, is_full() is space without fault, and get_code() reports disk_full before any fault (impl/query/query.ipp:83-104). Recovery from disk full is store::reload(): it takes the transactor exclusively, marks the store dirty, and reloads every storage, which clears space and discards orphaned staged extents (impl/store/store_reload.ipp:30-51, impl/memory/mmap_storage.ipp:153-183). The node drives this from chaser_storage once space is freed. Invariant (Storage-3). A refused allocation publishes nothing: logical is not advanced, so no row exists past the last successful claim.

Every query write holds the store's transactor, the shared side of a timed mutex (store.hpp:47, impl/store/store.ipp:281-284). Lifecycle operations take it exclusively, so they run only between writes: create, open and restore with try_lock; close, snapshot, reload and prune by waiting, raising wait_lock events while they wait. open takes the process lock (an OS file lock) and creates flush.lock, which exists only while the store is open (impl/store/store_open.ipp:29-118, locks/flush_lock.hpp). It loads the envelope before any table and fails on a schema mismatch. Stored bucket counts and filter k override configuration. close writes each table's body count into its head, unloads and closes every storage, and removes flush.lock only if no storage faulted (impl/store/store_close.ipp:30-100). A flush.lock found at open means the store was not closed cleanly, and only restore will open it.

A snapshot is the heads alone. Bodies are flushed in place and never copied; each head records its body's count, and restore truncates every body back to that count. Sources: impl/store/store_snapshot.ipp:30-82, impl/store/store_backup.ipp:31-127, impl/store/store_dump.ipp:28-88. Heads are written from memory, not copied as files, so the snapshot does not depend on the head files having been flushed. Each rotation step is a rename, so at every instant at least one complete snapshot exists in primary or secondary. Restore (impl/store/store_restore.ipp:29-204) requires the flush.lock left by an unclean close. It replaces heads/ with primary (or secondary, or recreates the store if neither exists), opens, and for each table verifies its head and truncates its body to the recorded count. The batch tables are dropped instead. Invariant (Snapshot-1). Restore yields a state that was reachable at the snapshot: every row a restored head publishes was fully written and flushed before the head was dumped, because bodies are flushed first and are append-only (Body-1). Invariant (Snapshot-2). Headmaps (candidate, confirmed, strong, state, envelope) have no body; their content is restored with the heads (primitives/headmap.hpp:32-38).

prune() requires the candidate and confirmed chains to coincide. It clears the prevout, pool and wtxid heads, snapshots with a zero count for the cache tables, truncates the prevout body, and shrinks the cache and batch bodies to reclaim disk (impl/store/store_prune.ipp). Pool records that can still confirm are compacted and kept.

dirty means the archive may hold a point spent more than once, so tx archival must detect duplicates (05 §2.1). It is set at open when the header table holds more than genesis, by a candidate pop (reorganization), by set_pooling, and by a reload after disk full (impl/store/store.ipp:233-243, impl/store/store_reload.ipp:42-47, impl/query/height.ipp:66). While clean, archival of a bypassed (milestone or checkpoint) block skips the duplicate search (impl/query/archive/chain_writer.ipp:214-220).

Progress is classified by the standard non-blocking definitions. An operation is wait-free if it completes in a bounded number of its own steps, and an algorithm is lock-free if, run long enough, some thread always makes progress, whatever the scheduling of the others. Code in which a thread can wait on another is blocking, and for blocking code the property that matters is deadlock-freedom. Non-blocking guarantees hold whatever the scheduler does; blocking guarantees assume that every thread keeps being scheduled, so that a lock holder eventually releases. Non-blocking (no scheduler assumption) Blocking (fair scheduling) Every thread progresses wait-free starvation-free Some thread progresses lock-free deadlock-free Progress only when running alone obstruction-free — Two things do not affect the classification. A lock that only provides an atomic read or write of one value is a primitive, interchangeable with an atomic. A join on the parts of one operation (a parallel query fanned out over the pool) blocks only the thread that started it. A lock counts when it is held across steps of an algorithm while independent operations wait on it.

Mechanism Progress Source Head reads (hash cells, array buckets, headmap cells) wait-free impl/primitives/hashhead.ipp:329-359, arrayhead.ipp:142-177, headmap.ipp:140-207 Headmap push (single writer, published by size) wait-free impl/primitives/headmap.ipp:283-322 Hash head push lock-free impl/primitives/hashhead.ipp:361-411 Headmap set (state merge and clear, strong replace) lock-free impl/primitives/headmap.ipp:367-402 allocate within capacity lock-free impl/memory/mmap_storage.ipp:457-470 Staged write completion (extent claim_) lock-free impl/memory/mmap_extent.ipp:118-155 Each lock-free step is a compare-exchange loop in which a failed exchange means another thread's exchange succeeded. Parallel queries fan out through standard library algorithms under a parallel execution policy (std::for_each, transform, transform_reduce, reduce, sort, all_of), whose join blocks only the initiating thread. The one other fan-out is the unspent output set commitment, which pipelines its sequential hash fold on a dedicated thread beside the parallel bucket fill (impl/unspent/unspent_serial.ipp:59-101); it is likewise joined within the one operation.

Memory map. These locks are private to one storage (mmap) and contend only among accessors of that storage. Lock Held across Waiters Source Remap lock (exclusive side) growing a storage's mapping every accessor of that storage memory/mmap.hpp:443-445, impl/memory/mmap_storage.ipp:436-450, :472-497, impl/memory/mmap_dispatch.ipp:33-72 Growth mutex the growth of one storage other writers that need growth memory/mmap.hpp:439-441 Extent ring mutex ring maintenance and a staged claim other staged writers of that body impl/memory/mmap_extent.ipp:161-200 Restore mutex restoring a released head segment head writers and the head worker impl/memory/mmap_head.ipp:572-580, :660-663 The write throttle parks a staged writer until the settle worker has written to disk (impl/memory/mmap_body.ipp:196-212). That is a wait on I/O, not on another thread's progress. Store and query. These locks are taken by queries and lifecycle operations. Lock Held across Waiters Source Candidate reorganization mutex a candidate pop candidate height readers (fork, sequence queries) query.hpp:1393, impl/query/height.ipp:69, impl/query/consensus/consensus_forks.ipp:53, :68, :124, impl/query/sequences.ipp:41 Confirmed reorganization mutex a confirmed pop confirmed height readers (fork, sequence queries) query.hpp:1394, impl/query/height.ipp:126, impl/query/consensus/consensus_forks.ipp:54, :95, impl/query/sequences.ipp:62 Transactor (exclusive side) create, open, restore, snapshot, prune, reload, close all writers store.hpp:303, §5 These locks are extremely low frequency and contention. Readers and writers take only their shared sides, which do not contend with each other. The reorganization mutexes are taken exclusively only by a chain pop, which occurs only in a reorganization. The transactor is taken exclusively only by: create, open and restore, which only try the lock, before any writer exists (impl/store/store_create.ipp:31, store_open.ipp:34, store_restore.ipp:31); snapshot (impl/store/store_snapshot.ipp:32); prune, which snapshots under the same hold (impl/store/store_prune.ipp:34); reload after disk full (impl/store/store_reload.ipp:32); close (impl/store/store_close.ipp:33). Files. Two file locks guard the store directory, not threads. Both are only tried, never waited on. Lock Taken Released Purpose Source Process lock (process.lock) create, open, restore close an exclusive OS file lock, so one process opens the store locks/interprocess_lock.hpp, impl/store/store_open.ipp:37, store_close.ipp:89 Flush lock (flush.lock) create, open close, if no storage faulted a sentinel whose presence at open marks an unclean close, which only restore accepts locks/flush_lock.hpp, impl/store/store_open.ipp:43, store_close.ipp:95, store_restore.ipp:41

By design every blocking lock is a leaf or is taken in a fixed order: The extent ring, restore and reorganization mutexes acquire no lock while held. The restore mutex is taken after the shared remap lock, by writers and by the head worker alike. Growth takes the growth mutex, then the remap lock exclusively, and holds no accessor while doing so. The fork queries take the candidate mutex before the confirmed mutex, both shared; a pop takes one exclusively. Lifecycle operations take the transactor exclusively only between writes; a writer holds its shared side only for the duration of a write. Invariant (Storage-4). No accessor or iterator on a storage is held while allocating on that storage. Growth waits for every accessor of the storage to release, so an accessor held across an allocation on the same storage deadlocks against it (impl/memory/mmap_storage.ipp:410-415, impl/query/query.ipp:50-58). This is the one rule deadlock-freedom depends on, and it binds only code inside the store. The query interface exposes no accessor or iterator (the accessor sets are protected, query.hpp:1297-1346), so no caller can hold one across a write. The store is deadlock-free for any use of its public interface. Starvation-freedom is not claimed: the shared mutexes make no fairness guarantee.

Companion to 02-primitives and 05-queries. Each table is declared in tables/<category>/<name>.hpp with its schema in tables/schema.hpp. The store owns them (store.hpp:367-406) and binds them to storages and settings (impl/store/store.ipp:42-198). Schema version {4,0,15,0} (tables/schema.hpp:62).

Arrows are foreign keys (navigation), labelled with the field that holds the link. Dotted arrows are searches through a hash head, labelled with the search key. Headmaps are indexed by the link of the table they annotate. Reading a block: header by hash, txs at the header link, then each tx, whose point_fk and outs_fk are the first of its contiguous ins and outs rows (ins_count, outs_count give the extent). Each ins row leads to the input (script and witness) and each outs row to the output (value and script). Invariant (Table-2). A transaction's ins and outs rows are contiguous and allocated before the tx row is written, so point_fk and outs_fk with the two counts determine them exactly (impl/query/archive/chain_writer.ipp:161-186).
