Architecture of libbitcoin-explorer: the command model, generation, parsing and output. Bitcoin Explorer (bx) is a command line tool built on libbitcoin-system. Each of its commands is a class derived from a common base, generated from one XML model that declares the command's name, category, options, positional arguments, configuration settings and help text. The bx executable finds the command named by its first argument, parses the rest of the command line, the environment and a configuration file into that command's bound members, and invokes it with an output and an error stream. Paths are relative to include/bitcoin/explorer/ in libbitcoin-explorer, at master 78ccbab8 (2026-10-27).

The console entry point forwards its arguments and the three standard streams to dispatch (console/main.cpp). BC_USE_LIBBITCOIN_MAIN is the libbitcoin-system macro that defines the platform main and supplies UTF-8 streams on Windows. BC_USE_LIBBITCOIN_MAIN int bc::system::main(int argc, char* argv[]) { return bc::explorer::dispatch(argc, const_cast<const char**>(argv), bc::system::cin, bc::system::cout, bc::system::cerr); } dispatch (src/dispatch.cpp) displays usage and the command list when there are no arguments. Otherwise it drops the program name and calls dispatch_command, which treats the first remaining argument as the command symbol. An unknown symbol is reported as an invalid command, naming the command that replaced it if formerly returns one. A found command is parsed, then helped or invoked. An exception escaping the command is reported as an invalid parameter and returns console_result::failure. parser metadata(*command); std::string error_message; if (!metadata.parse(error_message, in, argc, argv)) { display_invalid_parameter(error, error_message); return console_result::failure; } if (metadata.help()) { command->write_help(output); return console_result::okay; } return command->invoke(out, err); In Windows builds the input and output streams are swapped for binary std::cin and std::cout when the command declares requires_raw_input() or requires_raw_output(), and set to UTF-8 otherwise. The error stream is always UTF-8. The return value is a console_result (define.hpp): failure (-1), okay (0) or invalid (1). Positive values are domain specific, such as a validation command reporting an invalid result.

command (command.hpp) is the base of every command. It cannot be constructed directly, and each virtual has a default, so a derived class overrides only what applies to it. Member Purpose symbol() Static, lower case command name, such as tx-decode name(), category(), description() Name, category (such as WALLET) and help text obsolete() Excludes the command from the listed command names requires_raw_input(), requires_raw_output() Binary standard input or output load_options(), load_arguments() Named options and positional arguments load_environment(), load_settings() Environment variables and configuration file settings load_fallbacks() Reads unset arguments from standard input set_defaults_from_config() Applies configuration settings to defaulted options write_help() Writes command line help from the option and argument metadata invoke(output, error) Executes the command The base also holds the configuration settings shared by all commands, in [wallet] and [server] sections, each with a typed getter and setter (get_wallet_wif_version_setting() and so on). Help is produced by the libbitcoin-system config::printer, from the same metadata that the parser consumes.

Each command is a class in commands/, named for its symbol, that derives from command. Its options and arguments are bound to private option_ and argument_ structures, and exposed through typed accessors such as get_transaction_argument() and get_version_option(). Every command accepts --help (-h) and --config (-c). Each argument is declared both as a named option and as a positional argument with an instance limit, so it may be given either way (commands/tx-decode.hpp): virtual arguments_metadata& load_arguments() { return get_argument_metadata() .add("TRANSACTION", 1); } virtual void load_fallbacks(std::istream& input, po::variables_map& variables) { load_input(get_transaction_argument(), "TRANSACTION", variables, input); } The class declares invoke, and its definition in src/commands/ reads the bound values through the accessors and writes the result (src/commands/address-embed.cpp, simplified): console_result address_embed::invoke(std::ostream& output, std::ostream&) { const data_chunk& data = get_data_argument(); const auto version = get_version_option(); const auto ops = script::to_pay_key_hash_pattern(rmd160_hash(data)); const script script(ops); const auto hash = rmd160_hash(script.to_data(false)); output << payment_address(hash, version) << std::endl; return console_result::okay; }

generated.hpp includes every command header and declares three free functions over the full set of commands, defined in src/generated.cpp: Function Result find(symbol) A new instance of the command with that symbol, or null formerly(former) The symbol of the command that replaced a former name, or empty broadcast(func) Calls func with an instance of every command find compares the symbol against each class's static symbol(), so commands are constructed only on demand. broadcast lists the commands for usage (display_command_names), skipping obsolete ones. The help command uses find to load and write the help of another command.

The command headers are generated from model/generate.xml by the iMatix GSL templates in model/templates/ (model/generate.gsl). Implementations in src/commands/ are written by hand. Template Output gsl.command.hpp command.hpp, with the configuration settings gsl.commands.hpp commands/<symbol>.hpp, one per command gsl.generated.hpp, gsl.generated.cpp generated.hpp, src/generated.cpp data/gsl.bx data/bx, a bash command completion script test/gsl.generated__*.cpp Tests of broadcast, find, formerly and symbol The model declares each command with its arguments and options, the configuration sections, and the localizable resource strings that become the BX_* macros in generated.hpp: <command symbol="address-embed" formerly="embed-addr" output="payment_address" category="WALLET" description="..."> <option name="version" type="byte" configuration="wallet.pay_to_public_key_hash_version" description="..." /> <argument name="DATA" stdin="true" type="bytes" description="..." /> </command> Model types map to C++ types in model/primitives.gsl, either a libbitcoin-system type (system::config::hash256, system::wallet::hd_private) or one of the explorer config types (section 4.3). An option without a type is a bool switch. The stdin attribute generates the load_input fallback, an argument of type bytes read from standard input makes the command raw input, and an output of bytes makes it raw output. The configuration attribute generates set_defaults_from_config, and obsolete and formerly generate obsolete() and the formerly entry.

parser (parser.hpp) derives from the libbitcoin-system config::parser and supplies its metadata from the command instance. The sources are loaded into one variables_map, with the first stored value of a variable taking precedence (src/parser.cpp): Order Source Detail First Command line Named options and positional arguments Second Standard input load_fallbacks, for arguments not given on the command line Third Environment Variables prefixed BX_, declaring BX_CONFIG Fourth Configuration file The file named by --config or BX_CONFIG If --help is present only the command line is loaded, and help() returns true. Otherwise the parser notifies the bound variables and calls set_defaults_from_config, which replaces a defaulted option with its configured setting when that setting was not defaulted (commands/address-embed.hpp): const auto& option_version = variables["version"]; const auto& option_version_config = variables["wallet.pay_to_public_key_hash_version"]; if (option_version.defaulted() && !option_version_config.defaulted()) { option_.version = option_version_config.as<explorer::config::byte>(); } A parse error is returned as the error text and reported by display_invalid_parameter.

utility.hpp provides the fallback readers. load_input deserializes a parameter from the input stream when its variable was not set, and throws on failure. load_path reads a parameter from the file named by its variable, where - (BX_STDIO_PATH_SENTINEL) leaves the variable unset for standard input. write_file writes to the named file, or to the output stream when the path is empty or -.

Arguments and options are typed by config objects that round-trip through stream operators, as described in Config. Most are libbitcoin-system types. The types in config/ cover values specific to bx, each with a native value type and a pair of stream operators: Type Value Text form address std::string A valid payment address algorithm points_value::selection greedy or individual btc uint64_t Bitcoin decimal, read as satoshis byte uint8_t Decimal, not a character bytes data_chunk The entire stream, unencoded ec_private ec_secret Base16 electrum electrum::seed_prefix Seed prefix name endorsement data_chunk Base16, up to max_endorsement_size hd_key wallet::hd_key Base58 of hd_key_size bytes language system::language Word list language name sighash chain::coverage Signature hash type name signature message_signature Base64 of message_signature_size bytes witness witness_address::program_type Witness program name

A command writes its result to the output stream passed to invoke, and diagnostics to the error stream. Most commands write a single value in its text form through the value's operator<<, followed by a newline, such as base16(data) or a payment_address. A raw output command writes bytes to binary standard output. Structured results are JSON. write_stream (utility.hpp) serializes a system::json::value followed by a newline. Chain objects convert through the libbitcoin-system JSON conversions, and json.hpp adds conversions for the settings list and for a bitcoin_uri (src/commands/tx-decode.cpp): console_result tx_decode::invoke(std::ostream& output, std::ostream&) { write_stream(output, value_from(chain::transaction{ get_transaction_argument() })); return console_result::okay; } to_json(settings_list) nests the dot-delimited setting names into section objects under a settings key, as written by the settings command. display.hpp holds the fixed messages of the dispatcher: usage with version and command list, invalid command (naming the superseding command where one exists), invalid parameter, and connection failure.

Architecture of libbitcoin-network: net, sessions, channels and protocols, threading, transports and configuration. The network library (libbitcoin-network) is asynchronous networking for the Bitcoin peer-to-peer protocol and for client-facing services: HTTP, WebSocket, JSON-RPC, TLS and ZeroMQ (ZMTP). It provides the connection lifecycle, the wire encodings and the threading model, and leaves the behavior of a node or server to libraries that derive from its types. Paths are relative to include/bitcoin/network/ in libbitcoin-network, at master 001c1a32 (2026-10-27).

Object Type Role Network net (net.hpp) Owns the threadpool, the network strand, the address pool, the broadcaster, and the sessions Session session (sessions/) Creates channels of one kind (accept, connect, seed), starts them and attaches their protocols Channel channel (channels/), over proxy and socket (net/) One connection: reads, writes, timers, stop Protocol protocol (protocols/) One behavior on one channel, such as handshake, ping or address exchange Message messages/peer, messages/rpc, messages/http P2P messages, JSON-RPC values, HTTP bodies net attaches sessions, a session creates channels and attaches protocols to each, and each protocol holds its channel and its session:

net starts in two phases. start() attaches the manual session, loads the hosts file and attaches the seed session. run() connects the configured manual peers, then starts the inbound session and, once that has started, the outbound session. A derived network attaches its own sessions with attach<Session>(), or with attach_service<Session>() for client-facing services, which stop_services() can then stop independently of P2P. Both subscribe the session's stop() to the network's stop subscriber, which holds the session for its lifetime. The address pool (net/hosts.hpp) is owned by net and loaded from and saved to the file at settings::path. Peer sessions take, restore, fetch and save addresses through the network, on its strand.

Session Base Connections session_manual session_peer Connect to configured or requested endpoints, reconnect on stop session_seed session_peer Connect to seed nodes to populate the address pool session_inbound session_peer Accept peer connections on the configured bindings session_outbound session_peer Maintain a target count of peer connections drawn from the address pool session_server session Accept client connections on clear and secure bindings session declares create_channel(), attach_handshake() and attach_protocols() as pure virtual. session_peer implements them for channel_peer; session_server implements only the handshake, so a service derives from it and supplies its channel type and protocols. Acceptors and connectors (net/acceptor.hpp, net/connector.hpp) are created through the network, with SOCKS5 connection (net/connector_socks.hpp) and I2P SAM acceptance (net/acceptor_sam.hpp) as alternatives. Outbound connections are made in batches of connect_batch_size, raced with race_quality so that the first successful connection of a batch wins. The seed session completes with race_volume, once enough addresses have been received or every seed has finished.

proxy (net/proxy.hpp) owns the socket and implements reads, a queued and metered write path, stop, and stop subscription. channel adds an identifier and nonce, inactivity and expiration timers, pause and resume, and protocol attachment. The derived channels each own a dispatcher over an interface (section 4) and read one message type: Channel Options Reads Interface channel_peer tcp_server messages::peer frames interfaces/peer_dispatch.hpp channel_http http_server http::request interfaces/http.hpp channel_rpc<Interface> tcp_server rpc::request template argument A protocol is attached on the channel strand, and its lifetime is held by the channel's stop subscription (channels/channel.hpp, simplified): template <class Protocol, class SessionPtr, typename... Args> typename Protocol::ptr attach(const SessionPtr& session, Args&&... args) NOEXCEPT { auto protocol = std::make_shared<Protocol>(session, shared_from_base<channel>(), args...); subscribe_stop([=](const code& ec) NOEXCEPT { protocol->stopping(ec); }); return protocol; } socket (net/socket.hpp) holds the transport as a variant of io::socket, tls::stream, p2ps::stream and zmtp::stream. WebSocket is a framing mode of the clear or TLS socket, entered by upgrade. The transport setting carries the context that selects the TLS, P2PS or ZMTP upgrade.

Peer protocols are named for the protocol version level at which they apply (messages/peer/enums/level.hpp), such as protocol_ping_106 and protocol_ping_60001 (BIP31). session_peer::attach_handshake() attaches the highest configured version protocol, from protocol_version_106 to protocol_version_70016, and attach_protocols() attaches alert, reject, ping and address protocols according to the levels negotiated in the handshake. The seed session attaches protocol_seed_209 or protocol_seed_70016 instead, and the inbound session omits inbound address protocols. Protocol Level Messages Role protocol_version_106 106 version, verack The version handshake protocol_version_70001 70001 (BIP37) version.relay Handshake with transaction relay preference protocol_version_70002 70002 (BIP61) reject Handshake that rejects an obsolete or duplicate version protocol_version_70014 70014 (BIP152) send_compact Handshake that signals compact blocks protocol_version_70016 70016 (BIP155, BIP339) send_address_v2, witness_tx_id_relay Handshake that signals address v2 and witness transaction relay protocol_ping_106 106 ping Keepalive ping on a timer protocol_ping_60001 60001 (BIP31) ping, pong Ping with nonce, answered by pong protocol_alert_311 311 alert Logs received alerts protocol_reject_70002 70002 (BIP61) reject Logs received rejects protocol_address_in_209 209 address Stores received addresses protocol_address_in_70016 70016 (BIP155) address, address_v2 Stores received addresses, including v2 protocol_address_out_209 209 get_address, address Answers address requests (IPv4 and IPv6) protocol_address_out_70016 70016 (BIP155) get_address, address_v2 Answers address requests with v2 addresses protocol_seed_209 209 get_address, address Seeding: requests addresses, then stops protocol_seed_70016 70016 (BIP155) get_address, address_v2 Seeding with v2 addresses protocol_http HTTP methods Base of HTTP service protocols protocol_rpc<Channel> JSON-RPC Base of JSON-RPC service protocols A protocol subscribes to channel messages with SUBSCRIBE_CHANNEL, sends with SEND, and binds its handlers to its shared pointer. A handler returns true to remain subscribed. For example, the BIP31 pong handler (protocols/protocol_ping_60001.hpp): bool protocol_ping_60001::handle_receive_pong(const code& ec, const pong::cptr& message) NOEXCEPT { if (stopped(ec)) return false; if (message->nonce != nonce_) { stop(error::protocol_violation); return false; } nonce_ = acknowledged; set_pong(); return true; } protocol_http provides one handler per HTTP method and the standard responses, and protocol_rpc<Channel> provides result, error and notification sends. Both are bases for service protocols.

net constructs one threadpool (async/threadpool.hpp) of settings::threads_() threads sharing one io::context (io/context.hpp), each thread calling its run(). The context runs posted handlers, timer expirations (io::steady_timer) and socket completions (io::socket, io::acceptor, io/socket.hpp), waiting on an I/O completion port on Windows, kqueue on Apple and epoll otherwise (src/io/). Host names are resolved (io::resolver) by getaddrinfo on a resolver thread of the context. Objects that share state are confined to a strand (io::strand, io/strand.hpp) of that context, an executor whose handlers run in post order and never concurrently: Strand Objects Network strand (net::strand()) net, all sessions, hosts, the broadcaster Socket strand (socket::strand()) the socket, its channel, and the channel's protocols session::strand() returns the network strand, so all sessions are serialized with the network. Each socket constructs its own strand on the network's context, and proxy::strand() returns it. Members are documented as thread safe (const or atomic) or as protected by strand, and methods assert stranded(). Work that must not hold a channel strand is posted to the context with protocol::parallel(). Channel start crosses strands. The session pends the channel on the network strand, attaches the handshake on the channel strand, returns to the network strand when the handshake completes, attaches protocols on the channel strand, and completes on the network strand (session::start_channel() and its handlers in sessions/session.hpp).

A channel reads one message at a time. Each derived channel's receive() issues a read only if the channel is not stopped and no read is outstanding. On completion the channel opens a gate, notifies its dispatcher, and closes the gate (channel_peer::handle_receive(), channel_http::dispatch(), channel_rpc::dispatch()). The gate is a race_all whose completion handler posts receive() to the channel strand when the last reference is released, so the next read is armed only after every subscriber has released it (src/channels/channel.cpp, simplified): open_gate(); const auto code = dispatcher_.notify(request); close_gate(); if (code) stop(code); A protocol that retains gate() defers the next read until it releases the pointer. While a protocol holds the gate the channel is not reading, so gate() also starts a monitor that polls the socket for a half-closed connection every 10 milliseconds and stops the channel with peer_disconnect if the peer has gone (channel::monitor(), socket::poll()). The monitor ends when the read is re-armed. pause() holds the gate, or a gate of its own outside of a dispatch, and stops the channel timers. resume() restarts the timers and releases the held gate, or arms the read if none is held. A channel is created paused. The session resumes it after attaching the handshake, the version protocol pauses it on completing the handshake, and the session resumes it again after attaching protocols (sessions/session.hpp, protocols/protocol_version_106.hpp). Reads are not rate metered, as they are bounded by protocol correctness. They are bounded instead as follows: Bound Mechanism Setting Message size Parser and frame limits tcp_server::maximum_request Concurrency One read per channel, deferred by the gate Idle peer Inactivity timer, stops with channel_inactive tcp_server::inactivity_minutes (10) Channel lifetime Expiration timer, stops with channel_expired tcp_server::expiration_minutes (60) The inactivity timer arms once per window. Each read records its time (channel::reading()), and on expiration the timer rearms for the remainder of the window if a read occurred since it was armed, so activity costs a time stamp and not a timer reset. A zero setting disables the corresponding timer. Sends are throttled by rate. The proxy allocates each send bytes / rate_limit seconds, measured from the moment the write is issued to the socket, and defers the send's completion handler by whatever portion of that allocation the write did not consume (proxy::metered(), proxy::unconsumed()). The deferral is a deadline on the channel strand (throttle_). Since the write queue does not start the next send until the completion handler of the current one runs, the deferral throttles the channel without a queue of its own, and time spent idle between sends earns no credit. A channel is never stopped for exceeding the rate, it is only slowed. Setting Scope settings::rate_limit Bytes per second per channel, all sessions tcp_server::rate_limit Bytes per second per channel of the service settings::rate_limited(options) applies the more restrictive of the two, where zero is unlimited, so the limit is zero only if both are zero. A zero limit constructs no throttle. Stop is never deferred: unconsumed() is zero for a stopped channel, and stopping the throttle fires a pending deferral, whose handler reports the send's own result.

Every send of a channel passes through one write queue on the channel strand (src/net/proxy_queue.cpp). A send from any thread is dispatched to the strand as a pending entry holding a writer closure, its completion handler, and a cost. The first entry starts the write loop, and each completion invokes the entry's handler, pops it, and starts the next: void proxy::handle_write(const code& ec, size_t bytes) NOEXCEPT { const auto handler = std::move(queue_.front().handler); handler(ec, bytes); backlog_ = floored_subtract(backlog_, queue_.front().cost); queue_.pop_front(); if (!stopped()) write(); } The handler runs before the pop, so a send issued from the handler is queued behind the entry and does not start a second loop. One entry is one whole message, and its completion fires only when the message is fully written. A body that spans several writer buffers is written in a loop within the socket (socket::body_write()), and a chunked batch part writes its HTTP header and first chunk within one entry (proxy::handle_http_header_write()). No other write can start between the parts of a message, which is what prevents interleaving. Sends are of two kinds. A response (proxy::write(), reaching the socket as rpc_write, http_write or body_write) is solicited, paced by the request that provoked it, and is queued at zero cost. A notification (proxy::notify(), reaching the socket as rpc_notify or body_notify) is unsolicited, so the recipient can force it to accumulate, and it is charged against the channel backlog. Peer channels expose the same split as channel_peer::send() and channel_peer::notify(), and channel_rpc selects by type: a request model is a notification, a response model is a response. HTTP has no notifications, since it is half duplex; channel_http::notify() requires a WebSocket or a downgraded channel. Response Notification Proxy call write() notify() Reads Completes the request under its read gate, so the channel reads its next request only after the response is queued Independent of reads, so it may be sent while a request is in progress Cost Zero Estimated message size plus 256 bytes per entry During an open batch Stamped as a batch part and queued Deferred until the batch closes Over maximum_backlog Not applicable Channel stops with channel_backlog (ZMTP: dropped with message_dropped) The cost estimates the memory an entry pins, so a flood of small messages is charged more than its wire size. A charge is refused only when the queue is not idle and the backlog would exceed tcp_server::maximum_backlog (1 MiB by default), so one message is always accepted. The backlog is reduced as each entry is popped. A JSON-RPC batch is answered as one stream of parts. While a batch is open the proxy stamps each response as a batch part (the first carries the open), defers notifications to a separate deferred_ queue, and on reading the batch close queues the close part. When the close part is written the deferred notifications are moved to the write queue and the read is re-armed (proxy::handle_close_write()). A notification is therefore written only between whole responses or whole batches, and within each kind writes are in the order issued on the strand. WebSocket channels reject batches, as pipelined requests obtain the same result.

A request whose work is long, such as a store query, must not run on the channel strand, which would block every other operation of the channel, including its stop. The handler instead posts the work to the threadpool with PARALLEL (protocol::parallel()), passing the retained gate. The work runs off the strand and posts its result back to the strand with POST (protocol::post()), still carrying the gate, where the handler writes the response. For example, the Electrum balance query in libbitcoin-server (src/protocols/electrum/protocol_electrum_scripthash.cpp, simplified): void protocol_electrum::get_balance(const hash_digest& hash) NOEXCEPT { PARALLEL(do_get_balance, hash, gate()); } void protocol_electrum::do_get_balance(const hash_digest& hash, const gate_t::ptr& gate) NOEXCEPT { uint64_t confirmed{}, unconfirmed{}; auto ec = archive().get_balance(stopping_, confirmed, unconfirmed, hash); POST(complete_get_balance, ec, confirmed, unconfirmed, gate); } void protocol_electrum::complete_get_balance(const code& ec, uint64_t confirmed, int64_t unconfirmed, const gate_t::ptr&) NOEXCEPT { if (stopped()) return; send_result(...); } While the gate is retained the channel does not read the next request, so requests on one channel are answered in order and at most one is in flight. The gate is released when the completion handler returns, after the response is queued, and the read is then re-armed. The channel strand is free throughout the work, so the channel's timers, notifications, and stop proceed. Both bound methods hold the protocol's shared pointer, so the protocol outlives the work, but nothing waits on it. Stop stays fast in three ways: Mechanism Effect Socket stop flag stopped() is atomic and set before anything is posted, so it is visible off the strand Cancellation flag The protocol's stopping(ec) sets an atomic flag that the query polls, so the query returns early Stopped check The completion handler tests stopped() on the strand and abandons the result A response issued after stop is not queued (proxy::do_write()), and its handler is not invoked. A peer that disconnects while the work is in flight is detected by the gate monitor of section 2.2, which stops the channel and so cancels the query. The cancellation flag is a protocol member in libbitcoin-server (stopping_), not a network mechanism; the network provides the stopped state, the stop notification on the strand, and the gate.

protocol::stop(ec) stops the channel. proxy::stop() stops the socket, which sets the atomic stopped flag and cancels pending work, and then posts stopping(ec) to the channel strand. stopping(ec) stops the channel timers, releases a held gate, fires any throttle deferral, releases an HTTP parse in progress, clears the write and deferred queues without invoking their handlers, and notifies the stop subscribers, each protocol's stopping(ec) among them. Handlers test stopped(ec) on entry, which is true for an error code or a stopped channel. A stop on the channel strand while a batch response is open first releases the throttle and writes the batch close part, then stops the socket (proxy::do_stop()), so the client receives a well-formed response. A stop from off the strand, such as shutdown, is immediate. A WebSocket close or a channel expiration or inactivity stops the socket lazily, which allows a graceful WebSocket and TLS close; a subsequent stop terminates it directly. net::close() sets the closed flag and posts do_close(), which releases the sessions, stops the stop, service and connect subscribers and the broadcaster, and removes the threadpool's keep-alive. close() then joins the threadpool, so it must not be called from a pool thread (it aborts if the join fails), and then saves the hosts file.

async/ provides the primitives the objects above are built from: Type Behavior threadpool Threads sharing one io::context, kept alive until stop() subscriber<Args...> Handlers returning void; all notified, all dropped on stop() unsubscriber<Args...> Handlers returning bool; false desubscribes desubscriber<Key, Args...> Keyed bool handlers, with notify_one(key) race_all Completes when the last reference is released race_any Completes with the first finish() (thread safe) race_speed<Size> Completes with the first of Size finishers, at the last race_quality Completes with the first success, or with the last failure race_unity Completes at the last finisher, with the first failure if any race_volume Completes when a finisher reports a sufficient count enable_shared_from_base shared_from_this for derived classes The subscribers are not thread safe: every method is called on the owner's strand and every handler is invoked there. handlers.hpp defines the common handler types result_handler, count_handler and notify_handler. net/deadline.hpp wraps a restartable io::steady_timer, which completes with success on expiration and with operation_canceled on stop.

An interface (interfaces/) is a compile-time list of methods, each a name and its argument types, and the subscriber type for its handlers. The peer dispatch interface (interfaces/peer_dispatch.hpp) lists each P2P message by its command, such as method<"pong", messages::peer::pong::cptr>. Condensed, with most methods cut: struct peer_dispatch { /// Unsubscriber requires bool handlers, injects `code` parameter. template <typename... Args> using subscriber = network::unsubscriber<Args...>; /// dispatcher.subscribe(std::forward<signature>(handler)); template <class Message> using signature = std::function<bool(const code&, const typename Message::cptr&)>; /// Messages exchanged after the handshake completes. static constexpr std::tuple messages { method<"addr", messages::peer::address::cptr>{}, method<"block", messages::peer::block::cptr>{}, // ... method<"ping", messages::peer::ping::cptr>{}, method<"pong", messages::peer::pong::cptr>{}, // ... method<"tx", messages::peer::transaction::cptr>{} }; /// Handshake methods (exchanged before the handshake completes). static constexpr std::tuple handshake { method<"version", messages::peer::version::cptr>{}, method<"verack", messages::peer::version_acknowledge::cptr>{}, // ... }; }; The HTTP interface (interfaces/http.hpp) has the same form, one method per HTTP verb, with a subscriber of void handlers in place of the peer interface's bool (unsubscribing) handlers: struct http_methods { static constexpr std::tuple methods { method<"get", http::method::get::cptr>{}, method<"head", http::method::head::cptr>{}, method<"post", http::method::post::cptr>{}, // ... method<"unknown", http::method::unknown::cptr>{} }; /// Subscriber requires void handlers, injects `code` parameter. template <typename... Args> using subscriber = network::subscriber<Args...>; /// dispatcher.subscribe(std::forward<signature>(handler)); template <class Request> using signature = std::function<void(const code&, const typename Request::cptr&)>; }; Since the method list is a type, a dispatcher's subscribers, and the binding of each handler to its method, are resolved at compile time. The JSON-RPC interfaces of the server take the same form, with each method's parameters in place of a message type (see Server Architecture). rpc::dispatcher<Interface> (messages/rpc/dispatcher.hpp) holds one subscriber per method and notifies the matching subscriber of a request, whose method name and parameters are an rpc::request_t. A received peer frame is dispatched as a request whose method is its command and whose parameter is the deserialized message. The same mechanism dispatches HTTP requests by method and JSON-RPC requests by name. rpc::broadcaster<Interface> (messages/rpc/broadcaster.hpp) is a dispatcher over keyed subscribers, so a subscription can be removed by channel identifier. The network owns one over the peer broadcast interface (interfaces/peer_broadcast.hpp): addr, block, tx, and the internal diagnostics and terminator messages, which are never serialized. A protocol broadcasts with BROADCAST, which posts the message and its channel identifier to the network strand, and subscribes with SUBSCRIBE_BROADCAST, whose handler is posted back to the channel strand (protocols/protocol.hpp), or desubscribed once the channel has stopped. A terminator (broadcast/terminator.hpp) stops a channel identified by identifier or address, or the channels of slots at or above a count. A diagnostics broadcast collects one row of state from each targeted channel, on that channel's strand. wire_tx and wire_block carry transaction and block views to service channels, and net counts demand for them (demand_wire_tx(), demand_wire_block()).

Group Path Contents Peer messages/peer/ Each P2P message type with its command, deserialize() and serialize(); heading; registry RPC messages/rpc/ value_t, a JSON-RPC document model extended with fixed-width integers, any_t and embedded JSON; request and response types HTTP messages/http/, http_body.hpp, json_body.hpp HTTP/1.1 messages, the incremental parser and serializer, the flat buffer, bodies selected by content type, fields, status and media type enums any_t holds a type-erased shared pointer, which allows a deserialized message to pass through the dispatcher as a parameter and be received by its handler as its own type. The peer message codec (messages/peer/body.hpp) reads v1 frames and v2 packets into the same frame type, and the registry (messages/peer/registry.hpp) indexes the messages for per-message byte counts.

Every message is read and written through a body (messages/http/message.hpp): a type with a value_type, a reader that parses incrementally as bytes arrive (init, put, finish) and a writer that serializes incrementally into buffers (init, get). An http::parser drives a body's reader from received bytes and an http::serializer drives its writer (messages/http/parser.hpp, messages/http/serializer.hpp). messages/http/bodies.hpp defines the empty, data (chunk_body), string, span, buffer and file bodies, and the library defines bodies for JSON, JSON-RPC and P2P messages, and a variant body that holds any of them. Since a body does not depend on HTTP framing, the same bodies serve HTTP, WebSocket, raw TCP and ZMTP: the socket's rpc_*, peer_* and body_* operations drive a body directly, without an HTTP message around it (http::body_parser, http::body_serializer). Body Path Value Purpose json::body messages/json_body.hpp A JSON document, with an estimated size and a serialization buffer owned by the socket Reader parses and writer serializes JSON, both streamed rpc::body messages/rpc/body.hpp rpc::request or rpc::response, with batch state JSON-RPC, extending json::body with validation and batch framing; the reader reads requests, the writer writes responses, and the notifier writes notifications (requests) peer::body messages/peer/body.hpp A P2P frame: heading and type-erased message P2P messages, read from v1 frames or v2 packets, written as serialized v1 frames http::file_body messages/http/bodies.hpp An open file (http::file, messages/http/file.hpp) File responses, read from the file 4 KiB at a time (read_size) http::body messages/http_body.hpp A variant of all of the above and the http:: string, data, span, buffer and empty bodies Any message The JSON body defines no size, so a response is sent chunked rather than serialized first to compute a content length: serialization streams directly to the socket. Its writer's buffer belongs to the socket, which retains it across messages and can reduce it to the minimum (reclaim_buffer). The JSON-RPC body adds what JSON-RPC requires of a document: request and response validation, and the framing of batches, which the reader reports as it opens and closes and the writer is told by its caller. It tolerates the observed deviations of clients, such as the single value parameters of Electrum clients and the version 1 messages that btcd places within a version 2 batch, and records them for the channel to validate. Message termination is by transport: newline terminated over TCP, and by the frame over HTTP and WebSocket. The P2P body parses a message's heading and payload into a frame that holds the deserialized message, type-erased, with a parse context stamped by the channel and any fault detail. For BIP324 the payload of an already identified message is accepted directly. The variant body (http::body) holds one of the bodies, selected when its reader or writer is constructed, and passes every call through to it. For a request, the reader is selected by the Content-Type header (messages/http_body.hpp): Content type Body application/json rpc::request, or a plain json::body document where the caller sets plain JSON text/plain String application/octet-stream File for an attachment, otherwise data Otherwise Empty A body may also be preselected before the read, which is how the P2P and JSON-RPC bodies are used on transports without HTTP headers. The writer is selected by the value the caller assigns to the message, an empty body if none: Assigned value Writer rpc::response rpc::writer, a JSON-RPC response rpc::request rpc::notifier, a JSON-RPC notification JSON document json::body writer P2P frame peer::body writer String, data, file, span, buffer The corresponding messages/http/bodies.hpp writer None Empty The JSON and JSON-RPC writers hold their serializers, so they are not movable and are constructed in place within the variant. The writer also reports whether its output is binary (data, file, span, buffer and P2P) or text (string, JSON and JSON-RPC), which selects the frame type of a WebSocket write. Like the JSON body, the variant defines no size, so every variant message is chunked.

A socket (net/socket.hpp) carries every transport. Its transport is selected by a context (settings::transport), a variant of std::monostate (clear), a tls::context, a p2ps::context or a zmtp::context, and do_upgrade() applies it on accept and on a non-proxied connect. HTTP and WebSocket are layered over the clear or TLS socket, and detect() distinguishes HTTP from raw TCP on the same port from the first bytes. Transport Over Implementation Carries TCP io::socket Bitcoin P2P (v1), JSON-RPC over TCP (Electrum, Stratum v1) TCP/S TLS 1.3 tls::stream over tls::server The same, encrypted HTTP, HTTP/S TCP, TLS http::parser and http::serializer over the socket REST, JSON-RPC over HTTP WS, WS/S HTTP upgrade ws::reader and ws::serialize_header framing over the socket JSON-RPC over WebSocket P2PS TCP p2ps::stream Bitcoin P2P, BIP324 (v2) encrypted ZMTP, CurveZMQ (ZMTPS) TCP zmtp::stream, NULL or CURVE mechanism ZeroMQ publish, request and pipeline sockets SOCKS5 TCP connector_socks Outbound connections through a proxy (such as Tor) I2P SAM TCP acceptor_sam Inbound connections forwarded by an I2P SAM bridge The socket's operations are grouped by what they read and write: tcp_* fixed buffers, peer_* P2P messages, rpc_* JSON-RPC requests, responses and notifications, http_* HTTP messages (including progressive reads for batched JSON-RPC bodies), ws_* WebSocket frames, and body_* non-HTTP bodies.

Every transport begins as an io::socket (io/socket.hpp), held as the first alternative of the socket's variant (socket_t in net/socket.hpp). Upgrades move the TCP socket into a wrapping stream, and get_base() recovers it from any alternative through the stream's next_layer(), so shutdown, close and peer liveness always act on the TCP layer. Each socket owns a strand of the network context. Every public operation dispatches its work to that strand, and every completion handler runs on it, so one socket's I/O calls are never concurrent. The exception is accept(), which runs on the acceptor's (network) strand until its handler is invoked (src/net/socket_connect.cpp). Step Implementation Accept io::acceptor::async_accept into the socket's io::socket, then do_handshake() unless the acceptor is proxied Connect io::async_connect over the resolved range, trying each endpoint in sequence, or io::socket::async_connect per endpoint of the bound address family when a binding is configured Handshake do_upgrade() applies the context; inbound sockets are bounded by the connect timeout, which stops the socket on expiry Stop shutdown(shutdown_type::both) and close() on the strand The tcp_* operations move fixed buffers. tcp_read completes only when the buffer is filled (io::async_read), and tcp_write writes the whole buffer (io::async_write) (io/operations.hpp, src/net/socket_tcp.cpp). The SOCKS5 and SAM negotiations are written entirely with these operations. Body reads over TCP (body_*, rpc_*) parse the bytes already in a http::flat_buffer (messages/http/flat_buffer.hpp) and then read more with async_read_some, preparing the larger of the buffer's free capacity and the header limit, bounded by the buffer's max_size() (buffer_overflow if nothing remains) (src/net/socket_http.cpp). The body reader consumes what it parses and the residue stays in the buffer for the next read. A read whose total exceeds maximum_request fails with body_limit (src/net/socket_body.cpp). JSON-RPC over TCP (Electrum, Stratum v1) is newline terminated: rpc_write and rpc_notify set terminate on the message before writing it (src/net/socket_rpc.cpp). watch() and poll() share a 10 ms timer that checks the TCP layer for a received FIN (io::socket::half_closed()), reporting peer_disconnect. Cancellation of a socket operation (operation_canceled) is reported to the caller as channel_stopped. Setting (settings::tcp_server) Default Use maximum_request max_payload Bound on one read (body, HTTP body, WebSocket message, P2P payload, ZMTP frame) minimum_buffer 4 KiB Size retained buffers are reduced to when idle maximum_buffer 64 KiB Bound of the retained JSON serialization buffer connect_timeout_seconds 0 (network default) Inbound handshake bound, outbound connect bound

tls/ implements the server side of TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446). tls::server is a state machine that consumes transport bytes with receive() and produces them into output(), with x25519, P-256 or P-384 key exchange, ECDSA P-256 or P-384 server authentication, optional client authentication, and AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. It has no pre-shared keys or early data. tls::context holds the certificate chain, private key and verification policy shared by a server's connections, tls::schedule and tls::transcript the key schedule and handshake hash, tls::record the protection of one direction, and tls/codec.hpp the presentation language reader and writer. tls::stream (tls/stream.hpp) is the TLS socket. It takes ownership of the connected io::socket and holds one tls::server per connection, constructed from the context. A read receives socket bytes into an input buffer of one record (record_header_size plus maximum_ciphertext), passes them to receive(), and returns the readable application bytes. A write protects at most one record (maximum_plaintext, 16 KiB) and sends output(). Records produced by reads (alerts and key updates) are sent in order with written records, and a closure of the transport without close_notify is reported as tls_stream_truncated (src/tls/stream.cpp). The client role is not implemented: do_upgrade() fails an outbound TLS socket with tls_alert_handshake_failure, so TLS is a server transport only. settings::tls_server::initialize_context() creates the tls::context, loads the certificate chain (cert_path, a P-256 or P-384 leaf) and PEM private key (key_path, with key_pass if set), and, when cert_auth is set, requires a verified client certificate (set_verify(true, true)), adding each certificate file of that directory as a verification anchor (add_anchors()). The context is applied to the secured bindings (safes, safe_port). On accept, do_upgrade() moves the TCP socket into a tls::stream and runs its server async_handshake(). Since get_tcp() returns either the clear or the TLS socket, the tcp_*, body_*, rpc_* and http_* operations run unchanged over TLS. A lazy stop sends close_notify (async_shutdown()) before closing the TCP layer (src/net/socket_stop.cpp).

HTTP is the HTTP/1.1 implementation of messages/http/ over the clear or TLS socket. A request is read with an http::parser<true, http::body>, which consumes the start line, each field, each chunk line and each trailer field once complete, and body data as it arrives, so the variant body of section 5.2 selects its reader from the Content-Type header. A response is written with an http::serializer<false, http::body>, each of whose buffer sets is written with io::async_write. Reads use a caller-owned http::flat_buffer whose residue carries pipelined bytes to the next read (src/net/socket_http.cpp). Limit Value Body maximum_request (parser.body_limit()) Header The lesser of maximum_request and maximum_http_header (16 KiB) (parser.header_limit()) A request with an unknown method fails with bad_method, since dispatch of verb::unknown is reserved for WebSocket. A WebSocket upgrade request is returned to the channel with error::upgrade rather than dispatched (section 6.5). On a JSON-RPC port, detect() decides between HTTP and raw TCP from the first bytes without consuming them. Empty lines preceding a request line are skipped, and a first byte of { or [ (neither a valid method token character) latches the socket as downgraded(), after which it reads and writes newline terminated JSON-RPC as in section 6.2. Detection reads only when the buffer holds nothing but line breaks. The http_* operations read and write whole messages: http_read parses the header and body, and http_write serializes the response, its JSON body through the socket's retained buffer, which is reduced to minimum_buffer when the write completes. Batched JSON-RPC is read and written progressively instead, without materializing the batch: Operation Implementation http_read_header Parse into a caller-owned parser, completing when is_header_done() http_read_body Parse, completing when the body is done or the parse pauses http_read_some Parse, continuing a paused parse and completing once it progresses http_write_header http::serialize_header() written with io::async_write, once per message (chunked, no content length) rpc_write_chunk Each response part as chunk data (http::chunk_header(), the part, http::chunk_end), followed by http::last_chunk (0\r\n\r\n) after the part that closes the batch The JSON-RPC body reader pauses the parse at each element of a batch, which the socket reports as need_buffer. proxy (net/proxy.hpp) owns the parser across the message, delivers each element as a request carrying the message headers, absorbs the batch close, and stamps response parts with the batch state (src/net/proxy_actions.cpp). HTTP settings (settings::http_server) add the server name, permitted hosts and origins, and basic authorization credentials.

ws/ implements the server side of WebSocket (RFC 6455) over the clear or TLS socket, which remains the socket's transport. A socket becomes a WebSocket only by upgrade: http_read returns error::upgrade with the request, and the channel accepts it with accept_websocket(request) on the strand, which writes the handshake response and switches the socket to WebSocket framing (websocket()) (src/net/socket_ws.cpp, simplified): ws::response response{}; const auto ec = ws::accept(response, request.base()); response.set(http::field::server, BC_HTTP_SERVER_NAME); // bytes: the response, serialized. VARIANT_DISPATCH_FUNCTION(io::write, get_tcp(), io::buffer(bytes), error); if (error || ec) return error::operation_failed; ws_reader_.emplace(maximum_, true); websocket_.store(true); return error::success; ws::accept() (ws/handshake.hpp) validates a version 13 upgrade request and sets the response to switching protocols, or to an error status, so a refusal is an HTTP response and the socket remains HTTP. The handshake response carries a Server header of BC_HTTP_SERVER_NAME. ws::reader (ws/reader.hpp) assembles each data message from received frames, unmasking the payload into the caller's flat buffer as it arrives, validating text as UTF-8 and rejecting a message above maximum_request (message_too_big). It surfaces each ping, pong and close control frame once complete, and the socket logs each. A ping is answered with a pong (an unsent pong answers only the most recent ping), and a close from the peer is answered with its close code, after which the socket shuts down its send side and the read completes with websocket_closed. Frames are written unmasked with a header from ws::serialize_header() (ws/frame.hpp), from a queue in order, so control frames queue behind data frames. Operation WebSocket behavior ws_read One whole message into the flat buffer, in any number of frames, up to maximum_request ws_write One whole buffer as one message (a single frame with FIN set), text or binary http_read, rpc_read, body_read body_read of one whole message into the preselected body, with no HTTP header http_write, rpc_write, body_write body_write, each writer buffer one frame, the last finishing the message tcp_read Fails, since WebSocket reads frame messages, not sizes http_read_header, http_read_*, rpc_write_chunk Fail, since messages have no HTTP framing A body that spans several writer buffers is therefore delivered as one multi-frame message. Text is the default, and body_write takes the binary setting from the body's writer. JSON-RPC over WebSocket (btcd) is framed by the message and not newline terminated. A lazy stop sends a normal close frame (ws::close_code::normal), unless a close was already sent in answer to the peer, then closes TLS if present, then the TCP layer.

The v1 peer transport is the clear io::socket, read and written with the peer_* operations (src/net/socket_peer.cpp). Each message is a 24 byte heading (messages/peer/heading.hpp) followed by its payload: Field Size magic 4 command 12, null padded payload_size 4 checksum 4 peer_read makes exact reads into caller memory: first heading::size() bytes into a fixed array, then payload_size bytes into the channel's payload buffer, each with io::async_read. Between the two, the peer::body reader (src/messages/peer/body.cpp) parses the heading and rejects it with invalid_magic if the magic is not the network identifier, and with oversized_payload if the size exceeds the frame's maximum. Once the payload is read, the checksum is verified only if validate_checksum is set (default false), and the payload is deserialized by its registered command (registry::to_any). The channel stamps each read frame with these parameters (channel_peer::create_frame()): Frame field Source magic settings::identifier version The negotiated protocol version checksum settings::validate_checksum maximum maximum_request of the session's tcp_server settings The channel reduces its payload buffer to minimum_buffer after a read once the node is current. peer_write passes the frame to body_write, and the body writer serializes the whole v1 frame (registry::to_frame) into one buffer. On an inbound socket with a P2PS context, the first bytes have already been read to detect the peer's transport (section 6.7). For a v1 peer they are retained in the socket's detection buffer and drained into the first heading read.

p2ps::stream implements the BIP324 (v2) encrypted peer transport, with p2ps::cipher holding the ephemeral ElligatorSwift keypair, the directional ciphers and the session identifier. An inbound socket detects a v1 peer from the magic and command prefix (detected_v1()), and otherwise upgrades to the stream. The context (p2ps::context) holds only the network magic, which keys the v2 key derivation salt and the v1 detection prefix. It is applied to peer sockets when the node provides the encryption service (net::privacy_), to inbound, SAM and outbound sockets alike (src/net.cpp). Side Handshake (src/p2ps/stream.cpp) Detection (inbound) Read 16 bytes (detection_size, magic and command); a v1 peer matches the magic, version and five null bytes Responder The 16 bytes begin the peer's key, the balance is read, then the own key is sent ahead of the terminator Initiator Send the own key, read the peer's Both Derive the ciphers, send the garbage terminator and a version packet, scan for the peer's terminator within the garbage allowance, read version packets, skipping decoys The first packet received authenticates the peer's garbage as associated data, and bytes read past the terminator are replayed into the packet reads. After the handshake the stream is message oriented: async_read_message reads the 3 byte encrypted length, rejects a length above the lesser of the cipher's content maximum and maximum_request plus the 13 byte message type, reads the packet into the caller's buffer, decrypts it in place, and skips decoy packets. The message type is one byte: a nonzero short identifier, or zero followed by a 12 byte null padded command. async_write_message writes one message as one encrypted packet, using the registry's short identifier or its command. peer_read and peer_write select the stream when encrypted(). The payload span from the stream is passed directly to the peer::body reader's identified overload, which synthesizes the v1 heading for the channel (section 5.2).

zmtp::stream implements ZMTP 3.1 framing over a TCP socket: the greeting, the NULL or CURVE mechanism handshake, and one frame per read. Under CurveZMQ (ZMTPS) (zmtp::cipher), each frame is boxed into a MESSAGE command, so the layers above see the same frames. CurveZMQ (ZMTPS) is implemented for the server role only. zmtp::context holds the server keypair and the authorized client keys (any client if none). zmtp::role (zmtp/role.hpp) is the socket type a server channel advertises, which fixes the admitted peer types and the grammar of reads and writes: Role Socket type Admits publisher PUB SUB, XSUB puller PULL PUSH replier REP REQ, DEALER router ROUTER REQ, DEALER, ROUTER The handshake (src/zmtp/stream.cpp) sends the 64 byte greeting at once, then reads the peer's in two stages: the signature and major version (11 bytes), which must be 0xff, a tenth byte with its low bit set, and major version 3 or above, then the balance. The peer's mechanism must match the context's, and under CurveZMQ (ZMTPS) the peer must be the client. Mechanism Commands after the greeting NULL Send READY with Socket-Type, read the peer's READY CurveZMQ (ZMTPS) Read HELLO, send WELCOME, read INITIATE, authorize the client key, send READY The peer's Socket-Type must be admitted by the role, and its Identity property, if any, is retained. A refusal sends a best-effort ERROR command (400 for an unauthorized client). Handshake frames are limited to 8 KiB. A frame is a flags byte (MORE, LONG, COMMAND), a one byte length or, with LONG, an eight byte big-endian length, and the body. async_read_frame reads these with three exact reads into a caller-owned frame, failing a body above the caller's maximum (maximum_request) before reading it. async_write writes a caller-framed buffer. There are no public zmtp_* operations: rpc_read, rpc_write and rpc_notify select ZMTP when zeromq() (src/net/socket_rpc.cpp), and translate frames to and from JSON-RPC messages by role (src/net/socket_zmtp.cpp): A read collects parts until one without MORE, up to 32 parts. A command frame must be a whole message: PING and PONG become ping and pong, and for a publisher SUBSCRIBE and CANCEL become subscribe. A publisher also accepts a single part subscription prefixed 0x01 or 0x00. A puller reads a method part and one part per positional parameter. A replier requires the empty delimiter part and sets a null id. A router accepts an optional delimiter and sets the id to the peer's Identity. A response (replier, router) is the delimiter, then the result part or the error code and message parts. A notification is written by a publisher, or by a router behind an empty delimiter; PING and PONG are written in every role. Parameters are positional, one part each: integers little-endian, booleans one byte, strings as bytes, and shared chunks and streamable values written in place. Named parameters are not serializable. The parts of a message are framed into one allocation and written with one async_write. settings::zmtp_server applies the NULL context to the clear bindings and the CurveZMQ (ZMTPS) context, from the Z85 server secret key and the authorized client certs, to the secured bindings.

connector_socks (net/connector_socks.hpp) creates outbound connections through a SOCKS5 proxy (RFC 1928), with optional username and password authentication (RFC 1929). When settings::socks5::proxied(), the TCP connection is made to the proxy endpoint, and the socket is constructed as proxied, so its transport handshake is deferred until the proxy has connected the peer (src/net/connector_socks.cpp). The negotiation is a sequence of tcp_write and tcp_read calls on the socket's strand: Step Write Read Method Version 5, one method: none (0x00), or username/password (0x02) if credentials are set Version and the same method, else socks_method Authentication Version 1, username and password, each length prefixed and at most 255 bytes Version 1 and success, else socks_authentication Connect Version 5, CONNECT, reserved, then the target address and big-endian port Version, reply code, reserved, address type Bound address IPv4, IPv6 or length prefixed name, and port (discarded) The target is sent as an IPv4 or IPv6 address when the peer address is one, and otherwise by name (from the address or the endpoint host) for resolution at the proxy. Each nonzero reply code maps to its own error (socks_failure through socks_unsupported_address). On success the connector calls socket::handshake(), which applies the socket's context to the peer connection (for example P2PS), and the result is posted back to the connector's strand. settings::socks5 (username, password, socks) is part of the outbound and manual peer settings.

acceptor_sam (net/acceptor_sam.hpp) accepts inbound peers forwarded by an I2P SAM bridge (SAM v3). It listens on an ephemeral loopback port, and on accept, if no forwarding is established, establishes it over two control connections to the bridge (src/net/acceptor_sam.cpp): Connection Requests Session HELLO VERSION (3.1, or 3.2 with USER and PASSWORD when credentials are set), then SESSION CREATE STYLE=STREAM with a random session id and the stored destination key, or a transient ed25519 destination Forward HELLO VERSION, then STREAM FORWARD of the session to the loopback listener's port Requests are written with tcp_write. Replies are newline terminated lines, read one byte at a time with tcp_read (bytes after a line belong to the peer), bounded at 64 KiB, tokenized with quoted values, and mapped from RESULT to sam_* errors. A transient destination returned by the bridge is saved to key_path, so the address is retained across sessions. Both control sockets are watched, and if the bridge closes either, the session is torn down and recreated on the next accept. Each forwarded stream arrives on the loopback listener, prefixed by the peer's destination line. The acceptor is proxied, so the socket's handshake waits until the acceptor has read that line, decoded the destination (I2P base64 alphabet), and set the socket address to the SHA256 of the destination with port zero (set_address). It then calls socket::handshake(), which applies the P2PS context when configured, including v1 detection. settings::sam (username, password, bridge, key_path) is part of the inbound peer settings.

An acceptor (net/acceptor.hpp) creates inbound sockets. start() opens, binds and listens on a local endpoint, with address reuse, and an IPv6 listener is IPv6 only. accept() accepts the next connection and hands its socket to the session, which must call accept() again for the next one. Accepts are serialized on the acceptor's strand, and stop() cancels a pending accept. A TLS, P2PS or ZMTP acceptor creates its sockets with the transport context of its binding, and the socket upgrades on accept. The SAM acceptor (net/acceptor_sam.hpp) instead accepts the streams that an I2P bridge forwards to a loopback listener, reading the peer's destination from the line that prefixes each stream (see I2P SAM).

A connector (net/connector.hpp) creates outbound sockets. connect() takes an address from the pool (outbound session) or an endpoint from the configuration (seed and manual sessions), resolves a host name, and connects the socket. The connection races a deadline (race_speed of two): the first of the connect and the connect_timeout timer to complete wins, and the loser is cancelled, so a connect attempt cannot outlive its timeout. The SOCKS5 connector (net/connector_socks.hpp) derives from it, connecting to the proxy and negotiating the connection to the target before the socket upgrades (see SOCKS5). Sessions create their acceptors and connectors through the network (net::create_acceptor(), create_acceptor_sam(), create_connector(), create_connectors()), so a derived network can substitute its own. The outbound session creates a batch of connectors per attempt and races them, keeping the first successful connection.

settings (settings.hpp) holds the transport and peer settings common to all sessions (threads, timeouts, rate limit, black and white lists, protocol levels and feature flags, user agent, hosts file path) and one options struct per peer session. The option structs form a hierarchy: Struct Adds tcp_server Bindings, connection limit, inactivity and expiration, buffer and request sizes, backlog, rate limit secure_server Secure bindings (safes), clear and secure transport contexts tls_server Key and certificate paths, and the tls::context zmtp_server CURVE key and authorized client keys http_server Server name, allowed hosts and origins, credentials websocket_server As http_server peer_manual, peer_outbound, peer_inbound Manual peers, seeds and batch size, loopback and self addresses; SOCKS5 or SAM The config types (config/) parse and print settings values: Type Value authority IP address and port, with CIDR subnet; a zero port matches any port endpoint Scheme, host and port, where the host may be a DNS name address An address item with timestamp and services, the hosts file line format credential username:password[:method[,method]...] for HTTP basic authorization

logger (log/logger.hpp) is thread safe. write(level) returns a streaming writer that commits its message when destroyed, and fire(event) records an event and value. Messages and events are delivered to subscribers on the logger's own single-thread, low-priority threadpool. Objects derive from reporter, which holds the logger. Levels (log/levels.hpp) are news, session, protocol, proxy, remote, fault, quitting, objects and verbose, each with a macro (LOGN, LOGS, LOGP, LOGX, LOGR, LOGF, LOGQ, LOGO, LOGV) that compiles away unless its level is enabled at build time. tracker<Class> counts live instances at the objects level, and capture reads console input lines for subscribers.

Companion to 06-sessions-and-protocols and 07-header-protocols. Block-out is the block-serving side: respond to peer requests (get_blocks, get_data) with inventory / block bodies, and announce newly-confirmed blocks via inv so peers know to come ask. Four levels: 106 (protocol_block_out_106) — full implementation: serves get_blocks/get_data, announces new blocks via inv; an unservable request stops the channel. 70001 (protocol_block_out_70001) — BIP37: unservable items are accumulated and reported with one not_found instead of a stop. 70012 (protocol_block_out_70012) — suppresses inv-based announcement when the peer has opted into sendheaders (BIP130). 70014 (protocol_block_out_70014) — BIP152: serves compact blocks for compact get_data items and getblocktxn. File Lines Role src/protocols/protocol_block_out_106.cpp 313 Block serving + inv announcement; stop on unservable src/protocols/protocol_block_out_70001.cpp 74 not_found accumulation src/protocols/protocol_block_out_70012.cpp 75 sendheaders handler → sets superseded_ src/protocols/protocol_block_out_70014.cpp 140 compact block and getblocktxn serving

Invariant (BlockOut-Inherit-1). Each level is a strict superset of the one below. All 106 behaviour remains in effect; higher levels only change the unservable report, the announcement gate, and add compact serving.

// :46-66 void start() { subscribe_chase(...); SUBSCRIBE_CHANNEL(get_data, ...); SUBSCRIBE_CHANNEL(get_blocks, ...); protocol_peer::start(); } void stopping(ec) { unsubscribe_chase(); protocol_peer::stopping(ec); } The protocol does three things: Listens for chase::block from the bus → emit inv to peer. Listens for get_blocks from peer → reply with inv. Listens for get_data from peer → start a streaming send of blocks.

// :102-124 bool do_announce(header_t link) { const auto hash = archive().get_header_key(link); if (was_announced(hash)) return true; // anti-echo if (hash == null_hash) return true; // store inconsistency; logged only NOTIFY(inventory{ { { type_id::block, hash } } }, handle_send, _1); return true; } Invariant (BlockOut-Announce-1). A block is announced only if (a) it wasn't received from this peer (was_announced false), and (b) get_header_key(link) returned a non-null hash. Anti-echo discipline matches the header and tx out protocols. Invariant (BlockOut-Announce-2). Announcement is via a single inv containing { type_id::block, hash }. The peer then sends get_data to retrieve the block body if it wants it.

// :129-141, :294-306 inventory create_inventory(const get_blocks& locator) { if (!is_current_chain(true)) return {}; return inventory::factory(archive().get_blocks(start_hashes, stop_hash, max_get_blocks), type_id::block); } Invariant (BlockOut-Serve-1). Like header-out, block-out is gated on is_current_chain(true) — non-current nodes reply empty.
2.4 Inbound get_data (peer asks for block bodies)

// :146-166 bool handle_receive_get_data(ec, message) { if (!node_witness_ && message->any_witness()) { stop(protocol_violation); return false; } // A if (is_zero(message->count(blocks))) return true; send_block(error::success, zero, message, gate()); return true; } The old per-channel backlog and allow_overlapped setting are gone: each get_data starts its own send loop over the message's items, and the channel's gate (gate(), a libbitcoin-network read gate held across the out-of-line work) serialises outbound messages so concurrent requests cannot interleave or run unbounded.

// :171-234 void send_block(ec, index, message, gate) { if (stopped(ec)) return; // drain unservable items, skipping non-block inventory for (; index < items.size(); ++index) { if (!item.is_block()) continue; if (item.is_witness_type() && !node_witness_) { stop(protocol_violation); return; } link = query.to_header(item.hash); if (is_servable(item.hash, link)) break; if (!handle_unservable(item)) return; // 106: stop(not_found); 70001: accumulate } if (report_unservable(index, message, gate)) return; // 70001: SEND(not_found) then resume here if (index >= items.size()) return; block out{ { query.get_wire_block(link, witness), witness } }; if (!out.block.is_valid()) { if (handle_unservable(item)) report_unservable(add1(index), ...); return; } span<microseconds>(events::block_usecs, start); SEND(std::move(out), send_block, _1, add1(index), message, gate); } The continuation is send_block itself: each completed SEND triggers the next item. The loop terminates when the items are exhausted or on error / stop. Invariant (BlockOut-Stream-1). At any time, at most one SEND(block, ...) is in flight per request; the next is started only from the previous's completion callback. This is the natural back-pressure: a slow peer slows the send rate. Invariant (BlockOut-Servable-1). A block is servable iff its hash resolves to a stored header, it is associated, and it is not a pruned bypass block on a limited node (is_servable, :237-267). An unservable item at 106 stops the channel with not_found ("this block could not have been advertised to the peer", :270-280); at 70001 and above it is reported.

Two separate witness-gating sites: handle_receive_get_data (request-time) and send_block (per item). node_witness_ = node.provide_witness (protocol_block_out_106.hpp:39). Invariant (BlockOut-Witness-1). A node that does not provide witness drops any peer that requests witness data, at either the batch level or the per-item level. There is no path that serves non-witness data in response to a witness request.

handle_unservable accumulates the item instead of stopping (:41-51, when enable_not_found_), and report_unservable sends the accumulated run as one not_found message whose completion resumes send_block at the next index (:55-68). Invariant (BlockOut-NotFound-1). Unservable items are answered in request order, as a run preceding the next servable block, and nothing is produced until the prior write completes.

// :39-48 start: SUBSCRIBE_CHANNEL(send_headers, ...) // :53-63 handle_receive_send_headers: superseded_ = true; return false (one-shot) // :66-69 superseded(): return superseded_ The base handle_chase checks superseded() first (protocol_block_out_106.cpp:75-76): once true, the very next chase::block makes handle_chase return false, and the bus desubscriber removes this protocol from the event list. Invariant (BlockOut-Supersede-1). After the peer sends sendheaders, this protocol no longer emits inv-based block announcements. Header-based (or compact) announcement via protocol_header_out_70012/70014 takes over. Invariant (BlockOut-Supersede-2). Supersede is one-way: once true, never reset. superseded_ is a std::atomic_bool because the base reads it from its bus handler on the node strand while the derived class writes it from its channel handler.

handle_receive_get_data (:56-86) runs the base loop for block items, then answers every compact / witness_compact item that is servable with a compact block from make_compact_block (doc 06 §3.2). handle_receive_get_compact_transactions (:91-134) answers getblocktxn with the requested txs by differentially encoded index; an index past the block's tx count is a protocol violation, a missing tx body is a protocol2 fault.

Anti-echo (BlockOut-Announce-1). One in-flight send per request (BlockOut-Stream-1). Servability (BlockOut-Servable-1): only associated, unpruned blocks are served. Supersede monotone (BlockOut-Supersede-2).

The send loop drains the request as long as the peer accepts data and the store yields block bodies. Stop is non-blocking; an in-flight send completes through the channel's stop machinery (libbitcoin-network).

The protocol is strand-confined except for the superseded_ atomic. Single-threaded reasoning suffices per channel. The combined "announce via compact block OR headers OR inv, never more than one" property needs joint reasoning across protocol_block_out_70012, protocol_header_out_70012 and protocol_header_out_70014: they consume the same chase::block event, and the supersede flag plus the header-out fallback chain ensure at most one announcement per block per channel. A peer's behaviour (deciding to send sendheaders/sendcmpct, when to issue get_data, etc.) is an oracle in the model.
