A device (stream/device.hpp) declares a category from the ios tags. The category decides how make_stream buffers it: Device Container Category Behavior copy_source data_reference input_seekable, direct_tag Reads in place from the buffer copy_sink data_slab output_seekable, direct_tag Writes in place to the buffer flip_sink data_slab seekable, direct_tag Reads and writes in place at one position push_sink std::string, data_chunk sink_tag, optimally_buffered_tag Appends to the container through a buffer A direct device exposes its memory as a sequence of two character pointers. push_sink is indirect: it receives writes through do_write and sizes its buffer from the container's unused capacity, or 1024 bytes if there is none (stream/devices/push_sink.hpp): void do_write(const typename device<Container>::value_type* from, typename device<Container>::size_type size) NOEXCEPT override { container_.insert(container_.cend(), from, std::next(from, size)); }

make_stream<Device> (stream/make_stream.hpp) derives from std::istream, std::ostream or std::iostream according to the device category, and installs a device_buffer<Device>, a std::streambuf implemented in the module. For a direct input or output device the buffer's get or put area is the device's own sequence, so no copy is made between device and stream. An input/output device shares one position for reading and writing and is unbuffered. An indirect device is output only, and is buffered by optimal_buffer_size() and flushed on sync and on destruction. template <typename Device> using device_stream = std::conditional_t<device_buffer<Device>::input, std::conditional_t<device_buffer<Device>::output, std::iostream, std::istream>, std::ostream>;

system::istream<>, system::ostream<> and system::iostream<> (stream/iostream/) are not standard streams. Each holds three byte pointers and a one-byte state, and implements only the subset of the standard stream interface that the streamers use: rdstate, setstate, clear, tellg/tellp, seekg, peek, read, write and flush. The streamers are templates over the stream type, so the same streamer code compiles against either. A read is a bounds check and a std::copy_n (impl/stream/iostream/istream.ipp): auto bytes = possible_narrow_sign_cast<size_t>(count); if (is_overflow(bytes)) { if (state_ != goodbit) return; // Allow read to end if state was good (std::istream behavior). bytes = end_ - position_; setstate(badbit); } std::copy_n(position_, bytes, data); position_ += bytes; These are the fast aliases, and the ones chain types use internally. Fast streams are used extensively in libbitcoin. They are significantly faster than the standard streams, yet provide the same simplifying abstractions. They are generally passed through the reader and writer interfaces, which accept standard streams as well, so a function written against the interfaces serves either (see Streamers).

make_streamer<Device, Base> (stream/make_streamer.hpp) owns a make_stream<Device> and a streamer over it in one object, so a copy or push streamer is constructed from the container alone. The stream is held in a private base, stream_owner, so that it is destroyed after the streamer, whose destructor flushes into it.

No streamer operation throws; all are NOEXCEPT. A reader or writer is valid while its stream state is goodbit. Any failure sets all of eofbit, failbit and badbit, so that a state some standard streams treat as recoverable cannot be cleared by a later operation (impl/stream/streamers/byte_reader.ipp): template <typename IStream> void byte_reader<IStream>::invalid() NOEXCEPT { // If eofbit is set, failbit is generally set on all operations. // badbit is unrecoverable, set the others to ensure consistency. stream_->setstate(IStream::eofbit | IStream::failbit | IStream::badbit); } validate() calls invalid() after each stream operation that left any flag set. Exceptions from tellg and seekg on a standard stream are caught and converted to invalidation. Callers test the reader once, at the end, through operator bool. Reads past the end of an invalid reader return padded or empty values: integers and arrays are zero filled, and read_bytes, read_bytes_cptr and read_string return empty or null without allocating. set_position clears the invalid state before seeking.

A reader carries a remaining_ limit, unbounded by default. set_limit(size) bounds reads to the next size bytes, and a read, skip or peek beyond it invalidates the reader without reading from the stream. read_size(limit) reads a variable integer and invalidates if it exceeds limit, returning zero, so its result can be passed to a following read before the reader is tested. read_variable invalidates on a non-minimal encoding.

Chain types construct from a reader&. This includes block, header, transaction, input, output, point, outpoint, script, operation and witness (chain/). Constructors from a data_slice, a stream::in::fast or a std::istream wrap it in a reader and delegate (src/chain/transaction.cpp): transaction::transaction(const data_slice& data, bool witness) NOEXCEPT : transaction(stream::in::fast(data), witness) { } transaction::transaction(stream::in::fast& stream, bool witness) NOEXCEPT : transaction(read::bytes::fast(stream), witness) { } transaction::transaction(std::istream& stream, bool witness) NOEXCEPT : transaction(read::bytes::istream(stream), witness) { } from_data(reader&) reads fields in sequence without testing for errors between them, and passes the reader, converted to bool, as the object's validity. A superfluous witness invalidates the reader explicitly with source.invalidate().

Serialization takes a writer&. to_data(bool) sizes a data_chunk from serialized_size, and writes into it through a fast stream, so the buffer is allocated once. Hashing uses the same to_data(writer&) against a hash writer, so the serialized bytes are never materialized (src/chain/header.cpp): stream::out::fast stream{ digest }; hash::sha256x2::fast sink{ stream }; to_data(sink); sink.flush(); return digest; sha256x2_writer overrides do_write_bytes to feed its accumulator, and on flush writes the double SHA-256 digest through the base writer to the underlying stream, here the 32-byte digest.

Streamers are the typed read and write layer of the stream module. A streamer wraps a stream and reads or writes Bitcoin's serialized forms: little and big endian integers, variable length integers, hashes, byte vectors and strings. Every chain type serializes and deserializes through them. Paths are relative to include/bitcoin/system/ in libbitcoin-system, at master 0cd57fcf (2026-10-27).

The streamers implement three abstract interfaces (stream/streamers/interfaces/), with short aliases (stream/streamers.hpp): using flipper = byteflipper; using reader = bytereader; using writer = bytewriter; The chain types take these interfaces, reader& to deserialize and writer& to serialize, so a chain type is independent of the streamer and of the stream beneath it. The same to_data(writer&) writes to a std::ostream, to a fast stream over a byte buffer, or into a hash. Group reader writer Integers read_2_bytes_little_endian to read_8_bytes_little_endian, big endian forms, read_byte, peek_byte The corresponding write_* Variable integers read_variable, read_size(limit) write_variable Hashes read_mini_hash, read_short_hash, read_hash, read_long_hash, and shared pointer forms write_bytes Bytes read_bytes() (remaining), read_bytes(size), into a buffer, and shared pointer forms write_bytes Strings read_string(limit), read_string_buffer(size), read_line write_string, write_string_buffer, write_line Control skip_bytes, rewind_bytes, get_read_position, set_position, set_limit, is_exhausted, invalidate flush, get_write_position State operator bool operator bool A failed read or write invalidates the streamer, and every later operation is a no-op that returns a zero or empty value. A deserializer reads its whole object and tests the streamer once at the end (see Stream).

Each streamer is a class template over its stream type (stream/streamers/): Streamer Reads or writes byte_reader, byte_writer Bytes byte_flipper Bytes, read and write over one iostream bit_reader, bit_writer, bit_flipper Bit fields hex_reader, hex_writer Base16 text on the stream, bytes at the interface sha256_writer Bytes into a SHA-256 hash, written to the stream on flush sha256x2_writer Bytes into a double SHA-256 (Bitcoin) hash sha256t_writer<Tag> Bytes into a tagged SHA-256 hash

The combinations of streamer and stream are named by namespace in stream/streamers.hpp, for each direction and form: read::bytes, read::bits, read::base16, write::bytes, write::bits, write::base16, and hash::sha256, hash::sha256x2, hash::sha256t. Within each: Alias Stream istream, ostream A std::istream or std::ostream fast A fast system::istream<> or system::ostream<> copy A standard stream over a copy device on a buffer, by make_streamer push, text, data A standard stream that inserts into a container, a std::string or a data_chunk A chain type constructed from bytes wraps them in a fast stream and a fast reader (src/chain/transaction.cpp): transaction::transaction(const data_slice& data, bool witness) NOEXCEPT : transaction(stream::in::fast(data), witness) { } transaction::transaction(stream::in::fast&& stream, bool witness) NOEXCEPT : transaction(read::bytes::fast(stream), witness) { }

A hash writer is a writer, so any object that serializes can be hashed by serializing it into one. The serialization is never materialized: each write is absorbed into the hash, and flush writes the digest to the underlying stream. A header's hash is computed by serializing the header into a double SHA-256 writer over a fast stream on the digest (src/chain/header.cpp): hash_digest header::hash() const NOEXCEPT { if (hash_) return *hash_; hash_digest digest; stream::out::fast stream{ digest }; hash::sha256x2::fast sink{ stream }; to_data(sink); sink.flush(); return digest; } Transaction identifiers and signature hashes are computed the same way.

The unicode module makes UTF-8 the one string encoding of the library and of the applications built on it, on every platform. On Windows it converts at the process boundary, so portable code written against char and std::string compiles and behaves the same there as elsewhere. It also carries its own Unicode tables, with its normalization tables extracted from Python's unicodedata, so that passphrase normalization in wallet operations matches Python wallets such as Electrum exactly. Paths are relative to include/bitcoin/system/ in libbitcoin-system, at master 0cd57fcf (2026-10-27). Windows APIs accept UTF-16 (wchar_t) for text, not UTF-8. The library follows the UTF-8 Everywhere design: char holds UTF-8 throughout, and wide characters exist only at the edge, where the process meets the operating system. On other platforms the same names resolve to the standard facilities, so application code has no platform branches.

An application declares BC_USE_LIBBITCOIN_MAIN and implements bc::system::main as it would main, with UTF-8 argv. On Windows the macro defines wmain and forwards (unicode/utf8_everywhere/environment.hpp): int wmain(int argc, wchar_t* argv[]) { return libbitcoin::system::call_utf8_main(argc, argv, &libbitcoin::system::main); } call_utf8_main sets the global locale to UTF-8 for character conversion only, keeping numeric formatting classic, then converts _wenviron and argv to UTF-8 buffers, replaces environ for the duration of the call, and restores it afterward: std::locale::global(std::locale(std::locale::classic(), std::locale(utf8_locale_name), std::locale::ctype)); std::setlocale(LC_NUMERIC, "C"); auto backup = environ; auto environment = allocate_environment(_wenviron); On other platforms the macro defines main and forwards directly.

The macro also defines bc::system::cin, cout and cerr, used in place of the std streams. On Windows these are unicode_istream and unicode_ostream objects over std::wcin, std::wcout and std::wcerr; elsewhere they are references to std::cin, std::cout and std::cerr (unicode/utf8_everywhere/stdio.hpp). Component Windows behavior unicode_streambuf Translates UTF-8 narrow buffers to and from the wrapped wide std::wstreambuf, carrying a partial UTF-8 character on output to the next flush console_streambuf Sets the console input and output code pages to CP_UTF8, and replaces the std::wcin buffer with one that reads through ReadConsoleW set_utf8_stdio Sets stdin, stdout and stderr to _O_U8TEXT mode set_binary_stdin, set_binary_stdout Set the descriptor to _O_BINARY mode Console setup is performed once per process, and is skipped for a process with no attached console, such as a service. On other platforms these are no-ops, except set_console_echo and unset_console_echo, which use termios. Do not use std::cin, std::cout or std::cerr once the console streams are substituted. On Windows set_utf8_stdio puts the standard descriptors in _O_U8TEXT mode, which cannot be undone. In that mode the C runtime does not support narrow character I/O on those descriptors, so std::cin, std::cout, std::cerr and printf fault (an assertion in debug builds). All console I/O must go through bc::system::cin, cout and cerr (or cin_stream(), cout_stream(), cerr_stream()). The fault is Windows-only, so code that mixes the two can pass on other platforms and fail only there.

std::filesystem::path constructs from a narrow string using the ANSI code page on Windows. to_path and from_path construct and extract through std::u8string instead (unicode/utf8_everywhere/paths.hpp): std::filesystem::path to_path(const std::string& value) NOEXCEPT { return { cast_to_u8string(value) }; } extended_path fully qualifies a path and, on Windows, prefixes \\?\ when its length reaches MAX_PATH; elsewhere it returns the path unchanged. bc::system::ifstream and ofstream open through extended_path, so a long path works on every platform. module_path returns the executable path from GetModuleFileNameW, /proc/self/exe, or _NSGetExecutablePath, and default_config_path resolves under the common application data folder on Windows or SYSCONFDIR elsewhere.

unicode/conversion.hpp converts between UTF-8 (std::string), UTF-16 (std::wstring) and UTF-32 (std::u32string), for single strings and lists. One decoder and one encoder, selected by character size, implement all six directions. Conversion is strict: a truncated or overlong sequence, an unpaired surrogate, or a value above U+10FFFF yields an empty result, with no replacement or skipping. // Empty if any sequence is invalid (no replacement or skipping). template <typename CharOut, typename CharIn> static std::basic_string<CharOut> to_utf( const std::basic_string<CharIn>& in) NOEXCEPT The implementation uses neither std::codecvt nor a platform API. UTF-32 is the working form for character-level operations, since each char32_t holds one code point.

unicode/normalization.hpp provides the four Unicode normal forms, case conversion, and the character operations that wallet seed derivation requires. Function Operation to_canonical_composition NFC to_canonical_decomposition NFD to_compatibility_composition NFKC to_compatibility_decomposition NFKD to_lower, to_upper Full case folding (lower), simple 1:1 mapping (upper) to_non_combining_form Remove characters of nonzero canonical combining class to_non_diacritic_form Remove characters with the Unicode Diacritic property to_compressed_form Collapse ASCII whitespace, remove an ASCII space between CJK characters is_combining, is_diacritic, is_chinese_japanese_or_korean, is_whitespace, is_separator Character tests

A normal form decomposes each code point recursively through a two-level trie, applies canonical ordering (a stable sort of each combining run by combining class), and for NFC and NFKC recomposes through a sorted pair table. Hangul syllables decompose and compose algorithmically. Pure ASCII input is returned unchanged, and ASCII case conversion takes a direct path. static void normal_form(std::string& value, bool compatible, bool recompose) NOEXCEPT { const auto points = to_utf32(value); std::u32string out{}; out.reserve(points.size() * two); for (const auto point: points) decompose_one(out, point, compatible); canonical_order(out); if (recompose) compose(out); value = to_utf8(out); }

The library carries its own tables so that normalization gives the same result on every platform and matches the Python wallets it must interoperate with. The tables are extracted from Python's unicodedata, the same source Electrum normalizes with, which in turn extracts them from the Unicode Consortium's publications (the Unicode Character Database). A wallet passphrase is normalized before it is hashed into the seed, so the seed depends on the normalization as well as on the passphrase. Unicode normalization is a very large standard that changes with each Unicode version, so this dependency is inherently fragile: a passphrase outside ASCII can normalize differently under a different version of the data, or in a different implementation, and so derive a different seed, and with it different keys. Our approach is to align as closely as possible with early Electrum, the original seed phrase implementation, and to keep the tables fixed. If the Unicode standard or its use by Electrum, or by other wallets and tools, changes the result for a passphrase, that is an inherent break, one that the standards and their implementations themselves do not address. A passphrase of ASCII characters only is unaffected.

Caller Normalization Standard Matches bx commands wallet/mnemonics/electrum seeder Passphrase: NFKD, to_lower, to_non_combining_form, to_compressed_form; words: to_non_combining_form, to_compressed_form Electrum seed version system Electrum electrum-to-seed, electrum-new wallet/mnemonics/electrum validator Words: to_non_combining_form, to_compressed_form Electrum seed version system Electrum electrum-decode wallet/mnemonics/mnemonic seeder Passphrase: NFKD BIP39 BIP39 wallets (reference: python-mnemonic) mnemonic-to-seed words/languages Dictionary matching: NFKD and to_lower; Japanese joins with the ideographic space BIP39 word lists BIP39 wallets mnemonic-decode, mnemonic-to-seed, electrum-decode, electrum-new wallet/keys/encrypted_keys Passphrase: NFC BIP38 BIP38 wallets ec-to-ek, ek-to-ec, ek-to-address, ek-public-to-ec, ek-public-to-address, token-new The Electrum seeder follows Electrum's normalize_text step by step, each call annotated with the Python line it reproduces: // seed = unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', seed) // seed = seed.lower() to_compatibility_decomposition(phrase); to_lower(phrase); Electrum removes characters for which unicodedata.combining is nonzero, so to_non_combining_form tests the canonical combining class from Python's own database, not the Diacritic property, and the CJK intervals are Electrum's rather than a Unicode block list.

The wallet module of libbitcoin-system implements the standards that wallets share: keys and their encodings, addresses, mnemonics, message signing, partially signed transactions, output descriptors, compact block filters and silent payment scanning. It is a library of value types and functions. It holds no keys and opens no files or connections, and the caller supplies all entropy. Paths are relative to include/bitcoin/system/ in libbitcoin-system, at master 0cd57fcf (2026-10-27).

libbitcoin does not provide seed entropy. Every wallet class and function that creates a seed, key or mnemonic accepts its entropy from the caller. Software cannot provide entropy, and cannot ensure that it is provided by the compiler, operating system or hardware beneath it, so the library leaves its source to the application and to the user. The maybe_random function in crypto/ is named for this uncertainty, and is used only for ephemeral values such as network session keys, never for wallet seeds (see Crypto).

wallet/wallet.hpp includes every header of the module. The types are in namespace wallet, except ec_scalar and ec_point (namespace system), PSBT (wallet::psbt), and the block filter functions of wallet/neutrino.hpp (namespace neutrino). The wallet types are values. Each is constructed from its text form, its binary form, or the values it derives from, and a failed construction produces an invalid instance rather than an exception. As with the chain types, an instance does not change after construction, other than by being replaced through move or assignment. The exceptions are the math types ec_scalar and ec_point, which are accumulators, with compound assignment operators (+=, -=, *=), and bitcoin_uri, which is built up by setters. The bool operator reports validity, and a failed operation on ec_point or ec_scalar returns an invalid or zero value. Most types are copyable and comparable, and payment_address has a std::hash specialization so it can key unordered containers.

Each type with a text form has an encoded() serializer, a constructor from std::string, and stream operators that use the two, so the text round-trips. The stream extraction operators of the key, address, URI and PSBT types throw on invalid text, for parsing text from a stream (ec_private, from src/wallet/keys/): std::istream& operator>>(std::istream& in, ec_private& to) { std::string value; in >> value; to = ec_private(value); if (!to) throw istream_exception(value); return in; } The encodings come from the radix module: base58 for WIF, extended keys and payment addresses, base16 for public keys, bech32 and bech32m for witness and silent payment addresses, and base64 for PSBT. Mnemonics round-trip as word sentences, bitcoin_uri as a BIP21 URI, and descriptor as its expression with checksum.

A key or address carries the prefixes of its network as values, not as a global setting. context collects one network's prefixes, and the contexts btc_mainnet, btc_testnet and btc_regtest are predefined, btc_mainnet the default argument where a context is taken (wallet/context.hpp): struct BC_API context { /// Extended (hd) private/public key prefixes. prefix::hds hd; /// Witness address prefix. std::string p2w; /// Pay to key hash address version byte. uint8_t p2kh; /// Pay to script hash address version byte. uint8_t p2sh; /// WIF (legacy private key) version byte. uint8_t wif; /// Silent payment address prefix. std::string sp; ec_private packs its WIF and address version bytes into one 16 bit versions value, and hd_private its private and public prefixes into one 64 bit prefixes value. The classes are designed to forward these network parameters through every derivation, so the network is given once, where the root value is constructed. A derived HD key keeps its parent's prefixes in its lineage, hd_private::to_public gives the corresponding public prefix, and ec_private produces its payment_address with its own address version: const hd_lineage lineage { lineage_.prefixes, add1(lineage_.depth), fingerprint(), index };

The wallet module implements standards, not algorithms. Hashing, elliptic curve operations, ciphers and encodings come from the modules below it, and word lists from the words module. Standard Primitives used BIP32 HMAC-SHA512, secp256k1 point and scalar addition BIP38 scrypt, AES-256 BIP39 PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 (2048 iterations), SHA-256 checksum, NFKD SLIP39 Shamir over GF(256), RS1024 checksum Message signing Double SHA-256, ECDSA public key recovery BIP352 Tagged SHA-256, secp256k1, bech32m BIP158 SipHash, Golomb-Rice coding A BIP32 master key is the HMAC-SHA512 of the seed under the specified key, split into secret and chain code (src/wallet/keys/hd_private.cpp): // This is a magic constant from BIP32. static const auto magic = to_chunk("Bitcoin seed"); const auto intermediate = split(hmac<sha512>::code(entropy, magic)); return { intermediate.first, intermediate.second, prefixes };

The mnemonic types derive from words::languages, which holds the entropy, the words and the dictionary language, and provides sentence(), words(), validity and the stream operators. Each type selects its dictionaries from the words catalogs. Type Standard Words Dictionaries Produces mnemonic BIP39 12 to 24, in multiples of 3 en, es, it, fr, cs, pt, ja, ko, zh_Hans, zh_Hant Seed, hd_private electrum_v1 Electrum v1 12 or 24 en, pt ec_private, ec_public electrum Electrum v2 12 to 46 en, es, it, fr, cs, pt, ja, ko, zh_Hans, zh_Hant Seed, hd_private slip39 SLIP39 20 or 33 per share en Master secret, hd_private An electrum seed has a prefix (standard, witness, and the two factor forms) that states its use, and construction from entropy can grind the entropy until the words carry the requested prefix. slip39::to_shares splits a master secret into groups of shares, and slip39::to_secret recovers it from a threshold of groups.

wallet/message.hpp implements the legacy Bitcoin message signature, the format of Bitcoin Core's signmessage and verifymessage, which predates segregated witness and identifies the signer by a P2PKH address only. It signs a message with an ec_private, WIF or secret, and verifies a signature against a payment_address. The signature is a compact ECDSA signature with a prefix byte that encodes the recovery id and key compression. The signed hash is the double SHA-256 of the prefix "Bitcoin Signed Message:\n", the message length and the message. psbt::transaction parses and serializes BIP174 (version 0) and BIP370 (version 2) transactions. Input and output maps are structs of typed fields, and fields the type does not interpret are kept as raw entry pairs, so they survive a round trip. Its methods are those of the PSBT roles that need no keys: Method Operation combine() Merge the fields of another copy of the same transaction join() Merge the inputs and outputs of another transaction finalize() Convert complete signature sets into final scripts extract() The network transaction, once all inputs are final fee(), locktime() Values computed from prevouts and lock time fields Finalization covers legacy and version 0 witness scripts. Taproot fields are parsed and preserved but not satisfied. descriptor parses a BIP380 expression in a given context and produces the output scripts at an index, or the scripts with their key origins as psbt::derivation records for signing. The supported functions are pk, pkh, wpkh, sh, wsh, multi, sortedmulti, combo, tr (key path), addr and raw. points_value::select chooses outpoints for a spend from a set of valued outpoints, either the smallest sufficient set (greedy) or the individually sufficient outputs (individual).

neutrino::compute_filter computes a block's BIP158 filter, from a chain::block or from a chain::view::block read in place, and compute_header chains the filter headers. match_filter tests a filter against scripts or payment addresses. silent_payment is a BIP352 receiver, constructed from a scan secret, a spend key and labels. The static members summarize a transaction's inputs (the input hash times the sum of its eligible input keys) and collect the summaries of a block's transactions as columns. scan() finds the outputs of a transaction that pay the receiver, with the tweak and label of each, and match() tests only for the first output to the receiver (k = 0). keys() exposes the receiver keys to the batch scanner (crypto/secp256k1/batch/scan.hpp).

How libbitcoin is tested: testability, kinds of test, reference vectors, continuous integration and coverage. How libbitcoin is tested: code built for testability, the kinds of test, the platforms each change is tested on, and how coverage is measured. The mechanics of writing a test are in Test practices.

Code is written to be tested through its own interface. There are no test hooks: no test-only branches, no conditional compilation for tests, and no access granted to tests that other callers do not have. Mocks and fakes are injected to alter and detect behavior: Mocks. A test derives a mock from the class under test, or from one it depends on, and overrides what it alters or detects (mock_channel_peer, mock_proxy, mock_settings). Fakes. A test substitutes a working implementation of a dependency, such as the in-memory chunk_storage fake for the store's memory-mapped files. Settings. Behavior that depends on configuration is driven by the settings object the code already takes.

Kind Scope Suite unit A method or function, isolated to the extent practical. C++, in each repository's test/ component A group of units, such as a class. C++, in each repository's test/ functional A feature group, such as client-server communication. C++, in each repository's test/ performance The speed of a unit or component. C++, in each repository's test/, disabled by default acceptance Each server interface, as a client uses it. Python, in libbitcoin-server's endpoints/, against a live node The C++ suites run in every CI job, except the performance tests, which are compiled only when HAVE_PERFORMANCE_TESTS is defined. The acceptance suite is customer acceptance: it exercises each interface of a running bs as its clients do, over its own protocols.
A test case tests one thing, and its name states that thing: the method, the condition and the expected result. A failing test is then a diagnosis.

Line coverage. A GCC debug job in each repository's CI (GitHub Actions) is built with --coverage, and its lcov output is reported to Coveralls, excluding the paths listed in the repository's coverage element of the build model. Constant time. In the expanded matrix, libbitcoin-system and libbitcoin-explorer each run their constant-time tests under valgrind, in GCC 14 and Clang 18 release builds on Linux x64 and arm64. Valgrind reports any branch or memory access that depends on secret data (Crypto). Fuzzing. libbitcoin-system is a module of bitcoinfuzz, a differential fuzzer that runs the same inputs through several Bitcoin implementations and reports where their results differ. Mutation testing. Coverage shows which code ran, not whether a test would fail if it were wrong. Mutation testing changes the code and checks that a test fails. libbitcoin-system is tested on MutantHub.

Building Bitcoin Server (bs) and Bitcoin Explorer (bx) on Linux, macOS and Windows: build options, toolchains, libbitcoin-build, platform coverage and build status. Bitcoin Server (bs) is built from libbitcoin-server and the four libraries it depends on: libbitcoin-system, libbitcoin-database, libbitcoin-network and libbitcoin-node. Bitcoin Explorer (bx) is built from libbitcoin-explorer and the two libraries it depends on: libbitcoin-system and libbitcoin-network. Each repository's install script builds and installs its libraries in order, ending with its own.

A C++20 compiler. The versions tested in CI are listed in Toolchains. Git, to fetch the libbitcoin sources. The build tools of the chosen build system: autotools or CMake on Linux and macOS, Visual Studio on Windows. The prerequisites of each platform are listed on its page (Linux, macOS, Windows). No other libraries need to be installed (see Build options).

With the prerequisites installed, on Linux or macOS, a static release build installed under ~/libbitcoin, optimized for the build machine: $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server $ cd libbitcoin-server $ ./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static --hardware-optimized The result is ~/libbitcoin/bin/bs. bx is built the same way from libbitcoin-explorer: $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-explorer $ cd libbitcoin-explorer $ ./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static --hardware-optimized The result is ~/libbitcoin/bin/bx. On Windows, see Windows.

By default bs and bx are built for the baseline instruction set of its architecture (AVX2 by default on Windows, which can be lowered). Options such as --enable-avx2 or --enable-shani make them faster on CPUs that have those instructions, and unable to run on CPUs that do not. --hardware-optimized enables all that the build machine supports, so its builds run only on CPUs with the same extensions. Run bs --hardware on the target machine to see what it supports, and see Build options.

Linux, macOS and Windows: prerequisites and steps for each platform. Build options: the install script options and the build options shared by all three build systems. Toolchains: autotools, CMake and Visual Studio, and the compilers tested in CI. Platform coverage: platforms, compilers and build systems compared with Bitcoin Core. libbitcoin-build: the generator behind the build files, for maintainers.

libbitcoin-build is a maintainer tool. Building bs does not require it: everything it produces is committed to each repository. It is needed only to change the build files themselves, such as adding a source file, a target, a dependency, a build option or a CI job.

Every libbitcoin repository is built by three build systems (autotools, CMake and Visual Studio), tested by the same CI matrix, and installed by the same scripts. libbitcoin-build generates all of those files from one description, so that they stay consistent across the build systems and across the repositories. It covers six repositories: libbitcoin-system, libbitcoin-network, libbitcoin-database, libbitcoin-node, libbitcoin-server and libbitcoin-explorer.

For each repository it generates: Area Files Autotools builds/gnu/configure.ac, Makefile.am, the pkg-config .pc.in, and the test runner CMake builds/cmake/CMakeLists.txt, CMakePresets.json and the package config Visual Studio the solution, every .vcxproj and .vcxproj.filters, property sheets, NuGet configuration and the debugger visualizers Install scripts install-gnu.sh, install-cmake.sh, install-presets.sh and build-msvc.cmd CI the GitHub Actions workflows: ci.yml, ci-expanded.yml and version-tag.yml Editors the VS Code workspace and settings Sources the aggregate include header and version.hpp Repository .gitignore and CODEOWNERS It also fixes the versions every build uses. These include the C++ standard, the MSVC toolset, and the compilers and runner images of the CI matrix (see Toolchains). README build instructions are not generated.

The description is a single XML manifest, version4.xml. It declares each repository's targets (libraries, tests and binaries), their source roots, options, dependencies, compilers and CI jobs, along with the shared dependency, preset, build option and toolchain definitions. Templates written in iMatix GSL turn the manifest into the files above. The tool runs in three steps: Generate every artifact into output/version4. Copy the static Visual Studio property sheets and scripts. Copy the output over the sibling repository checkouts beside the libbitcoin-build checkout. $ ./generate4.sh On Windows, generate4.cmd does the same, and accepts repository names to limit the copy, for example generate4.cmd libbitcoin-node. GSL builds from source on Linux and macOS, and is available as a NuGet package on Windows.

Source lists are not kept in the manifest. The generator reads them from the sibling checkouts on disk, scanning each target's source roots. So: Adding a source file under an existing root needs no manifest change: add the file and regenerate. CMake finds new files by itself. Adding a source root or a target needs a manifest change. Do not hand-edit Makefile.am or the .vcxproj files. The generator also gives files that share a name distinct object names, which hand edits miss.

All six repositories must be checked out beside libbitcoin-build. A missing repository or directory stops the run partway. The scan reads the working trees, not git. Untracked files are included, and an empty directory inside a scanned tree empties the lists it would have filled. Clean the trees before regenerating. The copy overlays files and never deletes them. A file the generator no longer produces must be removed from the repository by hand.
Ubuntu 24.04 is the reference platform. CI builds and tests on it with GCC 13 through 16 and Clang 18 and 19 (see Toolchains). Other distributions work with the equivalent packages.

$ sudo apt install build-essential git autoconf automake libtool pkg-config curl CMake builds also require CMake 3.30 or later. Ubuntu 24.04 ships an older version, so install a current one from cmake.org.

$ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server $ cd libbitcoin-server $ ./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static The script clones libbitcoin-system, libbitcoin-database, libbitcoin-network and libbitcoin-node. It then builds, tests and installs each in order, ending with libbitcoin-server. The result is $HOME/libbitcoin/bin/bs. bx is built the same way from libbitcoin-explorer, whose script clones libbitcoin-system and libbitcoin-network: $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-explorer $ cd libbitcoin-explorer $ ./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static The result is $HOME/libbitcoin/bin/bx. Every script and option on this page applies to both. The dependencies are cloned into the current directory. Add --build-src-dir=<path> to put them elsewhere, --build-skip-tests to skip the test suites, and --build-skip-test-run to build the test suites without running them. The default prefix, /usr/local, requires sudo for the install step. A prefix in the home directory does not.
The CMake script takes the same options: $ ./builds/cmake/install-cmake.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static

A preset selects the configuration and link by name: nix-gnu-debug-static, nix-gnu-debug-shared, nix-gnu-release-static or nix-gnu-release-shared. $ ./builds/cmake/install-presets.sh --build-preset=nix-gnu-release-static The presets script chooses the install location itself, and the result is prefix/<preset>/bin/bs under the source directory.

The scripts use the compilers named by CC and CXX: $ CC=clang-19 CXX=clang++-19 ./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static CFLAGS and CXXFLAGS are kept and passed to every library. Hardware extensions are enabled with the hardware options, for example the ARM crypto extensions of a Raspberry Pi 5: $ ./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static --hardware-sha2 --hardware-aes See Build options for the hardware options.
macOS builds use the same scripts as Linux, with Apple clang from Xcode. CI builds and tests with the current Xcode on Apple silicon (see Toolchains).
Install the Xcode command line tools, then the build tools from Homebrew: $ xcode-select --install $ brew install autoconf automake libtool pkg-config cmake

$ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server $ cd libbitcoin-server $ ./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static The result is $HOME/libbitcoin/bin/bs. CMake works the same way with ./builds/cmake/install-cmake.sh and the same options. The scripts use clang and clang++ by default. bx is built the same way from libbitcoin-explorer: $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-explorer $ cd libbitcoin-explorer $ ./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-config=release --build-link=static The result is $HOME/libbitcoin/bin/bx. The notes in Linux about the source directory, skipping tests and passing compiler flags apply on macOS too.

On Apple silicon, --hardware-sha2, --hardware-sha3 and --hardware-aes enable the ARM crypto instructions, which every M-series CPU has. On Intel Macs, use the x86 options (see Build options). GPU acceleration is not available on macOS.

Options are given to the install scripts, which pass them to every library they build. The autotools form is --enable-<name> or --with-<name>, the CMake form is -D<name>=ON, and Visual Studio uses the Option-<name> property.

install-gnu.sh, install-cmake.sh and install-presets.sh accept: Option Purpose --prefix=<path> Install location (default /usr/local). Not used by the presets script. --build-preset=<name> CMake preset (presets script only, required). --build-config=<debug\|release> Debug (-Og -g1, assertions on) or release (-O3, assertions off). --build-link=<dynamic\|static> Build shared or static libraries (default both). --build-src-dir=<path> Where sources are cloned (default the current directory). --build-obj-dir=<path> Where objects are built (default obj in the current directory). --build-use-local-src Use existing source directories instead of cloning. --build-full-repositories Clone full history (default is a shallow clone). --build-skip-tests Do not build or run the tests. --build-skip-test-run Build the tests without running them. --build-parallel=<n> Number of parallel jobs (default the number of CPUs). --build-post-install-clean Remove dependency build files after installing. --hardware-optimized Optimize for the build machine's CPU (-march=native -mtune=native), with --build-config. See Hardware options. --noninteractive Do not prompt. --verbose Display the commands run. Any other option is passed to each library's configure step, which is how the options below are given.

Each option compiles code that uses an instruction set extension. A bs built with an option runs only on CPUs that have the extension. Run bs --hardware on the target machine to see which it has, and do not enable an option it lacks. All are off by default. --hardware-optimized (§1) enables every extension of the build machine's CPU instead. Portability: a build with --hardware-optimized runs only on CPUs that have every instruction set extension of the machine it was built on. To build for other machines, omit it, and enable only the extensions they all have.

Option Instructions --enable-sse41 SSE4.1 --enable-avx2 AVX2 (implies AES-NI) --enable-avx512 AVX-512 (F, BW, VL) (implies AVX2 and AES-NI) --enable-avxifma AVX-IFMA (implies AVX2, SHA extensions and AES-NI) --enable-avx512ifma AVX-512 IFMA (implies AVX-512, AVX2, SHA extensions and AES-NI) --enable-shani SHA extensions (implies AES-NI) --enable-sha512 SHA512 extensions (implies AVX2) --enable-aesni AES-NI and PCLMULQDQ --enable-vaes VAES and VPCLMULQDQ (implies AES-NI and AVX2)

Option Instructions --hardware-sha2 ARMv8 SHA-1 and SHA-256 (implies AES) --hardware-sha3 ARMv8.2 SHA-3, used for SHA-512 (implies SHA-1/SHA-256 and AES) --hardware-aes ARMv8 AES and PMULL The ARM options are install script options. Each option and the options it implies combine into one target flag, -march=armv8-a+<extensions> (armv8.2-a with --hardware-sha3), added to CFLAGS and CXXFLAGS. For example, --hardware-sha2 builds with -march=armv8-a+aes+sha2, and --hardware-sha3 with -march=armv8.2-a+aes+sha2+sha3. They cannot be combined with --hardware-optimized. The configure and CMake options --enable-sha2, --enable-sha3 and --enable-aes add no flags, and imply the same options as their install script options. Each checks that the compiler flags enable its extension, and configure fails if they do not. When building without the install script, give your own -march or -mcpu in CFLAGS and CXXFLAGS, including every implied extension, with the matching --enable options.

Option Default Purpose --with-cuda on NVIDIA GPU batch signature verification GPU support needs no CUDA toolkit to build. bs loads the NVIDIA driver when it starts, and uses the CPU when there is no driver or GPU. Only the libbitcoin-system scripts accept --without-cuda (-Dwith-cuda=OFF), including its build-msvc.cmd. The scripts of the other repositories build libbitcoin-system with GPU support. In Visual Studio, /p:Option-cuda=false disables it in any build.

Option Default Purpose --with-tests on Build the test suites. --with-console on Build bs. --with-web on Compile the web pages into bs. Without it, bs serves pages only from a configured path. --with-self-tests off Compile the built-in store tests into bs, which enable its -g/--get and -p/--put options and the [t]est built-in case console menu entry. --with-verbose off Compile in verbose logging (LOGV), in libbitcoin-network and every library and binary built on it. Debug builds enable it by default. --with-performance-tests off Compile the libbitcoin-system performance tests. --with-slow-tests off Compile the slow libbitcoin-system tests: scrypt, PBKDF2, the encrypted key tests, the bloom and sieve filter tests and a 1 GiB SHA vector. --enable-ndebug on Compile assertions out. --build-config sets it. --enable-isystem off Include the headers of libbitcoin dependencies with -isystem in place of -I, which silences their warnings.

The instruction set, GPU, --with-web, --with-self-tests, --with-verbose, --with-performance-tests, --with-slow-tests and --with-secp256k1 options are Option-<name> properties on the project property pages, or /p:Option-<name>=true (or false) on the build-msvc.cmd or msbuild command line. The others have no property: the tests and bs are projects in the solution, and the Release configurations define NDEBUG. For example, an AVX-512 build: $ builds\msvc\build-msvc.cmd --build-src-dir .. --build-config StaticRelease --build-use-local-src /p:Option-avx512=true Windows x64 and Win32 builds target AVX2 by default, which can be lowered (see Windows).

There is no required external dependency, and the Visual Studio projects use no NuGet package. libbitcoin implements secp256k1 and TLS itself, although secp256k1 can be replaced by an external library with the same public interface.

Option Default Purpose --with-secp256k1 on Use libbitcoin's native secp256k1 interface. --without-secp256k1 (-Dwith-secp256k1=OFF) compiles out the native interface and links an installed library with the libsecp256k1 interface in its place, such as bitcoin-core/secp256k1 0.8.0 or later, or UltrafastSecp256k1. Batch verification remains internal. Autotools and CMake. The library is found through pkg-config or CMake. --build-libsecp256k1 makes the install script build bitcoin-core/secp256k1 from source, with its ellswift, recovery and schnorrsig modules, along with the other dependencies. It is used only with --without-secp256k1. Visual Studio. /p:Option-secp256k1=false compiles out the native interface, and the library must be added to the link.

No build system enables link-time optimization (LTO), and it is not recommended with any toolchain. In measurements of the libbitcoin-system performance tests (November 2026), no form of LTO made secp256k1 signature verification faster, and verification dominates the time bs spends validating blocks. With MSVC, LTO made bs substantially slower. Compiler LTO flags secp256k1 verify time Other effects MSVC v145 /GL /LTCG +19% SHA-256 and SHA-512 hashing 10-85x slower (SHA-NI unchanged), ChaCha20-Poly1305 17x slower. bs.exe 7% larger, and each bs.exe link takes about 3 minutes instead of 1. MSVC v145 /GL /LTCG /Ob3 -2% The same result as /Ob3 without LTO. bs.exe 9% larger. Clang 18 -flto=thin no change Hashing of small inputs 3-16% faster, SHA-1 of 1 MB 10-12% slower. 13% more code, 11% longer test build. Clang 18 -flto no change AES and the secp256r1 and secp384r1 curves 4-7% faster. Test build takes twice as long. GCC 15 -flto=auto no change secp256r1 signing and verification, used by TLS, 20% slower. 21% less code. Each time is relative to a build by the same compiler without LTO: StaticRelease for MSVC, and a static -O3 release build for Clang and GCC. A positive change is slower. MSVC was measured on an AMD Threadripper PRO 9985WX, and Clang and GCC on an AMD Ryzen 7 7735HS.

The Visual Studio projects define ReleaseLTCG, ReleaseLEXE and DebugLTCG configurations, but no solution configuration selects them. With /GL, MSVC inlines functions only during the final link. By then the functions that libbitcoin forces inline have already been expanded into their callers, and MSVC no longer inlines even functions of one or two instructions, such as array element access and integer casts, which compilation without /GL inlines. In bs.exe, calls to such functions increase from about 3,000 to about 57,500. Adding /Ob3 (aggressive inlining) to an LTO build removes most of these calls. That restores StaticRelease performance but does not improve on it, and /Ob3 without LTO performs the same.

Requires autoconf, automake, libtool and pkg-config. Each library installs a pkg-config file, and the next library finds it through pkg-config, including the compiler flags for the hardware options it was built with.

Requires Visual Studio 2026 (MSVC toolset v145). The solution exposes the StaticDebug and StaticRelease configurations for x64, Win32 and ARM64. There are no package dependencies.

Windows x64 binaries can also be built on Linux with MinGW-w64 and autotools. install-gnu.sh cross-compiles when CC and CXX name the MinGW compilers and --host=x86_64-w64-mingw32 is given. No CUDA toolchain is required. The GPU verification kernels are part of the source, as compressed PTX (src/crypto/secp256k1/cuda/ptx.cpp in libbitcoin-system). At run time bs loads the NVIDIA driver library (nvcuda.dll on Windows, libcuda.so.1 on Linux), which compiles the PTX for the installed GPU. --with-cuda is on by default, and applies on x64 and arm64, except on macOS.

Visual Studio 2026 with the Desktop development with C++ workload. The Community edition is sufficient. Git. nuget.exe, from nuget.org, on the PATH. Build from a Developer Command Prompt for VS 2026, which puts msbuild on the PATH.

Clone the five repositories side by side: $ mkdir libbitcoin $ cd libbitcoin $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-system $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-database $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-network $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-node $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server Then build all five: $ cd libbitcoin-server $ builds\msvc\build-msvc.cmd --build-src-dir .. --build-config StaticRelease --build-platform x64 --build-use-local-src The script restores the NuGet packages and builds libbitcoin-system, libbitcoin-database, libbitcoin-network, libbitcoin-node and libbitcoin-server in order, then runs the tests. The result is bin\x64\Release\v145\static\bs.exe. bx needs only libbitcoin-system and libbitcoin-network beside libbitcoin-explorer: $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-system $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-network $ git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-explorer $ cd libbitcoin-explorer $ builds\msvc\build-msvc.cmd --build-src-dir .. --build-config StaticRelease --build-platform x64 --build-use-local-src The result is bin\x64\Release\v145\static\bx.exe, and the options below apply to both. Option Values --build-config StaticRelease or StaticDebug (required) --build-platform x64 (default), ARM64 or Win32 --build-skip-tests Do not build or run the tests --build-symbols default, disabled or public-only Other arguments are passed to msbuild. Build options are set as properties, for example /p:Option-cuda=false (see Build options).

Open builds\msvc\vs2026\libbitcoin-server.sln. It contains libbitcoin-server, its tests and bs, and references the other four libraries in their sibling directories. For bx, open builds\msvc\vs2026\libbitcoin-explorer.sln, which references libbitcoin-system and libbitcoin-network. Select StaticRelease or StaticDebug and build. Build options are on each project's property pages, under Configuration Properties.

Windows x64 and Win32 builds target AVX2 by default, so such a bs.exe requires a CPU with AVX2 (Intel Haswell, AMD Excavator or later). This is only a default, set by Option-arch, and can be lowered for an older CPU, for example to AVX or SSE2: $ builds\msvc\build-msvc.cmd --build-src-dir .. --build-config StaticRelease --build-use-local-src /p:Option-arch=StreamingSIMDExtensions2 Option-arch Instructions StreamingSIMDExtensions2 SSE2 AdvancedVectorExtensions AVX AdvancedVectorExtensions2 AVX2 (default) AdvancedVectorExtensions512 AVX-512 An extension option raises it as needed: Option-sse41 to at least AVX, Option-avx2, Option-avxifma, Option-vaes or Option-sha512 to AVX2, and Option-avx512 to AVX-512.

Options given on the command line apply to one build, and options set on the property pages are saved in the project files. To set options for every build on a machine, put them in a Directory.Build.props file in the directory that holds the cloned repositories (libbitcoin above). MSBuild imports this file into every project below its directory, so the options apply to all five libraries, whether built by build-msvc.cmd or in Visual Studio. The file is outside the repositories and is never checked in. For example, an AVX-512 machine with IFMA, AES-NI, VAES and the SHA extensions: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?> <Project xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/developer/msbuild/2003"> <PropertyGroup> <Option-arch>AdvancedVectorExtensions512</Option-arch> <Option-avx512ifma>true</Option-avx512ifma> <Option-avxifma>false</Option-avxifma> <Option-aesni>true</Option-aesni> <Option-vaes>true</Option-vaes> <Option-shani>true</Option-shani> <Option-cuda>true</Option-cuda> </PropertyGroup> </Project> A property not set in the file keeps its default, and a /p: property on the command line overrides the file. The build prints the resulting options at the start of each library's build.

Bitcoin Explorer (bx) for version 4 is in development. Commands may be incomplete or change before release. Bitcoin Explorer (bx) is the libbitcoin command line client. Its commands work offline, on keys, addresses, transactions, scripts and encodings, and online, querying a libbitcoin server. It is built on libbitcoin-explorer, which depends on libbitcoin-system and libbitcoin-network (see Developers). Each command is run as bx <command>, with bx <command> --help describing its arguments. Commands read their main argument from the command line or from standard input, so they can be piped together. For example, the key at BIP32 path m/0'/1 of a seed, and its legacy and segwit addresses: $ bx hd-new 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f | bx hd-private --hard --index 0 | bx hd-private --index 1 | bx hd-to-ec | bx ec-to-public 03501e454bf00751f24b1b489aa925215d66af2234e3891c3b21a52bedb3cd711c $ bx ec-to-address 03501e454bf00751f24b1b489aa925215d66af2234e3891c3b21a52bedb3cd711c 1JQheacLPdM5ySCkrZkV66G2ApAXe1mqLj $ bx ec-to-witness bc 03501e454bf00751f24b1b489aa925215d66af2234e3891c3b21a52bedb3cd711c bc1qhm6697d9d2224vfyt8mj4kw03ncec7a7fdafvt

Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. fetch-filter-checkpoint Retrieve compact filter checkpoint from a Libbitcoin server. fetch-filter-headers Retrieve compact filter headers from a Libbitcoin server. The distance between provided height and hash must be strictly less than 2000. fetch-header Get the block header from the specified hash or height. Height is ignored if both are specified. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. fetch-height Get the last block height. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. fetch-history Get list of output points, values, and spends for a payment key. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. fetch-public-key Get the EC public key of the address, if it exists on the blockchain. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. fetch-tx Get a transaction by its hash. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. fetch-tx-index Get the block height and index of a transaction. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. fetch-utxo Get enough unspent transaction outputs from a payment address to pay a number of satoshi. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. send-tx Broadcast a transaction to the Bitcoin network via a Libbitcoin server. subscribe-block Watch the network for all blocks. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. subscribe-tx Watch the network for all transactions. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. validate-tx Determine if a transaction is valid for submission to the blockchain. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. watch-key Watch the network for transactions in which a payment key participates. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection. watch-tx Watch the network for a transaction by hash. Requires a Libbitcoin server connection.

Command Description base16-decode Convert a Base16 value to binary data. base16-encode Convert binary data to Base16. base32-decode Convert a Base32 value to binary data. base32-encode Convert binary data to Base32. base58-decode Convert a Base58 value to Base16. base58-encode Convert a Base16 value to Base58. base64-decode Convert a Base64 value to binary data. base64-encode Convert binary data to Base64. bech32-decode Validate the bech32 checksum of Base16 data and recover its witness prefix, version and program. bech32-encode Add a prefix, version byte and checksum to a Base32 witness program. checked-decode Validate the bitcoin checksum of Base16 data and recover its version and payload. checked-encode Add a version byte and bitcoin checksum to Base16 data.

Command Description bitcoin160 Perform a RIPEMD160 hash of a SHA256 hash of Base16 data. bitcoin256 Perform a SHA256 hash of a SHA256 hash of Base16 data and then reverse the byte order. ripemd160 Perform a RIPEMD160 hash of Base16 data. sha160 Perform a SHA160 (also known as SHA-1) hash of Base16 data. sha256 Perform a SHA256 hash of Base16 data. sha512 Perform a SHA512 hash of Base16 data.

Command Description btc-to-satoshi Convert BTC to satoshi. curve-new Create a Base85 Curve ZMQ private key for use with a Libbitcoin server from entropy. curve-public Derive a Base85 Curve ZMQ public key for use with a Libbitcoin server. ec-add Calculate the EC function POINT + (SECRET * curve-generator-point). ec-add-secrets Calculate the EC function (SECRET + SECRET) % curve-order. ec-multiply Calculate the EC product (POINT * SECRET). ec-multiply-secrets Calculate the EC function (SECRET * SECRET) % curve-order. match-address Determine whether the provided client filter probabilistically matches the provided payment address. match-script Determine whether the provided client filter probabilistically matches the provided script. satoshi-to-btc Convert satoshi to BTC. tls-cert Create a self-signed PEM TLS certificate for a P-256 private key, for use with a Libbitcoin server. tls-new Create a PEM P-256 TLS private key for use with a Libbitcoin server from entropy.
Command Description hardware Display hardware compatibility. help Get the list of commands. settings Display all configuration settings. version Display version information.

Bitcoin Explorer (bx) runs with built-in mainnet defaults, and reads no configuration file unless one is given. Every command accepts -c <path> (--config <path>), or the path can be set in the BX_CONFIG environment variable: $ bx fetch-height --config bx.cfg $ export BX_CONFIG=~/bx.cfg $ bx fetch-height A command line option takes precedence over a configuration setting. The file uses the same syntax as the bs configuration file (Configuration File).
bx settings prints every setting with the value in effect, in configuration file form: $ bx settings --config bx.cfg

Setting Default Purpose wallet.witness_version 0 The witness version. wallet.witness_address_prefix bc The witness address prefix. wallet.wif_version 128 The wallet import format (WIF) key version. wallet.hd_public_version 76067358 The HD public key version (xpub). wallet.hd_secret_version 76066276 The HD private key version (xprv). wallet.pay_to_public_key_hash_version 0 The pay-to-public-key-hash address version. wallet.pay_to_script_hash_version 5 The pay-to-script-hash address version. wallet.transaction_version 1 The version of transactions bx creates. wallet.rule_fork_flags 4294967295 The consensus rule forks applied to scripts, all by default. server.url http://mainnet.libbitcoin.net:8181 The bs native interface used by the fetch-* commands. server.connect_retries 0 The number of times to retry contacting the server. server.connect_timeout_seconds 5 The time limit for each step of a request. A fetch-* command also accepts a server URL on its command line, which takes precedence over server.url.

The [wallet] settings select the encodings of keys and addresses. For testnet3, with a local bs serving its native interface (Block explorer): [wallet] witness_address_prefix = tb wif_version = 239 hd_public_version = 70617039 hd_secret_version = 70615956 pay_to_public_key_hash_version = 111 pay_to_script_hash_version = 196 [server] url = http://127.0.0.1:18180 The same [wallet] settings apply to testnet4, testnet5 and signet, and to regtest with bcrt as its witness address prefix. The server port is the bs native port on the chain: 18180 on testnet3, 48180 on testnet4, 58180 on testnet5, 38180 on signet and 28180 on regtest (Conventional Ports).

All options, grouped by purpose: Group Option Purpose Configuration -c, --config <path> Read settings from a configuration file -n, --net <network> Select the network (mainnet, testnet3, testnet4, testnet5, regtest or signet), by default the configured bitcoin.network (mainnet) Prompts -a, --accept Accept startup prompts without interaction Information -h, --help Display command line options -s, --settings Display the settings in effect, with their descriptions and defaults (Displaying settings) -v, --version Display version information -w, --hardware Display hardware compatibility (CPU features, GPU) Store -m, --make Create a new store in the configured directory, without running -b, --backup Snapshot the store (also available live from the console) -r, --restore Restore from the most recent snapshot Service -d, --daemon <value> Install (true) or uninstall (false) as a daemon/service -u, --user <credential> Daemon logon credential (defaults to the system account) Store scans -i, --information Display store information -f, --flags Display all fork flag transitions -k, --buckets Display hashmap bucket fill -l, --collisions Display hashmap collision statistics (time consuming) Each network's files are in a directory named for the network (mainnet, testnet4 and so on), the network directory. It is under the working directory, or under folders.root when that is configured: root = bitcoin puts the mainnet directory at bitcoin/mainnet. The store is in its store directory. The console log files (console_new.log, renamed to console_old.log when it reaches log.limit bytes), the events log (events.log) and the peer address cache (peers.cache) are in the network directory itself, unless [folders] places them elsewhere (Configuration File). Networks therefore never share files. bs creates the store if it does not exist, and -m creates it without running. Every run selects the network, by -n or by bitcoin.network in a configuration file. Without either, bs uses mainnet. The network can be set in the configuration file instead of by -n: [bitcoin] network = testnet4 $ bs --config bs.cfg Display command line help: $ bs -h Usage: bs [-abfhiklmrsvw] [--config value] [--daemon value] [--net value] [--user value] Info: Runs a full node bitcoin server. Options (named): -a [--accept] Accept startup prompts without interaction. -b [--backup] Backup to a snapshot (can also do live). -c [--config] Specify path to a configuration settings file. -d [--daemon] Install ('true') or uninstall ('false') as a daemon. -f [--flags] Scan and display all flag transitions. -h [--help] Display command line options. -i [--information] Scan and display store information. -k [--buckets] Scan and display hashmap bucket fill. -l [--collisions] Scan and show hashmap collision stats (may SIGKILL). -m [--make] Make new store in configured directory. -n [--net] Specify the network (mainnet|testnet3|testnet4|regtest|signet|testnet5), defaults to the configured network. -r [--restore] Restore from most recent snapshot. -s [--settings] Display all configuration settings. -u [--user] Daemon logon credential, defaults to system account. -v [--version] Display version information. -w [--hardware] Display hardware compatibility. Display version information: $ bs --version Version Information... secp256k1............ internal tls.................. internal tls 1.3 libbitcoin-system.... 4.0.10444 8a3cb4da libbitcoin-database.. 4.0.4814 167d381a libbitcoin-network... 4.0.7428 dd3e7777 libbitcoin-node...... 4.0.4343 efadf0b5 libbitcoin-server.... 4.0.3513 71a3750f compiled schema...... 4.0.29 Display hardware compatibility: $ bs --hardware Hardware configuration (x64)... aesni....... platform:1 compiled:1. vaes........ platform:1 compiled:1. shani....... platform:1 compiled:1. sha512...... platform:0 compiled:0. sse41....... platform:1 compiled:1. avx2........ platform:1 compiled:1. avx512...... platform:1 compiled:1. avxifma..... platform:0 compiled:0. avx512ifma.. platform:1 compiled:1. cuda........ platform:1 compiled:1. cuda ecc.... platform:1 enabled:0. build....... bs-linux-x64-avx512ifma platform shows whether the machine supports a feature and compiled whether this build uses it. A build does not have to be compiled for the hardware it runs on, though in many cases doing so significantly improves performance. Do not compile options that the hardware does not support, as the build will not run. The largest gains in initial block download come from shani (or sha2 on Arm), and otherwise from avx. build names the release build that matches the extensions compiled into this binary. When the machine supports a different set, a platform line follows, naming the release build that matches the machine. CUDA (GPU) support is compiled by default, except on macOS. cuda ecc reports whether the GPU's error correcting code (ECC) memory is enabled, which is set in your own environment. ECC is recommended but not required when using the GPU. When enabled it provides the same memory reliability as the main processor (see GPU error correction).

Commands typed into a running bs console (press <enter> after the character): Key Action m Menu of options and toggles c Close the node (graceful shutdown, same as <ctrl> c) b Backup the store (live snapshot) h Hold network communication g Go network communication i Info about the store e Errors in the store w Work distribution z Clear a disk-full condition (not required, automatically clears with sufficient space) Log on/off typed into a running bs console (press <enter> after the character): Key Digit Level a .0 Application n .1 News: startup, progress and notable events s .2 Sessions: connect and accept p .3 Protocols x .4 Proxies: sockets and channels r .5 Remote peer behavior f .6 Own node fault q .7 Quitting: connections and other components stopping o .8 Objects: lifetime tracking (debug builds only) v .9 Verbose detail Each log entry shows its level as a digit after the timestamp, for example .6 on a fault.

Paths take the platform's form, for example /data/bitcoin or D:\bitcoin. A relative folders.root is relative to the working directory, not to the configuration file. Every other relative path, of the other [folders] settings and of the TLS certificate and key files, is relative to the network directory, <folders.root>/<network>. An absolute path is used as is. Integer values may use commas as thousands separators, for example node.maximum_height = 900,000. Section map: Area Sections Files [folders] Logging [log] Store [database], [table.*] Chain [bitcoin], [forks], [wallet] Node [node] P2P network [network], [peer], [outbound], [inbound], [manual] Client-server [admin], [native], [bitcoind], [zmq], [btcd], [electrum], [sparrow], [esplora] Simple example config file: [folders] root = bitcoin console = log events = log The same settings can be written without section headers, by prefixing each name with its section: folders.root = bitcoin folders.console = log folders.events = log On mainnet this puts the store in bitcoin/mainnet/store and the log files in bitcoin/mainnet/log. The [folders] settings: Setting Directory of Default root The network directory, <root>/<network> The working directory store The store store console console_new.log and console_old.log The network directory events events.log The network directory peers peers.cache The network directory admin A custom admin site None, the embedded site native A custom block explorer None, the embedded site symbols Windows symbols (.pdb), Windows builds only symbols bs creates the store, console, events and peers directories. The admin, native and symbols directories are used only when they are set (symbols by default) and are not created.

bs -s (--settings) prints every setting with the value in effect for that run, each under its section and preceded by its description and default. The values are the selected network's defaults, the values derived from them (such as table bucket counts, Bucket autotuning), and any configured value, which is marked # configured. Combine it with -c to see what a configuration file does, and with -n to see a network's values: $ bs -c bs.cfg -s [node] # Maximum block height to populate, defaults to '0' (unlimited). maximum_height = 900000 # configured [table.header] # The number of buckets in the header table head, derived from expected and memory, defaults to '385181'. buckets = 385181 A setting with no value, such as an unset list, is printed commented out. Settings captured by an existing store (Settings fixed at store creation) are shown as configured; the store's values replace them when the store opens.
Configuring Bitcoin Server (bs): the command line, the configuration file, common setups, ports, services, performance, the store and the test chains.

The executable is bs (bs.exe on Windows), and the examples run the same on Linux, macOS and Windows. bs runs with built-in mainnet defaults. No configuration file is read unless --config is given. Run with defaults. The store is created in a mainnet directory under the current directory if it does not exist. $ bs With a configuration file: $ bs --config bs.cfg To run on testnet3, testnet4, testnet5, regtest or signet, with the store in a directory named for the network: $ bs -n testnet4 Until the chain is current, only the admin site accepts connections. P2P peers, the block explorer and the other client services wait (Until current).

The defaults suit most machines. These are the settings that most affect sync and query speed.

Setting Default Purpose network.threads 0 Threads that run the network: peer and client connections. 0 uses one per hardware thread, at most 32. node.threads 0 Threads that validate blocks. 0 uses one per hardware thread, which is two per core on a processor with hyperthreading (SMT). node.thread_priority true Run validation threads at high priority, ahead of other programs. false leaves them at normal priority. node.memory_priority true Keep the process at normal memory priority. false lowers it, so the operating system reclaims its memory first. database.turbo true Allow a single client query to use all processors, so large queries return sooner.
2. Signature verification and silent payment indexing

When a sufficient GPU is available, signatures are verified, and silent payment transactions indexed, in batches on the GPU, which is much faster than on a CPU. Run bs -w to see whether a GPU is available, and which processor features apply. Setting Default Purpose node.use_gpu true Use the GPU when one is available, for signature verification, silent payment indexing and silent payment scans. node.batch_verify 1,000,000 Signatures verified in each GPU batch. 0 disables GPU verification. node.batch_silent 1,000,000 Silent payment transactions indexed in each GPU batch. 0 disables GPU indexing. database.gpu_scan_minimum 65,536 Smallest silent payment scan, in transactions, sent to the GPU. Smaller scans run on the CPU, where they return sooner.

A GPU that supports error correcting (ECC) memory but has it off shows cuda ecc.... platform:1 enabled:0 in bs -w. Turn it on with nvidia-smi, as root on Linux or from an administrator prompt on Windows: $ sudo nvidia-smi -e 1 The change takes effect after a reboot, after which bs -w shows enabled:1. nvidia-smi -q -d ECC shows the current and pending modes, -i <index> selects one GPU of several, and -e 0 turns error correction off. On many cards it also reduces the memory available. platform:0 means the device has no error correcting memory, and there is nothing to enable.

Setting Default Purpose node.maximum_concurrency 50,000 Blocks downloaded concurrently. Blocks arrive out of order, and this window lets download run ahead of validation. 0 is unlimited. outbound.connections 100 Outgoing peer connections while syncing. More peers may be required to saturate a high bandwidth network connection. outbound.current_connections 10 Outgoing peer connections once the chain is current, when fewer are needed. 0 keeps outbound.connections.

On a Linux machine with more than one NUMA node (usually a machine with more than one CPU socket), disable the kernel's automatic NUMA balancing before you run bs. Ubuntu and most other distributions turn it on by default whenever the machine has more than one node. Check the node count and the current setting (1 is on, 0 is off): $ lscpu | grep NUMA $ cat /proc/sys/kernel/numa_balancing Disable it for the whole machine, both now and after reboots: $ echo 'kernel.numa_balancing = 0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-numa-balancing.conf $ sudo sysctl --system If you can't change the setting for the whole machine, start bs with interleaved memory placement instead: $ numactl --interleave=all bs --config bs.cfg Why it matters. With balancing on, the kernel repeatedly unmaps pages of a running process to sample which NUMA node is reading them, then moves each page to the node that reads it most. bs maps its store into memory and reads and writes it from many threads running on every socket. Pages that both nodes use keep getting sampled and moved, and the kernel's page-migration walks and lock spinning take the CPU time that validation needs. Measured on stratton. stratton has 2× Xeon E5-2683 v4 (32 cores, 64 threads, 2 NUMA nodes) and 256 GB RAM, running Ubuntu 26.04 with Linux 7.0. Download time is measured from the first block to height 345,000. Each row is a set of identical runs: Configuration Runs Download time (s) Slow runs Balancing on (default) 8 261 to 305 when fast; 443, 494 and more than 1,137 when slow 3 Balancing on, numactl --interleave=all 8 211 to 257 0 Balancing off (kernel.numa_balancing = 0) 8 235 to 264 0 With balancing on, about a third of all runs were slow. In the slow periods, the kernel's page migration took 40 to 59% of bs CPU time, and SHA-256 hashing took only 1 to 5%. In fast periods, migration took 0 to 2%. Machines with a single NUMA node are not affected.

Every service has an assigned port on each chain, clear and secure. A service listens only on the addresses given by its bind and safe settings (Listening), so the examples on this page give them explicitly. Only [admin] has a default address, 127.0.0.1 on its clear port. The P2P network uses its convention on each chain, so peers find the node without configuration. Each libbitcoin service uses its own block, 8N80 for clear connections and 8N43 for secure (TLS), so that bs can run beside bitcoind, Electrum servers and Esplora on one machine without conflict. Service Section Clear Secure P2P network [inbound] 8333 8333 Admin web [admin] 8080 8043 Native web and REST [native] 8180 8143 Bitcoind RPC and REST [bitcoind] 8280 8243 ZMQ [zmq] 8380 8343 BTCD RPC [btcd] 8480 8443 Electrum [electrum] 8580 8543 Sparrow [sparrow] 8680 8643 Esplora [esplora] 8780 8743 Stratum v1 [stratum_v1] 8880 8843 Stratum v2 [stratum_v2] 8980 – P2P has no separate secure port.
